News.title: One dead after Tesla strikes pedestrians in car park as four suffer injuries
News.content:
One dead after Tesla strikes pedestrians in car park as four suffer injuries

A car has crashed into pedestrians in a grocery store car park leaving one dead and four hospitalised

View 2 Images Car crash kills one and leaves four injured (Image: FOX LOCAL LA)

One person has been killed after being struck by a car in a grocery store car park.

‌



The incident took place in a car park of a Trader Joe's in Los Angeles on Thursday afternoon.

‌



Officials said the Tesla crashed into a security stand, killing one and injuring at least four others.

‌



View 2 Images The incident took place near busy Trader Joe's (Image: FOX LOCAL LA)

The store is based on Third Street and Fairfax Avenue.

‌



Los Angeles Fire Department crews responded to the crash near the Trader Joe’s in the Beverly Grove area around 1.20 pm, with police also attending the scene.

The LAFD confirmed that one person was pronounced dead at the scene as four others were treated by emergency services.

They have been rushed to hospital.

Article continues below

The driver reportedly lost control of her vehicle, causing her to hit a parked car and the pedestrians before smashing into the security stand, NBC reports.

The driver has been described as an 80-year-old woman, who has also been hospitalised.

This is a breaking news story, more to follow.

News.title: 'Nigel Farage's Reform UK conference descended into hypocrisy before it even started'
News.content:
'Nigel Farage's Reform UK conference descended into hypocrisy before it even started'

"The conference - the party's biggest yet, presumably booked in before they started slipping dramatically in the polls - doesn't even kick off properly until Friday"

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

It didn't take long for Reform UK's big party conference to descend into rank hypocrisy.

‌



The conference - the party's biggest yet, presumably booked in before they started slipping dramatically in the polls - doesn't even kick off properly until Friday. But today was their "business day" - a chance to woo fatcats and lobbyists before the rank-and-file members turn up.

‌



Deputy leader Richard Tice, opening proceedings, took the opportunity to have a pop at China and talk up British manufacturing. Presumably he hoped nobody would notice he was standing just a few yards away from a gift shop set up to flog piles of Reform-branded Chinese tat to Farage fans over the weekend.

‌



But the Mirror did. Sorry, Richard.

And it isn't just Chinese goods on sale at the nicknack stand. Goods from Bangladesh, India and Pakistan are also up for grabs. Only a handful of items carry a 'made in UK' label - including a tea towel. Just like "man of the people" Nigel lording it up in swanky private members clubs, it's another lesson in paying attention not to what Reform UK say, but what they do.

Because the two are often at odds.

‌



Zack seeks to crack his way into Parliament

Green leader Zack Polanski is hoping to finally turn his social media profile into a real job in politics - as he stands in the high-profile race to replace Keir Starmer as the MP for Holborn and St Pancras.

If he's selected, it will be the first real test of whether the Andy Burnham bounce has buoyed Labour enough to hold on to the seat in the face of a big name Green challenger.

And it'll be Polanski's first real test of whether he can convert TikTok likes and Instagram followers into votes. One to watch.

Article continues below

Speaking of awkward characters and dusty old buildings

The first trailer for the new Harry Potter HBO series has landed and it looks...almost exactly like the movies we know and love.

While different actors will portray JK Rowling's beloved magical misfits, the haunted halls of Hogwarts appear pretty much identical to the cinematic saga. Presumably this is so they don't have to mount a costly refurb of the franchise's bicoastal American theme park attractions to match reimagined sets.

The one thing missing from the new retelling is John Williams' iconic music - a thoroughly baffling decision.

News.title: Met Office forecasts temperatures to drop within days across 57 areas of UK - full list
News.content:
Met Office forecasts temperatures to drop within days across 57 areas of UK - full list

Temperatures are set to be below the average for this time of year across much of the UK next week

View 2 Images Temperatures are set to drop to below average in the second week of September (Image: Bristol Post)

Large parts of the UK are set for a dramatic change in temperatures as forecasts predict colder than average temperatures next week. Although meteorological autumn got underway from September 1, the coming weekend is expected to be warm with temperatures in the high 20s on Sunday.

‌



However, the Met Office is warning temperatures will drop back after the brief spell of warm weather. September 7 to 14 looks cooler than average, particularly across northern areas.

‌



In the update on the Met Office Youtube channel meteorologist Annie Shuttleworth said: “Temperatures are set to climb to the high 20s, but it’s pretty much a one-day only affair.”

‌



The warmer air isn’t expected to stick around, with conditions turning cooler again as low pressure pushes in. The forecaster explained: “It turns cooler again when we get more of a low pressure push in from the north.

View 2 Images Weather maps show large parts of the UK turning blue forecasting 'below average temperatures' from Sept 7 to 14 2026 (Image: European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF))

The meteorologist said: “After an anomalous warm day on Sunday, next week actually looks cooler than average across many northern areas and pretty close to average for early September across southern areas.”

‌



She added that the UK is in for a 'bumpy run' of conditions, with temperatures swinging as weather fronts move through: “It’s going to be quite changeable temperature-wise throughout the next 10 days.”

Before the temperatures change, northern parts of the UK are set for a windy weekend, which could carry on into the start of next week. The strongest winds look most likely across northern and northwestern areas at times.

The Met Office forecaster said: “We could see gusts of around 40 mph across some northern areas on Friday afternoon.”

‌



Looking ahead to Sunday, she added there is “the potential for quite a breezy day”, with model guidance showing “some inland gusts of around 40 miles per hour” across parts of northern England, southern Scotland and northwestern Scotland.

News.title: Nigel Farage secretly filmed celebrating foreign donations to Reform UK amid 'plot to break law'
News.content:
Nigel Farage secretly filmed celebrating foreign donations to Reform UK amid 'plot to break law'

Police have been urged to investigate explosive allegations that Nigel Farage and Reform UK had undeclared nationwide polls paid for by foreign donors, revealed in a year-long undercover investigation

View 4 Images Other political parties urged the police to investigate the claims (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/EPA/Shutterstock)

Police have been urged to investigate explosive allegations that Reform UK knowingly accepted foreign donations to pay for polls that weren't declared by the party.

‌



According to a year-long undercover investigation, senior party figures allegedly arranged for an American company to fund three influential polls that the party had commissioned.

‌



The report, by Channel 4 News and Verbatim, a group of investigative journalists, claimed the polls were then presented as being independent, making headline news and allegedly building support for the party ahead of May’s local elections.

‌



But, it claimed the public was not informed that Reform UK had commissioned the polls and would be arranging for an “off the book” backer to fund them. The three polls were said to cost £32,500 in total.

Reform UK accepts £4million from crypto billionaire pardoned by Donald Trump READ MORE :

View 4 Images Nigel Farage was filmed undercover celebrating secret new foreign donations

In a meeting over oysters and wine in Clacton, Mr Farage reportedly met with the undercover team in late July after the surveys had been published and paid for.

‌



According to the footage, Mr Farage said the polling was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck,” adding: “It worked. Boom.” Reform made significant gains in the local elections.

The discussion then allegedly turned to a potential future donation of £500,000 to Reform.

One of the undercover team - which included one posing as a rich American and his UK-based son “William Lockwood” - allegedly made clear that the plan would be for the UK-based son to make the payment and be the declared donor.

‌



This is despite the money originally coming from the US-based father, according to the sting. Such an arrangement would be illegal.

View 4 Images Nigel Farage poses with a tea towel at the merch shop at Reform's annual conference in Birmingham (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/EPA/Shutterstock)

The Liberal Democrats said it had written to the police and the Electoral Commission asking them to investigate. It's understood Labour also intends to report the allegations to the police. The Green Party also joined calls for police to probe the claims.

‌



Bob Posner, a lawyer and former Chief Executive of the UK Electoral Commission, called for criminal investigation as “serious criminal offences” may have been committed.

Mr Posner branded the facilitation of payments for polls by Reform figures as “shocking”, telling Channel 4: “From what I’ve seen it was commissioned by the party, it was polling for the party and hiding it means they’re hiding a donation”.

He added that it’s “against the law and the evasion of the rules, the attempt of evasion of rules, to take actions to further evasion of the rules, these are serious criminal offences”.

‌



Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said: “This scandal goes right to the top of Reform UK. Nigel Farage needs to urgently prove today that his top team haven’t broken the law and secretly plotted to undermine our democracy.

“It’s not just Farage’s secret £5 million ‘gift’. Time and again he and his mates think the rules don’t apply to them. The sleaze and scandal now engulfing him and his Party isn’t going away – it’s getting worse.

“It’s time to stop the deflections and desperate excuses. Farage and Reform must co-operate with the authorities to establish the truth and prove just how deep this scandal goes.”

‌



Lisa Smart, Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokesperson, said: "Farage has always behaved as though the rules apply to everyone but him. These new allegations against Reform look like the latest example, and must be dealt with swiftly by the authorities."

View 4 Images Bridget Phillipson branded the claims a 'scandal' (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

A HopeNotHate spokesman said: "Reform UK have been arrogant enough to think that the law doesn’t touch them; that they can get away with it. Now more than ever the party needs to be investigated thoroughly."

Article continues below

An Electoral Commission spokesman said: “The law requires political parties to report all permissible donations they accept with a value over £11,180 and all impermissible donations over £500. Information about any potential attempt to evade the controls on donations is for the police to consider.”

A Reform UK spokesman said: “Reform UK has been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. The party denies any wrongdoing.

“Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission.”

News.title: Driver 'runs from scene' of three-car crash as emergency services close road in Bootle
News.content:
Driver 'runs from scene' of three-car crash as emergency services close road in Bootle

Emergency services closed the road after being called out the three-car crash at a busy junction

View Image One driver is reported to have fled the scene of the crash in Bootle (Image: Submitted)

A driver ran from the scene of a three-car pile-up in Bootle on Thursday afternoon as emergency services raced to the scene.

‌



Debris was strewn across the busy junction after the smash, which saw three cars damaged. The road was closed while emergency services helped the remaining drivers and passengers.

‌



Southport Road was closed between Burnie Avenue and Wolfenden Avenue following the crash at around 5.30pm today. Photographs taken at the scene showed one car positioned sideways across the road, badly damaged with its front bumper and bonnet smashed. A second vehicle could be seen parked at the side of the road nearby.

‌



A Merseyside Fire and Rescue spokesman said that the occupants of two of the cars involved in the crash remained at the scene and were unhurt, but the occupants of a third vehicle had fled, Liverpool Echo reports.

He said: "Fire crews were called to a road traffic collision this evening on Southport Road, Bootle. Crews were alerted at 5.27pm and on scene at 5.34pm, with two fire engines in attendance.

Article continues below

"Crews arrived to find three cars involved in a collision at the junction with Kier Hardie Avenue, all vehicles were on all four wheels. "The occupants of one vehicle had left the scene before the arrival of crews, the occupants of the remaining two vehicles were out of the vehicles on arrival and uninjured.

"Crews isolated the battery to one vehicle and applied an absorbent material to the area to make the scene safe. Merseyside Police were in attendance managing traffic. Crews left the scene in the hands of police at 5.55pm."

The road had reopened after emergency services left the scene at 6.40pm.

News.title: Betting giant Paddy Power to shut up to 100 shops with 400 jobs at risk
News.content:
Betting giant Paddy Power to shut up to 100 shops with 400 jobs at risk

Paddy Power operate a total of 506 betting stores in Ireland and the UK right now with the proposed closures mean around one fifth of outlets could close

View 2 Images Up to 100 shops across the UK and Ireland could close (Image: Getty Images)

Up to 100 Paddy Power betting shops could be set to close before the end of the year, putting around 400 jobs at risk, owners Flutter Entertainment have announced.

‌



Those 100 stores would total around one-fifth of Paddy Power's entire Ireland and UK retail estate.

‌



Flutter blamed rising energy and rates costs, as well as the government's remote gaming duty rise have all taken a toll.

‌



“We are incredibly proud of our high street estate, and it remains a key part of our business in communities across the UK and Ireland. Unfortunately, we have had to take the extremely difficult decision to conduct this review," a spokesperson for Flutter UK and Ireland said.

"The high street trading environment has been challenging for a number of years given rising costs, fierce competition, economic uncertainty and the shift to online but we also face a material impact from the higher gambling taxes announced in last year’s UK budget.

"Our immediate priority at this time is to support those colleagues affected by this announcement."

‌



View 2 Images A punter places a bet in a bookmakers (Image: Getty)

Paddy Power owner Flutter posted tough Q2 trading results, with a $37m profit swinging to a $296m loss year-on-year for the New York Stock Exchange listed company, the Irish Mirror reports.

Flutter, who also own Sky Bet and Betfair, say that “impacted colleagues will be offered redeployment opportunities where possible”.

Article continues below

Paddy Power operate a total of 506 betting stores in Ireland and the UK right now

The Irish gambling company founded in 1988. Its product offering includes sports betting, online casino, online poker, and online bingo. Business operations are led from its headquarters in Dublin, alongside a satellite office in Malta.

Back in July, Betfred announced plans to close 132 stores, while William Hill owner Evoke are set to shut 270 of its betting shops.

News.title: Belfast fire - live: Harbour blaze chokes city with smoke as flames visible for miles
News.content:
The blaze involved around 4,500 tonnes of scrap cars at a metal recycling facility in Belfast Harbour

Fire crews tackled a blaze involving around 4,500 tonnes of scrap cars that broke out at Belfast Harbour shortly after midday on Wednesday

More than 50 firefighters worked through the night to bring a blaze at a scrap metal recycling facility in Belfast Harbour under control.

The blaze at the Clearway Disposals site on East Twin Road, in the shipyard area of the harbour estate, was reported at 12.14pm on Wednesday. On Thursday morning, Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service said crews remained at the scene of a "well-developed fire" involving around 4,500 tonnes of scrap cars.

A large plume of smoke spread across parts of east Belfast, including Victoria Park, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said.

Belfast Harbour says it handles more than 70 per cent of Northern Ireland's seaborne imports and exports, and around 25 per cent of the island of Ireland's sea trade.

News.title: Farage senior aide filmed suggesting way to avoid donations law
News.content:
Nigel Farage's senior aide suggested a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of Â£500,000 for Reform UK, according to undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4.

Dan Jukes was filmed meeting a man posing as the British-based son of a rich American businessman.

Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, his father would not be.

The undercover filming was done by a group called Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting. Channel 4 News say they have verified the material they were given and chose to broadcast.

Reform UK denies any wrongdoing and claims to have "been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign funded climate change activists".

The reporter posing as the son of the American donor is filmed raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Filmed standing outside a pub in Westminster, Jukes said "you do realise that you can do it?"

Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

"Actually that does strike me as a solution," Jukes continues.

He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before.

"That's one of the ways in which we do it," he is recorded as saying.

Reform UK have launched an internal investigation into Jukes. They would not confirm if he remained a party spokesperson.

Later, Channel 4 broadcast footage from a lunch in Clacton in Essex, with both the reporter posing as the UK-based son, and an actor â his supposed American father. Opposite them are both Dan Jukes and the Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Farage says "it's all above board" after the son has told him he has been in discussions with both Jukes and Reform's Head of Policy, James Orr about it for some time.

"I'll be the registered donor," the son says. "But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that's done and all those conversations are had the money is available."

"Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you," Farage is heard saying.

Orr is also now the subject of an internal Reform UK investigation.

News.title: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say
News.content:
The UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.

Approval for the Jackdaw project could come as soon as mid-September, just before Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.

The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups successfully argued that consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Jackdaw's owner says it will provide gas to supply up to 6% of the UK's demand at peak production, but environmental groups say it will only supply 2%.

Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and these updated estimates were put out for consultation in July.

News.title: Girl group Katseye are missing two members, but their tour still dazzles
News.content:
They may have been two members down, but the pop group Katseye received a hero's welcome as they played their first full concert in the UK.

The audience erupted with screams even before the show began, as the band broadcast their music videos on the O2 Arena's big screens, and the noise barely dipped for the next three hours.

It was proof that Katseye have become pop's biggest property (they're currently the most-streamed act on YouTube UK) even while singers Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza are on health-related hiatus.

The stage felt emptier without them, but their bandmates worked hard to fill the gaps, hyping up the crowd with a succession of bass-heavy pop anthems and jaw-dropping dance breaks.

"Are you happy to see us?" asked the band's youngest member, Yoonchae Jeong, as if the answer hadn't been obvious from the moment they appeared in a storm of laser lights and launched into the Brazilian funk workout of Hootie Frutti.

"I think you guys are our loudest crowd ever, literally," marvelled Megan Skiendiel.

"This crowd is unbelievable," added Lara Raj.

The concert was only the second date of the band's Wildworld tour - but fans already knew every twist and turn from social media.

There was even a cheer of relief when Daniela Avanzini survived a complicated lift in the dance routine for Gabriella. On the opening night, her dance partner dropped her., external

News.title: British army told to stop non-essential training exercises to save money
News.content:
The Army has been told to stop "non-essential" training exercises to save money, according to a defence source.

It will continue to train soldiers preparing to be deployed or on deployments - such as units sent to Estonia, the Falklands or Cyprus.

But units back in the UK and who are not preparing for a specific deployment have been told to cut back on collective training exercises due to financial pressures.

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces pressure to increase spending on defence.

The government is increasing defence spending to 2.5% of national income by next year, but is under growing pressure to reach a target of 3% by the end of the decade.

A defence source said the plans mean not doing what he called "nice to have training" - like large live fire exercises and rehearsing platoon attacks in UK training areas like Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire and Sennybridge in Wales.

It is understood planned exercises that were due to take place that are now cancelled include one involving the Royal Tank Regiment conducting live fire drills in Wales and a separate exercise involving tanks and Apache helicopters.

This was not the choice of the army, the source said. The pause is expected to continue for most of this year.

Other specific training aimed at modernising the Army â such as practising drone and counter-drone warfare is expected to continue.

The Army says it is prioritising the training that has been informed by lessons learnt from the war in Ukraine, and is reviewing each request for training on a case-by-case basis.

Though the government is increasing defence spending, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) is still struggling to fund all its investment plans.

Much of the new money has been earmarked for specific capital projects, including new weapons programmes. The part of the MoD's budget for training is still under significant pressure.

An Army spokesperson said: "Our training continues and we are prioritising activity that contributes most directly to readiness, deployability and operational effectiveness.

"We are also investing Â£2bn to transform training for the British Army over the next 15 years."

On Wednesday during Prime Minister's Questions, the chairman of the Commons Defence Select Committee, Labour's Tan Singh Dhesi, warned it was imperative to invest in the armed forces and urged Burnham to commit to reaching 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030.

The prime minister replied: "I've made that commitment very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time."

The government's wavering over defence spending was part of the downfall of Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer - with former Defence Secretary John Healey resigning his position in response to Sir Keir's plans on funding the armed forces.

Plans set out in the Defence Investment Plan (Dip) will see defence spending rise to 2.7% of GDP by 2027/28, but there are no firm details on how further increases will be achieved beyond that date.

The Treasury has consistently said the government will set out plans for reaching both 3% and 3.5% at the spending review, due to take place next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister to "cut welfare spending and invest that money in our defence". The party says it would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Faced with a choice between spending on military training and spending on benefits... Labour chooses more benefits," Tory shadow secretary of state for work and pensions Helen Whately said.

News.title: Watch: Gloria Steinem dedicated her life to fight for women's equality
News.content:
Gloria Steinem spent more than 60 years as one of the most prominent voices in the fight for women's rights.

She launched herself into the mainstream in the 1960s with an expose of New York City's Playboy Club, documenting the harsh conditions she faced working undercover as a Playboy Bunny.

A powerful and outspoken campaigner at a time of routine discrimination, Steinem faced sexist criticism and harassment from men throughout her long career.

Her lifelong battle saw many victories, including the US Supreme Court's 1973 Roe v Wade decision that guaranteed a woman's right to an abortion.

It also saw setbacks, like that same decision being overturned in 2022.

The feminist icon died on Wednesday at the age of 92, her foundation said in a statement. She never retired.

More on this story here.

News.title: 'Miracle' eagle with broken wing spotted back above Scottish coast
News.content:
A sea eagle that confounded experts by surviving into adulthood with a badly broken wing has been spotted back in the skies above Scotland's west coast.

The bird was dubbed the Isle of Mull's "miracle eagle" by charity the RSPB after it fell from its nest as a chick during a storm in 2023.

Experts that monitor the island's sea eagle population did not expect the male chick to survive, but it has now been spotted three years on - soaring above the island with the distinctive kink in its wing clearly visible.

Retired RSPB officer Dave Sexton, whose has worked with the island's sea eagles for more than 20 years, described the sighting as "incredible".

News.title: 'I lost my savings after a job interview scam'
News.content:
Jobseekers are being warned to be vigilant as scammers are targeting people on job listings websites to trick them into downloading bogus interview tools.

One victim was invited on LinkedIn by a fake recruiter to take part in a job interview process and downloaded a normal-looking document which turned out to be malicious software.

Within hours the hackers had drained his cryptocurrency accounts of Â£18,000 of savings and disappeared.

"It's a horrible feeling to be out a substantial amount - something I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy," the victim, who wanted to stay anonymous, said.

News.title: AI tools that take notes for GPs could miss vital information, study suggests
News.content:
The report concluded AI scribes can help with administrative work but more research needs to be done to understand how they work in specific healthcare settings and how their design supports both patients and clinicians.

It comes months after the BBC heard from doctors in the West Midlands, who said their workload had been significantly cut by using the transcription tool Heidi.

At one clinic in Dudley, the tool was credited with reducing a backlog of posting patient letters from six months to 14 days.

One of the key findings by the University of Edinburgh was that although AI tools can help capture what patients say, they can sometimes miss important aspects of consultations - such as facial expressions, gestures and emotional state.

The report said AI summaries tend to prioritise clinical information, which can come at the expense of the patients' stories and experiences of their illness.

It was also found that patients may be hesitant to reveal sensitive information - such as substance abuse, domestic abuse or mental health struggles - when they know the consultation is being recorded and processed by AI.

Researchers also highlighted that manual notetaking serves important functions for clinicians in their reasoning and reflection on what the patient has said.

Their report said using AI scribes could result in "cognitive offloading" for clinicians - which means the tools take on some of their mental effort.

This can have benefits, the report said, as clinicians can spent their efforts having more meaningful conversations with patients or concentrating on complex tasks.

However, it also said the tools can reduce memory recall and skill development and highlighted instances where clinicians do not recognise their own notes or remember the patient the next time they see them.

News.title: Weekend heat for parts of UK before more rain next week
News.content:
Temperatures are on the rise again in time for the weekend with areas of the south experiencing 27C on Sunday.

However, before that, wet and windy conditions are in the Friday forecast for many across the northern half of the UK.

Low pressure systems continue to roll in from the Atlantic across the far north of the UK, affecting mostly northern and western Scotland.

Meanwhile, high pressure will block and weaken these fronts across the southern half of England and Wales, where drought conditions and hosepipe bans continue.

News.title: Schools to close early for A66 crash funeral
News.content:
Supt John Wrintmore from Cleveland Police said there was potential for traffic disruption and delays from 15:00 to 17:00 on Friday.

"This will affect areas of South Bank, Normanby Road through Teesville, Ormesby and Marton, and Acklam Road," he said.

"We are working closely with highways departments from the local authority, who are leading on the traffic management for this event, in order to minimise disruption.

"As with any significant gathering, we have plans in place to ensure public safety and security, which is line with our usual process."

A spokesperson for Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council said: "A number of schools in the South Bank area will close earlier than usual on Friday afternoon due to anticipated traffic congestion and transport disruption associated with a local funeral taking place in the area.

"The decision was made after careful consideration of the potential impact on home-to-school transport and the departure of pupils, staff and families at the end of the school day.

"Schools have worked with the Local Authority and transport providers to consider arrangements for pupils, including those who travel to and from specialist educational settings.

"We recognise that early closure may cause inconvenience for some parents and carers, and we thank them for their understanding and cooperation."

The decision comes after a vigil, for one of the young men who died, last week was followed by disorder in Haswell, County Durham, where a number of cars were set on fire.

The incident prompted criticism from MPs and police.

The Volkswagen Passat involved in the collision was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash, according to the police watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.

A total of 27 people have been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following the crash.

News.title: Reform UK promises £80bn cuts to public spending
News.content:
Jenrick is due to give a major speech to the conference on Saturday but speaking at a fringe event with journalist Allister Heath, he sought to reassure voters that Reform's policies would be affordable.

He said it was important to "learn the lessons of [former Prime Minister] Liz Truss" who he said "basically went into a sweetie shop, took everything off the shelves and stuck it into a budget".

"Quite rightly the markets reacted very negatively to that."

Jenrick was a health minister in 2022 when Truss's plan to deliver large energy bill subsidies and Â£45bn of tax cuts shook market confidence in the UK's financial credibility.

Reform has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax but Jenrick suggested that would not be a priority, arguing relatively few people were affected by it.

"It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he said.

He said his party would retain the triple lock - the mechanism which ensures pensions rise by either 2.5%, the rate of inflation or the rate of average earnings, whichever is highest.

The triple lock is estimated to cost Â£15.5bn per year by 2030 but Jenrick said he could not look pensioners "in the eye" and cut their income "while there is so much waste in the public sector".

He said it would be "fundamentally unfair going to pensions before we have made hard choices elsewhere".

Jenrick has written to investors who hold government debt to set up meetings in London and New York to discuss what fiscal rules he would set with the aim of reducing the cost of borrowing.

The past few days have seen global borrowing costs rise, with the UK's costs increasing to a 28-year high.

Also speaking at the conference, the party's business spokesman Richard Tice set out a number of proposals aimed at increasing house building on brownfield sites - land that has previously been built on.

He said the party would consult on measures including scrapping stamp duty, capital gains tax and tax on rental income for a decade for homes built on brownfield sites.

Under the proposals, affordable housing requirements would be removed for brownfield developments outside major cities.

The party's policy document says its plans would reduce tax receipts but argued that additional homes built as a result would boost the economy.

Tice has also suggested cutting business rates for high street shops, offsetting the cost by increasing the tax for online retailers.

Reform's conference at the Birmingham NEC comes at the end of a turbulent summer which saw its leader Nigel Farage resign and then re-run in his Clacton constituency in a bid to end questions about a Â£5m gift he received before becoming an MP.

There is also a police investigation into donations made to the party.

The main business of the conference is expected to take place on Friday and Saturday, with speeches from Farage and other senior figures, as well as an address by the leader of the French far right National Rally party, Jordan Bardella.

News.title: Households warned gas price spike could pile fresh pressure on energy bills
News.content:
Households across the UK are being warned to brace for higher energy bills this winter as European countries scramble to replenish their natural gas stores before the weather dips.

Wholesale natural gas prices are already at three-year highs, which could lead to increased energy bills for businesses and consumers.

Europe, which delayed its summer stockpiling due to high wholesale costs sparked by the Iran war, had been gambling the conflict would end before winter and prices would in turn fall.

Storage levels are significantly lower than usual for this time of year, with countries facing the prospect of rushing to buy gas now or paying potentially higher prices when the winter comes.

The European benchmark natural gas price topped â¬75/MWh on Wednesday, its highest level since late 2022, the tail end of a spike caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Natural gas prices in the UK this week topped 185p per therm, also the highest since late 2022.

The price has jumped in the past week amid a return to hostilities between the US and Iran, with analysts fearing the renewed fighting will keep the key Strait of Hormuz closed even longer. Typically, around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) is transported through the waterway.

Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said he did not expect the waterway to begin reopening until early 2027.

Even then, there will be a lag before energy is flowing freely through the strait and pressure on energy prices are eased.

"The risks to gas prices are definitely tilted towards the upside," Hussain told the BBC, warning that the gas price would top â¬80 by the end of this year.

Hussain recalled interviews with gas storage operators at the outbreak of the US-Israeli war in Iran saying they would wait three to four months for the crisis to ease before stocking up.

"We are about six months into the strait being effectively closed and that obviously has not happened," he added.

Higher wholesale gas prices feed through to household energy bills by helping determine regulator Ofgem's price cap.

The energy price cap rose in July, and will increase by 4% in October, leaving a typical household paying Â£1,723. But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices could rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.

Dr Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, told the BBC on Thursday a fresh increase in wholesale prices would "increase pressure on our January price cap forecast".

However, he cautioned that there was "plenty of time to go" and a fall in wholesale prices could ease the pressure.

News.title: Badenoch accuses Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass
News.content:
Badenoch repeated existing Conservative plans to fund an increase in defence spending, including by reimposing the two-child benefit cap.

The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April, meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.

She said the final part of her party's plans to reach the 3% spending figure on defence had now been completed.

The Tories said this would include saving at least Â£4bn through reforms to housing benefit and removing the VAT exemption for Motability vehicles, saving Â£1bn.

"Alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos deal and re-purposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target," Badenoch said.

Housing benefit made up about 12% of the government's welfare bill this year, with Â£37.3bn forecast to be spent.

The Motability scheme, operated by a private company overseen by a charity, has historically given disabled people in receipt of eligible welfare benefits a 20% VAT discount on cars.

Last year, Rachel Reeves made the first changes to the Motability scheme in 50 years, removing about 50,000 premium cars like BMWs and Mercedes from the scheme and reinstating 20% VAT for most new cars, along with higher mileage charges.

Challenged over whether she was increasing child poverty to fund defence by reimposing the two-child benefit cap, Badenoch denied this.

"It is not going to increase child poverty. What increases child poverty is children's parents not having work or being paid low wages. We want to grow our economy," she told the BBC.

"Right now there are some people making choices not to have children because they can't afford it and paying for other people to have more children. That is not fair."

Responding to Badenoch's speech, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "These unserious plans are hardly surprising from the same Tory Party that hollowed out our Armed Forces, shrinking the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era.

"Andy Burnham has made it clear that his Labour government is determined to give our Armed Forces the investment needed to keep us safe.

"In just two years, Labour has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with funding already higher than at any point during 14 years of Conservative government."

It comes after Badenoch pressed Burnham over the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when she urged him to cut welfare spending and invest the money in defence.

Burnham also came under friendly fire from Labour MP Tan Dhesi at PMQs, who called on the prime minister to urgently commit to setting out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn't going to be enough," he said.

Burnham has insisted his government is committed to fully funding its defence plans, saying it will set out a pathway to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.

News.title: Burnham and Macron agree to scale up action on small boats
News.content:
Macron said: "This is a very strong relationship. For me it is extremely important, and I'm here with willingness and a commitment to get closer."

The French leader's visit to the UK was primarily to mark the Bayeux Tapestry's loan to the British Museum. He met King Charles at the museum on Wednesday, ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display next week.

In bilateral talks on Thursday, No 10 said Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

They also "discussed the UK's drive to get closer to Europe", while Burnham raised concerns about the potential impact of the Made in Europe procurement plan, being drawn up in Brussels to protect EU industries, on British sectors.

Burnham has previously called for closer ties with Europe, as had his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The pair also discussed establishing local assembly lines in Ukraine for the Scalp long-range missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile.

The leaders also discussed the situation in the Middle East and the need to ensure de-escalation in the Strait of Hormuz.

And Burnham raised Israel's move to open up tenders for the construction of settlement homes in a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank, saying it was "unacceptable and only served to undermine the prospect of the two-state solution".

The development in the so-called E1 area would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Plans to build there have long been internationally condemned, with settlements illegal under international law.

The arrival of the first foreign leader under the Burnham premiership is an important symbolic moment - it shows the relationship with Paris is an important priority.

But it also reflects an obvious reality - to further reduce small boats crossings, working with France will be essential.

France and the UK have been working extremely closely on Ukraine and Iran, trying to jointly influence the White House.

And Paris will be an important player as the UK seeks even stronger economic ties with Europe under the new No 10 administration.

The "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally - first seen earlier in August with a 15-metre long vessel carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK - are arguably the most pressing challenge facing the pair.

It follows a summer when the number of small boat arrivals in the UK fell to a seven-year low.

The town of Vail, an exclusive ski resort in the Colorado Rockies, is building a $189 million housing complex just to give workers an affordable place to live with a short commute.

“Thinking about people as the lifeblood of your town, even as infrastructure, this is an investment that’s important to us enough that we’ve invested significant dollars over the past few years,” Mayor Barry Davis told 9News during a tour of the construction site.

Crews broke ground on the locals-only 268-unit apartment complex, called “Southface Vail,” in June 2025, and it is expected to be completed in September 2028.

The project, which town officials began planning nearly a decade ago in 2017, will include 84 studio apartments, 100 one-bedroom apartments and 84 two-bedroom units across three four-story residential buildings. There will also be 257 parking spaces and amenities such as a fitness center, clubhouse and a dedicated bus stop.

And of course, there are the stunning views of Vail’s mountaintops.

open image in gallery Officials in Vail, a ski town in the Colorado mountains, are building a $189 million housing complex just to give workers an affordable place to live with a short commute ( Town of Vail )

“The views and the quality that goes into building something like this — it reinforces our values of how important the people that live and work in our town are to making our town work,” Davis said.

“You should have a great view, you should have a convenient commute to work, you should feel like a part of this community.”

Vail's hills, while breathtaking, will also pose a challenge for those working on the new complex.

The hillside that Southface will be built into has a slope of more than 40 percent, with Davis admitting, “This is an engineering feat.”

open image in gallery Crews broke ground on the locals-only 268-unit apartment complex, called 'Southface Vail,' in June 2025, and it is expected to be completed in September 2028 ( Town of Vail )

The average cost to rent an apartment in Vail is $3,620 per month, compared to the national average of $1,962 a month, according to online real estate marketplace Zillow.

Southface apartments will cost between $1,600 and $2,500 per month, 9News reported.

Every unit in the complex must be occupied by at least one full-time employee of a business in Eagle County, where Vail is located, and it must be their primary residence.

The town already has experience building affordable housing for local workers following the Timber Ridge Village project.

Timber Ridge Village includes seven multi-family buildings with more than 300 units. One building is currently open, and the rest are scheduled to open on a rolling basis.

Initial work will begin over the next two weeks on the Trump administration’s controversial 250-foot triumphal arch project, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced on Thursday.

“This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World,” he wrote on X, arguing that various commissions and Congress have proposed that some kind of monument adorn the site for more than a century.

“Despite Congress’s intent, the site became and remains today a barren traffic circle lacking any monumental treatment and significant historic value,” he added. “In fact, the passage extending from Arlington Memorial Bridge to Arlington National Cemetery was meant to serve as an Avenue of Heroes.”

The arch is one of Trump’s many D.C.’s project. It is set to be topped with winged sculptures, on an empty traffic circle near the Memorial Bridge over the Potomac River, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery.

Burgum’s announcement comes as the legal status of the arch is under scrutiny.

open image in gallery An artist’s rendering shows the Trump administration’s proposed triumphal arch in Washington, DC. Works is slated to start over the next two weeks ( National Park Service )

The National Capital Planning Commission has yet to offer its final approval for the project, while Democrats argue the administration needs congressional approval to move forward.

The arch also faces a lawsuit from veterans, who argue the arch will tower over the nearby military cemetery and disrupt their experience.

“Frankly, I’m befuddled as to what sort of legal authority the administration thinks it has behind it,” Nicolas Sansone, of Public Citizen, which is representing the veterans, told The Washington Post on Thursday.

Democratic Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia also criticized the announcement.

“Burgum and the Trump Administration are disregarding the risks and rushing this towering monument to Trump’s vanity because they believe Republicans will get crushed in November," he told USA Today. “This project is not even close to being ready for prime time."

open image in gallery Critics of the arch argue it lacks legal permission and will disrupt the carefully planned view between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery ( AP )

The Trump administration, for its part, argues it does not need congressional approval to move forward because Congress ratified a 1924 report calling to build a pair of monumental columns at the site.

The White House also claims support from a Supreme Court decision this week, which allowed construction to move forward on the new White House ballroom because the National Trust for Historic Preservation lacked standing to challenge the project.

The Trump team moved Thursday to dismiss the case trying to stop the arch.

Justice Department lawyers noted the challengers' “distaste for the perceived symbolism of the proposed arch does not establish a concrete and particularized injury” meriting a lawsuit.

The arch, which would stand nearly 90 feet taller than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, would be among the most significant and large-scale projects from President Trump to renovate Washington, alongside his changes to the White House, his renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and his effort to beautify various D.C. parks and statues.

Fox News let go of host Maria Bartiromo for leaking company information to the Trump administration, according to a report.

Thursday’s announcement stunned the media world with little explanation of why she was no longer with the network. In a brief statement, Fox said: “We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 ½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter,” and said her departure was effective immediately.

Hours later, media watchdog Status provided more details. According to the outlet, after Trump gave a speech in July about election interference, Fox News officials ordered the network’s top stars to stay clear of Trump's unsubstantiated claims. Several outlets noted that Fox gave little airtime to Trump’s speech in the hours and days that followed.

Bartiromo then leaked the company directive to the White House, according to Status. It's unclear if she reached out first, or the Trump team made the request.

By sharing the information, Bartiromo violated the terms of her employment agreement, Status noted.

open image in gallery Maria Bartiromo has departed Fox and a report says she was let go after leaking company information to the Trump administration ( Getty )

Bartiromo has yet to speak out on her dismissal. The Independent has contacted the White House, Fox News and Bartiromo’s reported attorney for comment.

Bartiromo, and had been linked to the vacant role of press secretary for the Trump administration following the departure of Karoline Leavitt.

However, Vanity Fair’s Washington Correspondent Aidan McLaughlin downplayed the suggestion on X, stating: “Bartiromo is not leaving for a job in the Trump admin, I’m told.”

Fox announced that Thursday’s Mornings with Maria on the Fox Business channel would be the final episode. As of tomorrow, the show will be rebranded as Mornings with Fox Business and will be helmed by a rotating cast of anchors.

The Friday show Maria Bartiromo's Wall Street will also be rebranded as Fox Business Network's Wall Street, and will be hosted this week by Cheryl Casone.

This weekend’s Sunday Morning Futures will be hosted by Jason Chaffetz, with a new host set to be announced at a later date.

open image in gallery Bartiromo was known favorite of Trump - but its doesn’t appear she is heading to his administration ( AFP/Getty )

Bartiromo, who had become one of the network’s most prominent hosts over the last decade, was known as a vocal supporter of President Donald Trump.

In April, Trump told her during an interview that he was “very surprised” that crude oil prices were “only” at $92 per barrel and predicted that the war could “be over very soon.”

“If you told me that we were going to be at only 92 a barrel, $92 a barrel, I would have been very surprised. All right, and you know what? I'm very happy, and it's going to come dropping down very big as soon as it's over,” he said.

Last June, Bartiromo was mocked after misleadingly sharing a fake Trump social media post.

During an interview with former Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) following the nationwide “No Kings” protest, Bartiromo quoted the fabricated post as she said: “I love the way the president handled it because, congressman, he put out a tweet. He writes: ‘A huge thank you to all the No Kings protesters yesterday. I was very concerned that a King was trying to take my place but thanks to your tireless efforts I am still your president! Great job all!’”

Turning back to Crenshaw, Bartiromo gleefully added: “The president had fun with that!”

News.content:

Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy trial have been struggling to agree on a verdict following a trial over whether she should be held criminally responsible for killing her three young children at her Massachusetts home in 2023.

Both sides agree that she did it. But her attorneys argue that Clancy was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and that poor mental healthcare exacerbated her condition. Prosecutors argue that she intentionally planned the killings.

Over 21 days of testimony, the jury heard from dozens of witnesses, including doctors, first responders, relatives and even Clancy’s former husband.

If convicted, Clancy's sentence could be as severe as life in prison. If found not guilty, she may be released or remain confined in a mental health facility. If the jury is unable to reach a verdict, the judge could declare a mistrial.

As the jury deliberates, here are key moments from the trial:

___

EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.

___

Judge declined to remove a juror

Before sending the deadlocked jury home Thursday, Judge William Sullivan declined a defense request to remove one of the jurors following heated discussions from both sides.

Earlier, the jury's foreperson sent the judge a note saying a single juror won’t follow the court’s instructions about reasonable doubt.

Details of the jury room conflict weren’t revealed and only briefly discussed in open court, but it raised the possibility that a single holdout was standing in the way of a verdict.

Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington said the juror should have been dismissed from the case. Sullivan said removing a deliberating juror is a sensitive undertaking.

The judge questioned each juror individually in private, then reread his instructions about reasonable doubt in court.

Reddington said afterward outside the courthouse that the juror would be questioned again by the judge Friday.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said in court that she believed Sullivan’s instruction was appropriate and no further action was necessary.

Jurors have struggled to agree on a verdict

Jurors have sent notes to the judge at least three times since they began deliberating Aug. 27.

On Tuesday, the fourth day of deliberations, jurors sent a note in the morning saying they could not unanimously agree.

The note did not elaborate, and there were no clues as to whether a majority of jurors were leaning toward a conviction or acquittal. It also did not provide any insight into the tone of deliberations or whether they had been cordial or acrimonious.

Sullivan asked jurors to keep deliberating.

On Wednesday they sent the court another short note saying they were still at an impasse. Sullivan again told them to keep trying.

Clancy's former husband made anguished 911 call

Clancy's former husband, Patrick Clancy, was first to take the stand.

In emotional testimony, he described the day he found his wife after she tried to kill herself.

Lindsay Clancy had sent him out to get takeout food and medication for their daughter, which prosecutors argue was an excuse to get him out of the house.

He came home to find the house unusually silent, before finding blood throughout the main bedroom and a window open.

Jurors listened to the 911 call Patrick Clancy made after finding his wife outside in the snow. Clancy can be heard speaking with his wife, then tells the dispatcher he’s going to check on the children.

Moments later, he howls and cries after finding his children in the basement. The confused dispatcher repeatedly asks what happened.

“She killed the kids!” he yells.

Everyone knew Clancy was struggling

Clancy's mother, mother-in-law, sister, friends and co-workers testified that Clancy struggled with her mental health after giving birth to Callan, the youngest of her three children.

Clancy's mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, said she and her former daughter-in-law were close. Both worked as labor and delivery nurses. She described Lindsay as a wonderful mother.

But Susan Clancy testified that Lindsay had become anxious, paranoid and suicidal, and that the psychiatric care she was getting wasn't helping.

“She felt unwell. She had insomnia. She was losing her appetite. She was very anxious and sad,” Susan Clancy said. “She was begging for help.”

Lindsay Clancy’s mother, Paula Musgrove, testified that her daughter was scared of sleeping alone, became paranoid and believed the medications she was taking “were destroying her mind.”

“Mom, will you please come up and stay with me for a bit? I’m really sick. Something is wrong,” Clancy wrote in an October 2022 text message that Paula Musgrove read in court. “I had horrible insomnia all night, and I just don’t know how I am going to get through the day. … It’s just really scary, and I don’t want to be alone.”

The defense questioned the quality of Clancy's medical care

Clancy saw several doctors about her declining mental health, and eventually checked herself in to a psychiatric hospital.

Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argued that she was misdiagnosed and overmedicated.

As he cross-examined one of her psychiatrists, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Reddington questioned her expertise, prescribing decisions and use of 25-minute video appointments with limited time for talk therapy.

At one point, Reddington implied that Tufts was a box-checking “robot.”

“What did you do? You had a woman who was telling you she felt hopeless,” he asked as they discussed an appointment about two months before the killings.

“I told her that this was something we could address, that there was hope, that there are treatments, that there are different types of programs,” Tufts said, “so she knew that she still had options and a reason to hope.”

Clancy said she heard a voice telling her to kill

Paul Zeizel, a clinical and forensic psychologist who visited Lindsay Clancy in the hospital after she killed the children, testified that he overheard her saying that a disembodied male voice had told her she had no choice but to kill her children and then herself. Zeizel said he believed Clancy wasn't responsible for her actions because of her deep mental illness.

Prosecutors called a rebuttal witness, forensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun, who said he didn’t believe Clancy had hallucinated voices.

“One of the things that she said when I asked about what happened, is that in the course of strangling each child, she said, ‘Go to God, baby. Go to God,’” he said. “That was part of her expectation that she and the children would be together in heaven with God.”

Dr. Gregory Saathoff, a senior psychiatrist for the FBI’s Behavioral Analysis Unit, testified for prosecutors that Clancy “had the capacity to know right from wrong.”

The lawyers got the last word

After testimony was complete, each side got about an hour to make their closing argument to the jury.

Reddington showed the jury a photograph of the Clancy family, looking happy, and a second one of Lindsay Clancy in the hospital.

“How does this turn into this?” Reddington asked. “How? Because of the damn medicine and the lousy medical care that she got.”

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said criticizing the mental health system was “a distraction.” She said Clancy chose to kill her children because doing so would make it easier to kill herself.

“She was depressed. She was exhausted. She was done. She didn’t want to try anymore. She felt damaged,” Sprague said. “But those kids, those kids were her protective factor. Those kids were keeping her from ending her misery.”

Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton and Oprah Winfrey are among a slew of politicians, celebrities, writers and activists who are lauding Gloria Steinem as a revolutionary and inspiring figure.

The celebrated author and activist, who became one of the most visible symbols and potent voices of the U.S. women’s movement, died Wednesday at her home in New York City. She was 92.

Kamala Harris

“To know her as a person is to know someone who was kind, sharp, and witty. She was invested in young women and keeping the door open for the next generation of leaders, and her advocacy was always about fighting for the strength, intelligenc, and dignity of women everywhere. She showed incredible support for women running for office, and I will always be grateful for her encouragement and support in my campaign for the presidency.” — the former vice president, on Facebook.

Hillary Clinton

“Gloria Steinem was, at heart, an optimist. Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that’s a moral choice she made every day. Even though we’ve faced setbacks to women’s full participation and equality in America and around the world, I want Gloria’s voice to remain in our heads.” — the former secretary of state, on social media.

Oprah Winfrey

“Every woman who has ever walked into a room knowing she belongs there; every woman who has demanded equal pay, equal respect, ownership of her own body, and the right to make her own choices; every girl who has grown up assuming that her dreams are hers to pursue — whether she knows Gloria Steinem’s name or not — is living, in some measure, inside the progress Gloria helped create.” — the media mogul and television producer, on social media.

Nancy Pelosi

“May it be a comfort to all of us who loved Gloria that her extraordinary legacy will live on in every generation that carries her fight forward.” — former Speaker of the House, on X.

Jane Fonda

“For decades, she trudged through every airport in the country, in sandals and a trench, carrying her own suitcase, packed with a few black clothes, hair curlers, and steam iron, in order to speak to women — at conferences, town halls, consciousness raising groups. No group was too small to deserve Gloria’s time. This is how she built the new women’s movement.” — actor and activist, on Instagram.

Barbra Streisand

“From the first moment I met Gloria in the 1970s, I was deeply impressed by her. She stood for everything I believed in: equality for women in the workplace, a woman’s right to choose, greater political representation for women, and a thoughtful, determined response to every form of gender-based discrimination. She gave voice to these issues with fierce intelligence and steely determination, but also with wit, empathy, and humility. What made her so extraordinary was not only the strength of her convictions, but the humanity and grace with which she expressed them.” — singer and actor, on social media.

Jill Biden

“Gloria Steinem understood that women’s equality begins with the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, health, and futures. For decades, she fought to make that freedom real for generations of women and girls. She spoke up when it was difficult, listened to those whose voices too often went unheard, and never stopped pushing our country forward.” — the former first lady, on social media.

Melinda French Gates

“Generational change doesn’t happen by accident or fate — it takes leaders like Gloria Steinem who work hand in hand with so many others to build a lasting movement.. What a light she was for me and so many others. What a debt we owe her.” — the philanthropist and businesswoman, on social media.

Julie Taymor

“She got tremendous joy out of being with other people, with other women, and improving their lives. ... She understood about working from the bottom up — and she never really wanted credit for any of it. She always said if she wasn’t alive, there would still be a women’s movement. I think she underestimated her power. She was very modest. She had not an ounce of, you know, narcissism or ‘me, me, me’ about her. And she was able to really make change.” — the director of “The Glorias,” a 2020 biopic of Steinem, in an interview with The Associated Press.

Julianne Moore

“The time I spent studying Gloria Steinem in order to play her was one of the most edifying of my life. Everything I watched, everything I read, everything I observed about her gave me a template for how I wanted to behave.” — the actor, who played Steinem in the 2020 film “The Glorias,” on Instagram.

Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex

“Privately, she was even better than you would imagine — spending Thanksgiving with our family, introducing me to one of my best friends (forever the champion of female friendship), loving our children with her whole heart, counseling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit.” — Duchess of Sussex, on Instagram.

Roxane Gay

“Gloria was one of a kind. Genuine, generous, curious, thoughtful. She lived a staggering life and her passing is a staggering loss tempered only by the ferocity of her legacy.” — the writer, on Instagram.

Abigail Disney

“Everything Gloria did was rooted in kindness. It flowed through her political activism.” — her friend and fellow activist, to the AP.

Rachel Cargle

“Gloria, you changed my life. You seeded a fire in me that would result in my own activism. I am forever grateful to have learned from what you offered the world.” — the author and social justice activist, commenting on Instagram.

Harvey Fierstein

“An unstoppable visionary who demanded an equal role for females in a male dominated world and worked tirelessly, for decades, to bring that change about. The greatest irony was how many women she had to battle as they cowered behind their male owners. But battle she did. Equal rights! Freedom to choose! Access to political power! Equal pay for equal effort.” — the actor and playwright, on social media.

Jill Filipovic

“I have done what I wanted to do with my life. That would not have been possible without Steinem and the scores of other feminists who it is no exaggeration to say radically reshaped America and the world.” — the author and feminist, in her Substack newsletter.

People are being urged to nurture their pensions much like growing plants or vegetables.

It comes as new findings reveal that one in three adults (33 per cent) do not know what is inside their pension pot.

Additionally, more than half of those surveyed (52 per cent) admitted they have never checked their pension balance.

The study was commissioned by Pension Attention, an industry-led campaign coordinated jointly by the Association of British Insurers (ABI) and Pensions UK.

According to the research, which surveyed 2,000 UK adults via OnePoll in July and August, nearly three in 10 people (29 per cent) have no idea how much money they will require for retirement.

The initiative has explored several themes over the years, with its latest campaign securing support from giant vegetable growers.

Kevin Fortey, a Guinness World Record breaker who is also known as “Mr Giant Veg”, said: “One tiny seed, given enough time and a bit of care, can grow into something incredible. I think pensions are much the same.”

Pensions minister Torsten Bell said: “Some people love growing vegetables, but everyone should get involved with growing their pension savings.

“What you plant today shapes what you’ll harvest at retirement.

“So take a few minutes now to check in on your pension, your future self will thank you for it.”

Pensions minister Torsten Bell ( Jordan Pettitt/PA )

Mark Smith, a spokesperson for the Pension Attention campaign – which offers guidance on checking pensions at pensionattention.co.uk, said the initiative aims to give people “the tools and confidence to tend to their financial future”.

David Meliveo, chief commercial officer for People’s Pension, said: “Starting your pension savings early gives your investments longer to grow, but you don’t need to sow the seeds with large amounts.

“Small, regular contributions can build momentum over the years, helping to cultivate a healthier retirement fund for the future.

“With more than 11 million people already saving through automatic enrolment from the age of 22, many workers are off to a strong start.

“Taking simple steps to engage with your pension, such as tracing old pension pots and using your provider’s app, can help you better understand how your savings are progressing and support better retirement planning.”

Laura Stewart-Smith, head of pension engagement at Aviva, said: “Your pension is one of the most important investments you’ll ever make.

“Taking a few minutes to understand how much you’ve saved and whether you’re on track for retirement can make a significant difference to your financial future. Small steps today can have a big impact over the long term.”

Becky O’Connor, head of pensions at PensionBee, said: “Having a workplace pension – or a personal pension if you are self-employed – makes it easier to look after your long-term financial security. Starting early and maintaining consistency is important.

“Thankfully, the stock market does a lot of hard labour on behalf of savers, alongside tax relief and any employer contributions. Together, these features are the bedrock of decent retirement savings that can hopefully be enjoyed for many years to come.”

Helen McGinty, head of financial advice distribution at Skipton Building Society, said: “People should think about building a financial buffer that gives them options.

“That might mean exploring early how long your existing savings would last under different retirement ages, a look at your current spending and how you see it changing when work stops, or planning when you could increase contributions.

“Many people also don’t know much they’re contributing every month and whether they’re on track, but checking in more often will allow you to make those adjustments early.

“It’s also important to consider how best to spread your pension pot across your lifetime, especially as health and lifestyle needs change.”

Ed Wood, financial planning director at Rathbones, said: “Too many people are effectively growing a pension they know very little about.

“What we hear time and again from clients is that the challenge isn’t just building retirement savings, it’s understanding whether those savings will deliver the retirement they actually want.”

He added: “The key is not perfection, but engagement. Small, consistent actions over time can make a big difference to retirement outcomes and help people approach later life with greater confidence.”

News.title: The Grand Tour review – The top bods at Amazon will be stressing about whether they’ve picked the right trio
News.content:

Back in 2002, when the BBC launched a reboot of its motoring show, Top Gear, producers had to scour the side alleys of TV to find its presenting trio. Jeremy Clarkson, who co-devised the format, was best known for presenting Robot Wars. Richard Hammond appeared on the dodgy-sounding satellite channel, Men & Motors. And James May, who joined in the second series, had been languishing on Channel 4, co-hosting their rival show, Driven. The casting proved inspired, but times have changed. It’s perhaps no surprise then, that Amazon’s reboot of The Grand Tour – the last great vehicle for Clarkson, Hammond and May – has plucked its stars from that new gold mine: social media.

They are James Engelsman and Thomas Holland – really? Another famous Thomas Holland(er)? – the YouTubers behind Throttle House, a leading channel for petrolheads, and Francis Bourgeois, a trainspotting TikToker who exploded into prominence during the pandemic. Together, the trio will travel the world, embarking on car-fuelled adventures and hoping that some of that old chemistry rubs off. “Have fun with this,” Clarkson advises, as the new trio arrive at Diddly Squat Farm for some convenient cross-promotion, “and don’t f*** it up!” Their first trip takes them to California, to the “dwindling world of petrol sports cars”, where they each get behind the wheel of a brand-new muscle car that’s defying the onslaught of electric vehicles. There’s a Ford Mustang, an American classic with an eye-watering price tag; a sleek Corvette that can ease up to 150 mph; and, finally, the Hennessey Venom, a roadster with horsepower that could turn Shadowfax grey. “With acceleration like this, I feel like I’m flying a fighter jet,” Bourgeois observes, as he roars off in the Venom.

When Amazon snaffled up the Top Gear presenters and launched The Grand Tour, they took a beloved part of the BBC show – the foreign specials – and made that the focus of the series. With carte blanche, the stunts could be bigger than ever. But they were also glossier, less prone to the haphazard disasters of the original. And this new iteration of The Grand Tour feels even less chaotic. They cruise serenely through Bombay Beach, rope Jenson Button in for a performance test at the Thermal Country Club, and participate in a slickly choreographed relay race with a team of aerobatic jets. “I felt the need,” Engelsman observes as his Corvette streaks off, “the need for the toilet.”

It is all rather safe. Engelsman and Holland clearly know each other well (the latter, a Canadian, is the most polished on-screen performer), but most of the charisma is left to Bourgeois. He might be an acquired taste (his enthusiasm for trains is either charming or irritating, depending on your cynicism levels), yet he clearly offers something distinctive. He has the nerdy qualities of James May coupled with Richard Hammond’s most effusive moments of childlike wonder. During one sequence where the team drives alongside a freight train, hauling its load through the Californian desert, his face lights up with a level of delight I have never, personally, experienced. “We’re in a Francis Bourgeois dream right now,” one of his co-hosts observes. It does slightly raise the question of whether Bourgeois might be more invested in the whole endeavour if they ditched the cars and travelled by train.

But for the most part, the opening episode of this relaunch is fine. The dynamic between the new presenters has yet to settle but will develop over time. Top Gear and The Grand Tour are shows that required their hosts to make tightly scripted, carefully planned sequences look spontaneous and effortless. That ease has yet to come; at times the new hosts come across as stilted. And it is not quite clear what the show wants to be. On the one hand, the season opener is a rallying cry for the fossil fuel industry (“petrol powered performance isn’t going to be driven out of town any time soon,” they declare, proudly). At the same time, there are a few jokes that might test the patience of their proprietor, Mr Bezos. “What part of the American dream does your car represent?” Holland asks Bourgeois, staring at his gaudy £2.1m ride. “The new American dream,” Bourgeois deadpans back. “Being a billionaire.”

Social media stars front the new series of ‘The Grand Tour’ ( Prime Video )

Will audiences who loved the original trio be converted by this new gang? Will their social media followings translate to Prime subscriptions? These are questions that the top bods at Amazon will be stressing about. “This is not an easy job,” Holland observes at the end of his first episode. He’s right. As the BBC have found in their attempts to recast Top Gear, the stakes are high. With this new generation of The Grand Tour, Amazon has played it as safe as possible – which, for some viewers, might undermine the whole point of a motoring adventure show.
