World.title: Liberia: Weah Visits Jailed Former VP Taylor Amid Drug Trafficking Charges
World.content:
Monrovia — Former President George Manneh Weah has arrived at the Monrovia Central Prison to visit former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor, who is being held on pretrial detention in connection with the government’s US$317 million cocaine investigation.

Taylor is facing several charges, including drug trafficking and money laundering. She has denied the allegations.

Weah arrived in Liberia Wednesday evening to a rousing welcome from supporters after spending several months abroad. Speaking shortly after his return, the former president condemned the charges against his former vice president, describing them as “bogus,” and promised to visit her at the prison.

True to his promise, Weah arrived at the Monrovia Central Prison Thursday afternoon, where he was greeted by scores of supporters gathered outside the facility.

The prison compound was heavily guarded by police as Weah, accompanied by senior officials of the Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC), made his way inside to meet Taylor.

Among those accompanying the former president are CDC Chairman Janga Kowo and former Speaker of the House of Representatives, Dr. Bhofal Chambers.

The visit comes amid heightened political tensions surrounding the government’s prosecution of Taylor and other suspects in the massive cocaine investigation.

Weah is expected to address journalists following his meeting with Taylor.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-President Weah Declares Democracy Under Threat, Defends Jewel Howard Taylor, Vows to Rally Opposition Unity
World.content:
MONROVIA — George Manneh Weah’s return to Liberia was always likely to carry political significance. But his first major intervention after months abroad has revealed something more consequential than the former president’s homecoming: he appears ready to re-enter the country’s political conversation at a moment when one of his closest political allies, former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor, is facing serious criminal charges and detention.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

For Weah, the Howard Taylor case is no longer simply a legal matter involving a former member of his administration. It has become a test of how far he is willing to go for a political partner he has repeatedly treated as family, and whom he now publicly calls his “sister.”

Standing before reporters and supporters at his Rehab residence in Monrovia following his return from abroad, Weah delivered an unusually forceful denunciation of the government’s handling of Taylor’s case.

He described the charges as “bogus and unacceptable,” accused authorities of tampering with the rule of law and warned that Liberia cannot afford a justice system that appears selective. “What’s happening to the former Vice President is wrong. The rule of law is being tampered with,” Weah said.

The language was unmistakably political. But it also exposed the difficult position in which the former president now finds himself. Taylor is not merely a former vice president. She was Weah’s constitutional partner throughout his presidency from 2018 to 2024, serving beside him through the triumphs, controversies and political battles that defined his administration.

Now she is facing allegations connected to Liberia’s investigation into a major cocaine seizure, including drug trafficking and money laundering charges that she has denied.

Weah’s decision to publicly challenge those proceedings places him in a potentially delicate confrontation with the administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai.

His remarks suggest that his answer may extend beyond visiting Taylor in detention or issuing public statements of solidarity. “I intend to visit her,” Weah said, making clear that he wants to personally empathize with his former vice president. But the former president also linked Taylor’s situation to what he sees as a broader threat to Liberia’s democratic order.

By placing the Taylor prosecution inside a larger argument about the rule of law, Weah is attempting to transform what could otherwise remain an individual criminal case into a national political debate about justice, democracy and the conduct of government.

His argument is that Liberia cannot afford a justice system in which political identity determines who is prosecuted and who is protected. “We need to be honest with the law,” he said. “We have to be fair.”

If Weah’s position is interpreted as opposition to the prosecution simply because Taylor served in his administration, his democratic argument could lose force. But if he succeeds in separating his demand for due process from the question of Taylor’s guilt or innocence, he could establish a broader political argument capable of resonating beyond the Coalition for Democratic Change.

Weah and Taylor entered Liberia’s highest political office together after the 2017 elections, forming one of the country’s most consequential political partnerships in recent history. Whatever disagreements may have emerged during or after their administration, Taylor remained closely associated with the Weah presidency.

Now, with Taylor facing prosecution, Weah’s public defense can be viewed as a measure of political loyalty. The former president’s return comes at a particularly sensitive moment because his political influence remains significant within the opposition community.

The reception he received at Roberts International Airport was, in itself, a political statement. Supporters turned out in large numbers to welcome him home, giving Weah an opportunity to demonstrate that his political base has not disappeared despite his absence from Liberia. He interpreted the reception as evidence of the continuing strength of the opposition. “The strength of our opposition political parties,” he said, referring to the supporters who came to receive him.

Beyond defending Taylor, the former president used his return to call for a broader opposition gathering. He wants opposition actors to sit around a table, listen to one another and develop a common approach to what he describes as threats to Liberia’s democracy. “The voice of the people, the opposition, we need to listen to each other and find a way to move forward,” he said.

Liberia’s opposition has often been stronger in numbers than in cohesion. Political parties and personalities have historically competed for influence, sometimes making it difficult to construct a sustained opposition coalition outside election cycles.

Weah now appears to be arguing that the moment requires something different. He wants the opposition to organize around democratic principles rather than simply around the next presidential election.

Weah remains the most prominent figure associated with the CDC, but his effort to rally a wider opposition community will require him to work with politicians whose ambitions may not necessarily align with his own.

Some may see him as the natural leader of the opposition. Others may regard his political dominance as precisely the problem that a broader coalition would need to overcome. That makes Weah’s call for unity both necessary and complicated. “We all need to stand up to protect democracy,” he said.

His message is particularly significant because he framed his own conduct following the 2023 presidential election as evidence of his commitment to democratic continuity. Weah recalled that he accepted the election result after losing to Boakai by a relatively narrow margin.

His point was clear that he believes his acceptance of defeat demonstrated that Liberia’s democratic institutions can function even when political competition is intense.

That argument could become a central part of his political narrative as he seeks to reassert himself. If Weah wants to present himself as a defender of democratic institutions, his supporters and political opponents alike will expect his proposed opposition movement to operate according to those same principles.

And perhaps most importantly, it means convincing opposition leaders that his call for unity is about strengthening the opposition rather than simply restoring his own political influence.

The former president’s proposed meeting will have to confront the practical questions that have often weakened opposition politics: Who speaks for the opposition? What issues unite the various parties? How will disagreements be resolved? Will the coalition support a single candidate in 2029? And, perhaps most importantly, can political leaders subordinate individual ambitions to a common objective?

For now, Weah appears to be building the argument that Liberia needs an organized political counterweight to the Unity Party-led government. His criticism of the administration over Taylor’s prosecution gives that effort an immediate rallying point. But the former president is also taking a significant political risk.

The harder he pushes the Taylor issue, the more the government may frame his intervention as an attempt to shield a former administration official from accountability.

The more he broadens the matter into a democracy debate, however, the more he places himself in a position where he must explain precisely what reforms or safeguards he wants.

His strongest position would be to insist that Taylor receive a fair and transparent judicial process while allowing the courts to determine the merits of the allegations. That would enable him to defend his former vice president without appearing to place her beyond the reach of the law.

His weakest position would be one in which political loyalty is allowed to substitute for evidence. Weah’s own words appear designed to avoid that trap. He did not simply say Taylor should be released because she served as his vice president.

The former president also raised questions about developments within the government’s own system, suggesting that reports of officials being removed while remaining connected to prosecutions raise concerns about the credibility of the process.

His comments indicate that he intends to scrutinize not only Taylor’s case but the broader machinery through which the government is pursuing its investigations. That could place Weah on a collision course with the administration in the months ahead. And if that happens, Taylor’s case could become the first major issue around which Liberia’s opposition begins to regroup.

World.title: Liberia: War Crimes Court Office Chief Urges Boakai to Recall Lawmakers for Special Session to Pass Court Bill Before U.N. General Assembly This Month
World.content:
Jallah Barbu, Liberia’s war crimes court office chief, said time is running out to establish the court.

Summary

War Crimes Court Cffice chief Jallah Barbu has urged President Joseph Boakai to recall lawmakers from their annual constituency break for a special session to act on legislation establishing the court.

Barbu wants action before Boakai attends the U.N. General Assembly starting on September 8, as Liberia prepares for a prominent international role on the Security Council.

The call comes as survivors and advocates call for urgent action on a national fund to provide reparations for people still living with the consequences of Liberia’s civil wars.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

PAYNESVILLE CITY, Montserrado County—Jallah Barbu, executive director of the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, has urged President Joseph Boakai to exercise his constitutional power by recalling lawmakers from their annual constituency break to act on legislation establishing the long-promised court.

Speaking Saturday at a Paynesville hotel during the 17th anniversary celebration of the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association, the country’s largest group representing victims and survivors of the civil wars, Barbu said lawmakers cannot wait.

“Mr. President, please, we begging you. These people they not coming until October,” said Barbu in Liberian English, drawing applause from an audience that included war victims and survivors. “Call them back right now to pass this law here. Don’t waste time. Call them back let them pass the law before you go to the GA[United Nations General Assembly]. It can happen.”

The appeal adds new urgency to Liberia’s long-running effort to establish a court for crimes committed during its civil wars, with competing proposals still before lawmakers more than two decades after the conflicts ended. Advocates see Boakai’s appearance at the U.N. General Assembly as an opportunity to demonstrate progress on accountability as Liberia assumes a more prominent international role, including its two-year term on the U.N. Security Council and its scheduled presidency of the Council in December. Transitional justice was not a stand-alone pillar of Liberia’s campaign for the Council’s seat, but key members of the international community have made it clear that they expect Liberia to have made meaningful progress on wartime justice before it takes is seat as chair on the Security Council. They also flag this as an important opportunity to encourage international support for the court.

The Legislature, which has the constitutional authority to establish courts, is considering six proposals: bills from the Liberian National Bar Association and a civil society coalition led by the Independent National Commission on Human Rights; separate proposals from Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah; and two bills from the government’s court office establishing a War and Economic Crimes Court and a National Anti-Corruption Court.

In May, Boakai renewed efforts to establish the courts. The Office subsequently submitted its bills, but lawmakers went on their annual constituency break in July without passing them.

Fighters from the United Liberation Movement of Liberia (ULIMO) shoot their way through downtown Monrovia, 1996. (AP Photo/Jean-Marc Bouju)

The Constitution gives the president authority to convene the Legislature in an extraordinary session when the public interest requires it. Since taking office in January 2024, Boakai has recalled lawmakers from legislative breaks three times, although one recall, in August 2024, followed a request from lawmakers themselves. The current break began July 17 and runs until the second Friday in October.

For court advocates, passage would give Boakai tangible progress to point to internationally on an accountability process that has remained unfinished since Liberia’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission recommended a special criminal court in its 2009 final Report.

But for Rebecca Sonyah, 70, the significance is far more personal.

Sonyah, the mother of Peterson Sonyah, executive director of the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association, lost her husband — Peterson’s father — and six other relatives in the St. Peter’s Lutheran Church massacre, in which an estimated 600 men, women and children were killed. Peterson and nine others survived the carnage. Sonyah, who said she was inside the church’s school building when the massacre unfolded, was left to raise Peterson and four of his siblings on her own.

Sonyah said she had previously advised her son against advocating for the court but changed her mind as the campaign became a national issue.

“The war crimes court [is] important because people fini doing the killing they are free,” Sonyah told FrontPage Africa/New Narratives on the sidelines of Saturday’s event. “So many years have gone by. Other people just grieving in their hearts. Some people caused people suffering. Then they sitting down relaxing, enjoying. So, whatever you do, you have to pay the consequence.”

Bodies of a woman and child at St. Peter’s Lutheran Church in Monrovia. Decomposing a long with those of hundreds of refugees massacred by soldiers of slain President Samuel Doe on July 30. This photography was taken by Mark Huband in 1990.

Even among court supporters, there is no consensus over the final legislation. One major disagreement concerns appeals. Karnga-Lawrence and Jallah want appeals from the proposed court ultimately routed through Liberia’s Supreme Court. In a 2025 interview with FrontPage Africa/New Narratives, Jallah also sought to restrict international participation, saying foreign lawyers and judges could serve as “consultants to Liberians” but could not appear before the court unless otherwise agreed by the Supreme Court.

But international and national experts have dismissed the idea that the court could happen without internationals playing key roles. United Nations and other key officials from European governments have warned that they would not recognize the court unless it was a hybrid domestic/international court separate from Liberia’s legal system. Tiawan Gongloe, a veteran human rights lawyer, rejected the argument that the Supreme Court’s constitutional status prevents a special court from having its own appeals chamber.

“All constitutions in the world have a clear provision that the Supreme Court is the highest in the land. Sierra Leone and Rwanda have the same provisions in their constitutions, yet they had war crimes courts that had appeal chambers,” said Gongloe, under whose tenure as national president of the Liberian National Bar Association the organization submitted its hybrid court bill in 2021. “Liberia cannot have that unique,” Gongloe said. “We don’t want this ‘made in Liberia’ that makes us look bad all the time. We are a party to the Geneva Convention. We are a member of the international community.”

The event was well attended by advocates for a war crimes court, as well as victims and survivors of Liberia’s civil wars. Credit: Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

The Office’s proposal has also faced criticism. Among the concerns are provisions allowing the prosecution of former child soldiers recruited between the ages of 15 and 18 for atrocities allegedly committed after they turned 18. The bill also includes genocide, terrorism and mercenarism within the proposed court’s jurisdiction.

Another issue raised during discussions over the bill has been the appointment of the proposed court’s registrar, one of its most senior administrative officials.

“There’s no perfect document in the world,” Barbu said. “Our own document is not perfect, but it will address our situation.”

Before lawmakers left for their constituency break, both chambers had begun considering the proposals. Boakai’s bills were referred to House committees, while more than 40 representatives participated in a two-day technical deliberation in Buchanan in June. The Senate Judiciary Committee separately began consultations aimed at harmonizing the competing proposals. Neither chamber passed legislation before the break.

Lawmakers said they needed time to consult constituents. But a soon-to-be-released FrontPage Africa/New Narratives survey found just 4 percent of 1150 respondents in 11 counties said they were aware that their lawmakers had held any consultations with citizens on the proposed court.

The delays have fueled frustration. At Saturday’s gathering, Barbu urged supporters to begin a sit-in at the Capitol Building.

“We beg you. Make it your duty to join us at the Capitol Building,” he said. “When they come, let them see us. When they going, let them see us.”

Victims and advocates are also pressing for reparations and assistance. Gongloe called for a National War Victims Relief Fund, proposing that Liberians at home contribute LD$100 annually and working Liberians abroad contribute US$1, with the government matching the total fivefold. He said the money could support medical care and microloans.

“Taking care of victims of the war is a different agenda,” Gongloe said.

In response, Barbu made a dramatic gesture, giving Gongloe the first LD$100 towards the fund. Patmillia Doe Paivey, a commissioner of the Independent National Commission on Human Rights, quickly took the note and promised a proposal for the fund would be announced in days.

The Liberia Massacre Survivors Association separately called for US$250,000 in annual government funding, beginning in fiscal year 2026/2027, to document survivor testimony and massacre sites, support memorialization and transitional justice education, and provide livelihood assistance.

“To support LIMASA [Liberia Massacre Survivors Association] is to invest in Liberia’s peace and dignity,” the group’s statement said.

The event also honored several people, including advocates and journalists, for their service to humanity and their advocacy and reporting highlighting the plight of victims and survivors of Liberia’s civil wars.

Bowoulu Taylor Kelley, vice president of the Association of Female Lawyers of Liberia, who delivered the keynote address, said justice must be accompanied by practical support for survivors.

“Hope is a widow hearing, at last, that her loss is seen. Hope is a nation saying to its wounded citizens: ‘you are not forgotten, you are not alone, and what happened to you matters,’” Kelley said.

She called for accessible health care, trauma-informed counseling, livelihood and education opportunities, support for widows, orphans, people living with war-related disabilities and elderly survivors, memorials, preservation of testimony and reparations.

“Restoring hope requires practical commitments,” Kelley said.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Cooperation Development Agency. The funder had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Pres. Boakai Sacks Justice Minister, Solicitor General Amid $336M Cocaine Bust Probe
World.content:
Monrovia — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has removed Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh and Solicitor General Cllr. Augustine Fayiah from their posts, abruptly reshuffling the leadership of the Ministry of Justice at a critical stage in Liberia’s investigation and prosecution of suspects linked to the country’s largest-ever cocaine seizures.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The Executive Mansion announced Wednesday that Cllr. Betty M. Lamin-Blamo has been appointed as the new Minister of Justice, while Cllr. Abrahim Boimah Sillah, Sr. will serve as Solicitor General.

The shake-up comes as the Ministry of Justice, under Tweh and Fayiah, has been at the center of the government’s legal response to two major cocaine seizures with a combined estimated street value of more than US$336 million.

The timing of the changes is likely to draw scrutiny, given that the investigation and prosecution remain active and several suspects are facing serious criminal charges.

Among those charged is former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor, who has been accused by the government of drug trafficking and money laundering in connection with the broader narcotics investigation. She has denied the allegations.

The government has also charged other suspects in connection with the drug cases, while investigators continue efforts to establish the full network behind the massive consignments.

Tweh and Fayiah had been publicly associated with the government’s legal handling of the cases, including the announcement of charges and the prosecution of suspects before the courts.

The Executive Mansion, however, did not link their removal to the cocaine investigation.

Instead, Presidential Press Secretary Atty. Kula B.N. Fofana said the changes form part of President Boakai’s “ongoing efforts to strengthen key institutions of Government and enhance the effective delivery of public services.”

The President said the two outgoing officials will be reassigned to other levels of government, although the Executive Mansion did not immediately specify their new assignments.

Major Legal Shake-Up

The removal of the two top Justice Ministry officials means the administration is changing both its political and prosecutorial leadership at a moment when the government faces the challenge of sustaining several high-profile narcotics prosecutions.

Cllr. Lamin-Blamo now takes charge of the ministry responsible for representing the government in criminal proceedings and overseeing the broader administration of justice. Cllr. Sillah will assume the Solicitor General’s role, including responsibilities tied to the government’s litigation and prosecution functions.

Analysts say the changes could have significant implications for the handling of the cocaine cases, particularly as prosecutors move forward with ongoing proceedings and investigations.

The first major seizure involved 237.6 kilograms of cocaine, valued at more than US$19 million, intercepted in Liberia.

A second and larger seizure involved approximately 3,971 kilograms of cocaine, with an estimated value of US$317.68 million, bringing the combined estimated value of the two consignments to more than US$336 million.

The seizures have triggered intense public and political scrutiny, including calls for an independent investigation into the identities of those behind the shipments and possible political or institutional connections.

The government’s handling of the investigation has also generated controversy following the arrest and prosecution of Howard Taylor, with opposition political actors and her defense team questioning aspects of the case.

New Leadership Takes Over

The Executive Mansion provided no detailed explanation for the timing of the Justice Ministry changes beyond the need to strengthen government institutions.

In addition to the Justice Ministry appointments, President Boakai made changes at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission, the Ministry of Local Government and the National Transit Authority.

At Gender, Children and Social Protection, Angel M. Morris was appointed Deputy Minister for Public Affairs, while Harrison K. Sorsor was named Assistant Minister for Research, Policy and Planning.

Alex Chersia Grant was appointed Commissioner of the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission, while Christopher Ben Bailey was appointed Superintendent of Grand Gedeh County.

Benedict Yeke Harleysion, Sr. was also reappointed Chairman of the National Transit Authority Board.

The Executive Mansion said nominees requiring legislative approval will be subject to Senate confirmation.

But for the Justice Ministry, the immediate question is whether the leadership change will alter the government’s approach to Liberia’s unprecedented cocaine investigation—and whether the new legal team will continue the prosecutions already underway without interruption.

World.title: Liberia: Senator Snowe, Mercy Ahun, and Roy Onyango Chosen to Provide Strategic Leadership for Africa’s Immunization Advisory Council
World.content:
MONROVIA — Bomi County Senator Edwin Melvin Snowe Jr. has been appointed First Vice Chair of the Continental Immunization Advisory Council (CIAC), placing the Liberian lawmaker in a key leadership position within a continental body responsible for providing strategic guidance on immunization and related public health priorities across Africa.

The appointment, formally communicated by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), brings Senator Snowe into the leadership of the CIAC alongside two other officials selected to guide the council’s work.

Under the new leadership arrangement, Dr. Mercy Ahun has been appointed Chair of the Continental Immunization Advisory Council, while Senator Snowe will serve as First Vice Chair. Mr. Roy Douglas Onyango Otieno has been appointed Second Vice Chair.

The appointments, according to the CIAC Secretariat, reflect Africa CDC’s confidence in the three leaders’ experience, leadership capabilities and commitment to advancing immunization, primary healthcare and health security across the continent.

For Senator Snowe, the appointment represents an expanded role in regional and continental public health discussions at a time when African countries continue to strengthen vaccination systems, improve access to essential healthcare services and respond to emerging health security threats.

In formally notifying the three appointees, the CIAC Secretariat congratulated them and requested confirmation of their acceptance of the appointments.

The Secretariat said the newly constituted leadership team will have a central responsibility in guiding the strategic direction of the council and helping ensure that its deliberations produce practical and evidence-informed recommendations for African Union Member States.

As First Vice Chair, Senator Snowe is expected to work closely with the Chair and Second Vice Chair in shaping the council’s agenda and supporting the effective coordination of its activities.

The leadership team will also be responsible for shaping plenary agendas, facilitating balanced and evidence-informed deliberations, building consensus among council members and helping ensure that recommendations produced by the CIAC remain independent, actionable and responsive to the priorities of African Union Member States.

The appointment therefore places Snowe at the center of continental conversations concerning immunization policy, primary healthcare and health security.

The CIAC is part of Africa CDC’s broader efforts to strengthen continental health systems and support African countries in addressing public health challenges through evidence-based policies, technical guidance and coordinated action.

The council’s work is particularly significant as African governments continue to confront challenges involving vaccine access, immunization coverage, healthcare delivery and preparedness for public health emergencies.

The appointment of Senator Snowe also adds a Liberian voice to the leadership of a continental platform dealing with issues that have direct implications for the country’s healthcare system and public health priorities.

Liberia, like other African countries, has continued to rely on partnerships and coordinated interventions to strengthen routine immunization, improve healthcare delivery and protect vulnerable populations against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Through his new continental role, Snowe will be expected to contribute to discussions aimed at translating Africa’s immunization commitments into practical outcomes for governments and communities.

The CIAC leadership is also expected to help strengthen collaboration among experts and representatives involved in immunization policy while ensuring that recommendations are grounded in scientific evidence and remain relevant to the needs of individual African countries.

The Africa CDC Secretariat has scheduled the council’s next meeting for Tuesday, October 6, 2026.

Ahead of that meeting, the Secretariat is seeking to convene a one-hour virtual leadership briefing involving Dr. Ahun, Senator Snowe and Mr. Otieno.

The briefing is intended to prepare the newly appointed leadership team for the upcoming council meeting and allow the three officials to discuss their responsibilities, strategic priorities and expectations ahead of the October gathering.

The Secretariat has asked the three leaders to confirm their availability for the briefing and agree on a convenient time before October 6.

Africa CDC, in congratulating the three appointees, expressed confidence that their leadership will help strengthen the council’s ability to translate continental immunization commitments into measurable results for African Union Member States and communities.

The Bomi County Senator has served in Liberia’s national political space for several years, and his new appointment gives him an opportunity to contribute to continental policy discussions extending beyond the traditional boundaries of national politics.

His role on the CIAC is expected to require engagement with health experts, policymakers and representatives from across Africa as the council works to promote stronger immunization systems and more effective primary healthcare interventions.

The appointment of Snowe alongside Dr. Ahun and Mr. Otieno also signals Africa CDC’s intention to establish a leadership team capable of guiding the council through complex discussions surrounding immunization and health security.

The three leaders are expected to work collectively to facilitate consensus among council members while ensuring that the council’s recommendations are independent, practical and responsive to the priorities of African countries.

With the next CIAC meeting scheduled for October, attention will now turn to the new leadership team as it prepares to assume its responsibilities and help shape the council’s agenda for the period ahead.

World.title: 15 year old among maternal deaths- Kasempa
World.content:
A 15-year-old is among 21 women in Kasempa District of North-western province who have died to pregnancy, labour and delivery complications since 2023, with six maternal deaths recorded so far this year.

North-western Provincial Nursing Officer, Florence Mutondo says the district’s maternal death toll has held steady at six per year since 2024 which was concerning.

Ms Mutondo said this during a stakeholders meeting in Kasempa district of North-western province.

“Kasempa District recorded three maternal deaths in 2023, when the province lost 57 women overall, rising to six deaths in 2024 as the provincial toll eased slightly to 55 and remaining at six in 2025, when the provincial figure climbed to 64. The district has again recorded six deaths so far this year, with the province’s toll standing at 44 and the year not yet over,” Ms Mutondo added.

“As it stands, Kasempa district has lost a total of 21 women due to pregnancy, labour and delivery complications from 2023 to date, with the youngest aged 15 and the oldest 41. The majority of the deceased were below the age of 30,” She said.

Ms Mutondo said some maternal deaths occurred outside health facilities, raising concern over delays in seeking skilled medical care.

“Not all of them died at facilities, some died at their houses. Out of the six women who have died this year, two died outside our health facility. This is disheartening, seeing the efforts that government has put in place to improve maternal health,” She said.

Ms Mutondo, however, commended Kasempa District for surpassing the national target of 95 percent antenatal care (ANC) coverage across all trimesters, despite North-western Province as a whole falling short of the target.

“As a country, we have a target of 95 percent ANC all-trimester coverage. The province has not achieved that 95 percent coverage. However, Kasempa district has surpassed the target, outperforming other districts in the province, which is very commendable,” She said.

Ms Mutondo further expressed concern over teenage pregnancies, saying Kasempa district has continued to rank among the districts with the highest teenage pregnancy rates over the past three years.

World.title: Mungwi residents hail govt. for infrastructure boost
World.content:
Residents of Lusenga area in Mungwi District in Northern Province have commended the government for constructing a 1 by 2 classroom block at Lusenga primary school at a cost of over K800, 000.

Martin Chanda said construction of the first ever government infrastructure is a great milestone for the people in the area.

Mr Chanda said the 2025 CDF project is almost complete, noting that the classroom block will not only increase learning space for the pupils but also motivate teachers to work hard.

Mr Chanda has since commended Sinkop Engineering and construction company Ltd for exhibiting quality workmanship.

And Maureen Mukupa noted that the new 1 by 2 classroom block will help address the shortage of space, noting that previously, the school with an enrolment of over 400 pupils, was using a 1 by 2 classroom constructed by the community.

World.title: Over K5million worth Sinda CDF projects unlocked
World.content:
The SindaTown Council has unlocked K5.59 million for 11 new developmental projects aimed at improving education, water supply, sanitation and transport infrastructure in Kapoche and Sinda constituencies.

The projects, funded under the 2026 Constituency Development Funds (CDF), include the construction of Mwembezi and Chimunsi bridges, completion of a one by three classroom block and staff house at Tikondane Primary School and drilling and equipping of boreholes and installation of Mark II hand pumps.

The package also includes the provision of 20 bunk beds and 40 mattresses to Mng’omba Day Secondary School, construction of a fence at the new Sinda Civic Centre and a water scheme at Sinda Local Court.

Speaking during the contract signing ceremony at the new Civic Centre, Sinda Town Council Director of Human Resource and Administration Ernest Kalimbanya,who represented Council Secretary Mary Chongo, urged contractors to prioritise local employment.

Mr Kalimbanya said engaging local people will ensure communities directly benefit from the projects beyond the infrastructure being delivered.

He also warned contractors against exploiting local workers, stressing that employees should be paid fairly and promptly in accordance with the law.

Mr Kalimbanya challenged contractors to deliver quality works within agreed timelines and adhere strictly to required specifications and standards.

He further urged contractors to minimise environmental damage by avoiding unnecessary tree cutting and rehabilitating areas disturbed during construction.

The council has reaffirmed its commitment to ensuring that CDF projects meet required standards and translate into improved service delivery and socio-economic benefits for communities.

World.title: International community continues to toast HH victory
World.content:
The international community has continued to toast President Hakainde Hichilema on his victory.

French President Emmanuel Macron has congratulated President Hichilema on his re-election as President of the Republic of Zambia.

Mr Macron says the relations between France and Zambia have deepened in recent years through fruitful dialogues in areas such as debt financing, health and sustainable management of natural resources.

He notes that the numerous ongoing and upcoming projects between the two countries are promising for the citizens of Zambia and France, particularly the young people.

Meanwhile, the Organisation of African, Caribbean and Pacific States (OACPS) has also congratulated President Hichilema on his re-election.

In a congratulatory message, OACPS Secretary General Moussa Batraki commended the people of Zambia and institutions for the peaceful and orderly conduct of the electoral process.

World.title: Zambia reaffirms commitment to cancer treatment
World.content:
Zambia has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening cancer treatment and oncology services in the region.

Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary (PS) Kennedy Lishimpi

says this commitment is demonstrated through investments in specialised cancer treatment infrastructure, equipment and technology.

Dr Lishimpi disclosed this in Lusaka today when he opened a two-day oncology symposium which being held at Inter-continental.

The PS stressed that the ongoing efforts include the recent commissioning of an upgraded radiotherapy and imaging section equipped with modern technology by President Hakainde Hichilema.

Dr Lishimpi stressed that government is also decentralising cancer services, with the Ndola Cancer Treatment Centre nearing 85 percent completion, while construction of a similar facility in Livingstone is expected to be on board soon.

He called for greater collaboration among oncology experts and partners to improve the quality and safety of cancer treatment.

He explained that the objective is to establish a stronger and more coordinated cancer-care system that enables patients to access appropriate services as close to their communities as possible, while specialised centres provide advanced and complex treatment.

He also called for increased focus on cancer prevention and early detection, saying early diagnosis improves the chances of timely intervention and better treatment outcomes.

The PS challenged the participants to use the three-day meeting starting today up to September 5th, 2026 to go beyond information sharing and identify practical measures that can be implemented in their respective institutions.

Meanwhile, Chief Scientific Officer at University of Texas Albert Koong, disclosed that his institution has collaborated with the Cancer Disease Hospital (CDH) for more than 15 years alongside providing capacity building, technical and equipment support to Zambia.

Dr Koong stated in an interview that the partnership has culminated in the opening of a modern radiotherapy centre at CDH, University Teaching Hospital in Lusaka.

He explained that the partnership with government through the Ministry of Health has the potential to transform the radiotherapy centre at CDH into a world class regional cancer treatment and training centres in Africa.

World.title: Kapata highlights Zambia’s investment opportunities
World.content:
Ministry if Information and Media Director Spokesperson, Henry Kapata says the presence of five African heads of state at President Hakainde Hichilema’s inauguration has put a spotlight on the growing network of billions of dollars in infrastructure, energy, trade and investment opportunities built around Zambia’s geographical position.

Mr Kapata says President William Ruto of Kenya, President Samia Suluhu Hassan of Tanzania, President Emmerson Mnangagwa of Zimbabwe, President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah of Namibia and President Duma Boko of Botswana joined other international representatives at National Heroes Stadium on September 1.

He observed that their presence was significant because each country sits within an increasingly connected economic network around Zambia. Railways, highways, bridges, border posts, electricity interconnectors, pipelines, mining supply chains and trade corridors are creating physical links between Zambia and markets stretching from the Indian Ocean to the Atlantic.

Mr Kapata indicated that President Nandi-Ndaitwah has already indicated Namibia’s willingness to work closely with Zambia to strengthen the infrastructure needed to make trade between the two countries smoother saying the relationship is part of a wider western connection that includes the Walvis Bay route and the Lobito Corridor, opening Zambia to Atlantic markets.

The Ministry of Information and Media Director Spokesperson told the media that to the east, Tanzania is central to the revival of the Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority, or TAZARA.

He said Zambia, Tanzania and China have signed a US$1.4 billion agreement to revitalise the railway, strengthening the connection between Zambia’s Copperbelt and the Port of Dar es Salaam.

“China’s involvement also demonstrates how Zambia’s regional infrastructure agenda is attracting partnerships beyond Africa, ” said Mr Kapata.

On the United States, Mr Kapata says the United States is similarly connected to Zambia’s western economic ambitions through its support for the Lobito Corridor and broader cooperation around critical minerals and infrastructure.

He said the corridor is intended to create a faster route from the mineral-rich Copperbelt region towards Angola’s Atlantic coast.

On Zimbabwe, Mr Kapata noted that the country provides another dimension of the network, saying the two countries are deepening cooperation in energy, transport and border infrastructure, including the Batoka Gorge Hydroelectric Scheme, a proposed 2,400-megawatt project to be shared equally between Zambia and Zimbabwe.

“The two countries are also working to improve cross-border movement and trade through their major border posts,” he said.

For Botswana, Mr Kapata said it provides the southern connection saying the Kazungula Bridge has already changed the movement of goods across the Zambezi, while Zambia and Botswana are working towards improving border operations and increasing the volume of traffic through the corridor.

He noted that the objective is increasingly clear: trucks should move more efficiently, goods should move in both directions and the infrastructure should generate greater economic activity on either side of the border.

Mr Kapata said Kenya adds an eastern market and a wider gateway to East Africa. Zambia’s ambition to produce 10 million tonnes of maize, three million tonnes of soya beans and one million tonnes of wheat creates a need for large regional markets.

Mr Kapata further added that Kenya, with its significant food demand and established logistics and commercial networks, is one of the markets Zambia can increasingly connect to through improved regional infrastructure.

World.title: ZAMRA, NHRA sign clinical trials MoU
World.content:
The Zambia Medicines Regulatory Authority (ZAMRA) and the National Health Research Authority (NHRA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding aimed at speeding up the approval and monitoring of clinical trials in the country.

ZAMRA Director-General Makomani Siyanga said the agreement will reduce regulatory delays, harmonise requirements and strengthen the protection of participants involved in clinical research.

Speaking during the signing ceremony in Lusaka today, Mr Siyanga said the two institutions will work together in authorising and monitoring clinical trials, medicine safety monitoring, sharing regulatory information and building capacity.

He says the collaboration will also allow the two agencies to undertake joint inspections of clinical trial sites and rely on work conducted by each other, reducing the regulatory burden on researchers.

Mr Siyanga said the agreement is part of efforts to address gaps identified during a World Health Organisation-assisted global benchmarking assessment, particularly in the regulation of clinical trials.

He said the initiative is also critical to Zambia’s efforts to attain WHO Maturity Level Three, which would strengthen the country’s national regulatory system for medicines and vaccines.

Mr Siyanga said attaining the status would help open regional, continental and global markets for locally manufactured medicines, with potential socio-economic benefits for the country.

He described clinical research as the heartbeat of drug development, saying the partnership will help ensure that research is conducted efficiently while safeguarding the rights and safety of participants.

Mr Siyanga has further called on researchers, academic institutions and pharmaceutical innovators to take advantage of the improved regulatory cooperation.

He has also urged the media to widely disseminate information about the agreement to researchers, pharmaceutical manufacturers, ethics committees and the general public.

And NHRA Director and Chief Executive Officer, Professor Victor Chalwe assured researchers, sponsors, ethics committees and research institutions that the agreement is intended to make the regulatory process more predictable, transparent and efficient.

Professor Chalwe said NHRA is committed to ensuring that Zambia remains a competitive, credible and ethical destination for clinical research, while ensuring that the protection of research participants remains at the centre of regulatory activities

World.title: Zambia records slight HIV decline
World.content:
Zambia has recorded a slight decline in the number of people living with HIV, from 1.311 million in 2023 to an estimated 1.308 million in 2025.

Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary Kennedy Lishimpi disclosed this during the dissemination of the 2025 HIV Spectrum Estimates in Lusaka today.

Dr Lishimpi revealed that women account for 64 percent of people living with HIV, while also representing 61 percent of new HIV infections.

“These estimates are more than technical projections, they provide the foundation of our national HIV response,” Dr Lishimpi said.

He said Zambia had made significant progress in reducing mother-to-child transmission of HIV, with the rate declining from 34.4 percent in 2005 to 6.12 percent in 2025.

Dr Lishimpi noted that the country must intensify efforts to reach the World Health Organisation’s elimination threshold of below five percent.

He said children living with HIV had declined from 137,000 in 2005 to 59,000 in 2025, while new pediatric infections fell from 23,000 to 2,700 during the same period.

Dr Lishimpi further added that AIDS related deaths had also declined from 66,000 in 2005 to 16,000 in 2025, largely due to increased access to antiretroviral treatment.

He noted that advanced HIV disease remains a major challenge, particularly among people who have not tested, interrupted treatment or experienced treatment failure.

Dr Lishimpi said the Government remains committed to reducing new HIV infections to below 10,000 by 2030 through stronger prevention programmes and the introduction of new technologies.

He said the Government will scale up long acting HIV prevention methods, including cabotegravir and lenacapavir, while continuing voluntary medical male circumcision.

“Let us use this evidence to accelerate impact and ensure no one is left behind,” Dr Lishimpi said.

Meanwhile, UNFPA Country Representative Seth Broekman has called for increased investment in HIV prevention programmes targeting adolescent girls and young women.

He commended Zambia for progress in reducing adult HIV prevalence and new infections, as well as surpassing the UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets.

Mr Broekman, however, warned that declining external HIV financing and rising health system costs could threaten progress if prevention programmes are not adequately funded.

“Strategic investment in prevention will save lives, protect human capital and reduce long-term treatment costs,” he said.

Mr Broekman said Lusaka and Copperbelt provinces account for about 43 percent of Zambia’s HIV burden, while some districts continue to record prevalence rates above 15 percent.
