UBS argues that Venezuelan output will take years to recover and that the impact on prices will be limited in the short term

Leading financial analysis firms have tempered the White House's forecasts on the Venezuelan oil agreement announced by Donald Trump on Friday, which grants a company part-owned by the US government control of seventeen fields holding some 65 billion barrels of reserves for a hundred years.

UBS argues that Venezuelan output will take years to recover and that the impact on prices will be limited in the short term. The Swiss bank says prices “continue to react mainly to developments in Hormuz” and has not revised its forecasts for the sector as a result of the deal. The White House had maintained the transaction would substantially reduce petrol prices for American consumers.

Timelines are the main obstacle. The consultancy Rystad Energy calculates that Venezuela will not recover its historic production peak — three times current levels — until 2050, and that doing so would require investment of 85 billion dollars. UBS adds that new transport infrastructure, technical capacity and a stable environment will be needed after years of underinvestment, sanctions and power cuts.

Despite holding the world's largest proven reserves, some 300 billion barrels, Venezuela extracts around 1.1 million barrels a day and ranks twentieth among world producers, behind Angola and level with Colombia, according to the International Energy Agency. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Wednesday in Caracas that output would more than double in the coming years.

Companies are responding unevenly. Chevron, which never fully left the country, announced on Wednesday an investment of 7 billion dollars over five years aimed at doubling its production by 2031, the largest commitment by a US company since January. Spain's Repsol, mentioned by acting president Delcy Rodríguez when she set out the terms of the deal, expects to triple its own. ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips, which left in 2007 after part of their assets were nationalised, maintain that conditions for a return do not exist.

Doubts also persist over the deal's durability. Citi considers that greater transparency and broader political legitimacy will be needed for it to survive a future change of government in Washington. UBS warns of possible litigation, given that the agreement provides for US companies to take over projects previously operated by Russian and Chinese firms. Both the Venezuelan opposition and sections of chavismo have criticised the operation.

On Venezuela's possible departure from OPEC, analyst Homayoun Falakshahi of the firm Kpler said it “would be a great victory for Trump”, though it could increase internal pressure on the interim government.

World.title: Lenín Moreno and a former Chinese ambassador convicted over bribes at Ecuador's largest dam
World.content:
Lenín Moreno and a former Chinese ambassador convicted over bribes at Ecuador's largest dam

3rd Thursday, September 2026 - 08:11 UTC Full article

The ruling is a first-instance decision and is not final. Moreno, 73, announced he will appeal, remains in Ecuador and has not been detained

A court of Ecuador's National Court of Justice on Friday sentenced former president Lenín Moreno to five years in prison for bribery, in the case over kickbacks linked to the construction and financing of the Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant. The same sentence was handed to China's former ambassador in Quito, Cai Runguo, and to former representatives of the Chinese state builder Sinohydro, Yang Huiju and Song Dongsheng.

The ruling is a first-instance decision and is not final. Moreno, 73, announced he will appeal, remains in Ecuador and has not been detained. “I have not received a single cent from Sinohydro,” he said outside the court. If the conviction is upheld, his paraplegia and age would mean he serves house arrest. The ruling also imposes a lifetime ban from holding public office.

The court, made up of judges Manuel Cabrera, Daniella Camacho and Julio Inga, found it proven that Moreno acted from the vice-presidency, which he held between 2007 and 2013 under Rafael Correa, to favour the awarding and financing of the project. According to prosecutors, Sinohydro channelled some 76.1 million dollars in bribes between 2009 and 2018, equivalent to 4% of the contract's value. The company Comercial Recorsa, linked to businessman and Moreno family friend Conto Patiño, received more than 75 million dollars from Panama.

Of the twenty-one defendants, twenty were found guilty. Patiño received five years. Moreno's wife, Rocío González, his daughter Irina, his brothers Edwin and Guillermo and his sister-in-law Martha González were convicted as accomplices and sentenced to two years and six months each. Former Coca Codo Sinclair managers Luciano Cepeda and Henry Galarza received three years. Financial reparations imposed on those convicted total more than 163 million dollars.

The trial ran for 31 sessions, with 29 witness statements, twenty expert reports and ninety documentary exhibits. Former vice-president Jorge Glas, who is serving a sentence in a maximum-security prison, testified for the prosecution and said he had received calls from Moreno about the project's progress and financing even though, in his account, those matters fell outside his remit. Moreno placed responsibility for the contract on Glas and argued that without charges against a senior official in charge of it the bribery case has no basis.

Coca Codo Sinclair, with 1,500 megawatts of installed capacity, supplies around 25% of Ecuador's electricity demand. Construction began in 2010 and it was inaugurated in 2016. The state took delivery despite 17,600 documented fissures, and regressive erosion of the Coca river threatens its facilities. Neither Sinohydro nor the Chinese government has commented on the ruling.

World.title: Norway prepares to open The Whale Museum, 190 miles north of the Arctic Circle
World.content:
Norway prepares to open The Whale Museum, 190 miles north of the Arctic Circle

3rd Thursday, September 2026 - 00:48 UTC Full article

The low, curved concrete roof, which is covered in stones, doubles as a viewing platform, giving visitors a chance to spot the many species of whales

By Sarah Kula for the Smithsonian Magazine



Called The Whale, the new venue is under construction in Andenes, a village on the northern tip of the island of Andøya, roughly 190 miles above the Arctic Circle. It’s scheduled to begin welcoming visitors on June 4, 2027, inviting guests to explore the majestic marine mammals through science, art, storytelling, sound and architecture.

Designed by Copenhagen-based architecture firm Dorte Mandrup, the building is a big part of the experience. The structure rises “as a soft hill on the rocky shore—as if a giant had lifted a thin layer of the crust of the earth and created a cavity underneath,” according to the company’s website.

The low, curved concrete roof, which is covered in stones, doubles as a viewing platform, giving visitors a chance to spot the many species of whales—including sperm whales, humpback whales, orcas, minke whales and long-finned pilot whales—that spend time in the area, reports Travel + Leisure’s Evie Carrick. Depending on the season, they might also get to experience the midnight sun or the northern lights.

Inside, the space will be divided into several “experience areas.” Visitors will walk among five life-size wooden sculptures depicting individual orcas known to swim in Norwegian waters, an installation intended to create a tangible connection with the animals.

A massive suspended whale sculpture will introduce guests to the creatures’ size, sounds and behavior, with a focus on their social nature and similarities to humans—including communication, cooperation and caregiving.

Another gallery will delve into the 90 modern-day whale species, highlighting the roughly 50-million-year evolutionary journey that transformed their ancestors into animals adapted to life in the sea.

Why whale watching in Andenes? According to the museum, whale-watching operators in the village began taking visitors out to see whales in 1988, making Andenes a pioneer of the industry in Norway.

Nearly four decades later, whale watching remains a major draw, with roughly 50,000 people visiting each year to see these marine giants.

Guests will also be able to do an anatomical deep dive in a gallery featuring bones, baleen, whale blood and other biological specimens. They'll learn incredible facts such as that scientists have found that a diving whale's heartbeat can slow to a remarkable two beats pwe minute.

Another gallery will be designed as an immersive underwater experience that puts visitors in the midst of the ocean food web, from whales feeding on krill, squid and herring to nursing, dying and sinking to the seafloor, where their remains become a key part of the deep-sea ecosystem.

Meanwhile, yet another gallery, named Soundscape, will be a dark, multisensory installation that combines whale calls, ocean sounds, weather and light to showcase whale communication. The museum will also devote one area to humanity’s complicated relationship with whales, including the history and consequences of industrial whaling as well as the different roles whales have played in human cultures over the years.

Finally, a gallery called “Horizons” will show how whale habitats and migration routes intersect with shipping and other human activity, emphasizing the interconnectedness of the world’s oceans.

World.title: Eight Months After Maduro's Capture, Venezuela's Oil Boom Has Outrun Latin America's Sovereignty Debate
World.content:
Eight Months After Maduro's Capture, Venezuela's Oil Boom Has Outrun Latin America's Sovereignty Debate

3rd Thursday, September 2026 - 00:31 UTC Full article

Photo: EFE/Henry Chirinos

When Colombian former President Gustavo Petro convened an emergency CELAC session in the first week of January, the assumption in most South American foreign ministries was that the region would answer the United States with one voice. Eight months later, the answer is still fragmented — and Venezuela's oil is flowing north at a rate not seen in two decades.

From Southern Spear to a fait accompli



The operation that removed Nicolás Maduro on 3 January 2026 began as a counter-narcotics campaign. US helicopters struck Fuerte Tiuna and the La Carlota air base in Caracas, and the Venezuelan leader was flown to the United States under the banner of Operation Southern Spear, a 2025 anti-drug deployment that had quietly acquired a regime-change function. Washington justified the raid under an “unable or unwilling” reading of self-defence, arguing that Caracas had ceased to control narco-terrorist networks operating from its territory.

The legal architecture of that argument matters more to the region than the raid itself. As geopolitical analyst Alexander Dubowy argued in an assessment of the operation, the prohibition on the use of force in Article 2(4) of the UN Charter “remains formally intact, but it is increasingly treated as a language game.” For a continent that built its diplomatic identity on non-intervention — from the Estrada Doctrine to the Contadora process — that is not an abstraction. It is a precedent with a filing number.

Venezuela's own institutions moved quickly to normalise the outcome. On 4 January, the Supreme Tribunal of Justice ordered Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez to assume, in an acting capacity, “all the attributes, duties and powers inherent to the office of President… to guarantee administrative continuity.” The court pointedly stopped short of declaring the presidency permanently vacant, which under the constitution would have forced elections within 30 days. Continuity, not legitimacy, was the objective.

The region split, and stayed split



Petro's emergency meeting produced no joint declaration. Colombia, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, Uruguay, Cuba, Nicaragua and Venezuela itself pushed for a rebuke of Washington. Argentina led the bloc that blocked it, joined by Paraguay, Peru, Bolivia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Panama, the Dominican Republic and Trinidad and Tobago.

The rhetorical distance was striking. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva called the strikes “a very serious affront to the sovereignty of Venezuela,” and Brazil joined Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Uruguay and Spain in a 4 January statement expressing “profound concern and firm rejection” of unilateral military action. Uruguay's foreign ministry invoked the UN Charter directly. President Javier Milei, by contrast, posted that “liberty advances” and called the capture “excellent news for the free world,” backing US control of Venezuelan oil sales within days. Paraguay's Santiago Peña said the operation could “only bring good news.” Peru's José Jerí framed it as the start of “a new era of democracy and freedom.” In Chile, outgoing President Gabriel Boric condemned the strikes while president-elect José Antonio Kast called Maduro's detention “great news for the region” — a split screen inside a single country.

That division was not a temporary reflex. It has hardened into the region's operating condition, and it has left Mercosur, CELAC and UNASUR's successor structures without a usable common position on the most consequential hemispheric event since the Panama invasion of 1989.

The commercial facts moved faster than the diplomacy



While ministries debated language, the barrels moved. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said on 8 January that Washington had “maximum leverage over the interim authorities in Venezuela right now” and that “their decisions are going to continue to be dictated by the United States of America.” The arrangement has since been formalised through ordinary diplomatic channels: US chief of mission Laura Dogu met Foreign Minister Yvan Gil on 31 January to define a bilateral roadmap.

The numbers explain the durability. Venezuelan output is running at roughly 1.25 million barrels per day, with US refineries absorbing more than 500,000 bpd — up from about 135,000 bpd at the end of 2025. Washington is shipping more than 100,000 bpd of naphtha south for blending with Venezuela's heavy crude. Export volumes are up 19.7% on the year and fuel output 12.9%. The Financial Times has reported more than US$13 billion in Venezuelan oil revenue collected under US administration in 2026, against a US$3 billion disbursement authorised in April. Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit described it as “a beautiful energy partnership.”

For South America, the strategic implication is uncomfortable. A country holding 303 billion barrels of proven reserves — some 17% of the global total — has had its export policy relocated to Washington without a treaty, a vote, or a regional mechanism to review it. Colombian and Brazilian heavy-crude producers now compete against volumes priced by a foreign administrator. Caribbean refiners face a supply chain whose terms are set outside the hemisphere's own institutions.

What the next eight months test



The open question is not whether the intervention was lawful — that argument is now largely retrospective. It is whether Latin America can build any collective instrument that survives disagreement between its two largest economies. Mercosur's EU negotiations, the region's energy corridors and the South Atlantic's security architecture all depend on the answer.

Regional analysts tracking the hemispheric fallout have argued that multipolarity without shared rules produces not balance but disorder. Venezuela in 2026 is the case study, and this analysis of US intervention and multipolar disorder offers a fuller reading of how that disorder is reshaping the balance of power across the Americas.

This article was contributed by Eagle Intelligence Reports, a geopolitical analysis publication covering foreign policy, security and strategic risk.

World.title: ‘A pact with organized crime’: Opposition’s response to Sheinbaum’s second year report
World.content:
Listen to this article

In a 67-minute speech at the National Palace on Tuesday, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report. A month shy of completing her second year in office, she touted achievements across a wide range of areas and declared that her administration is “transforming public life in this country.”

Later on Tuesday, prominent opposition politicians presented a fundamentally different view of the state of the nation, asserting that Mexico, as a country, has not in fact improved under the leadership of Sheinbaum and her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador (2018-24).

While opinion poll results show that Sheinbaum is a highly popular president, millions of Mexicans oppose her government.

In speeches in a general session of Congress on Tuesday, two of Mexico’s best-known opposition politicians, Sen. Ricardo Anaya of the National Action Party and Sen. Alejandro Moreno of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, outlined some of the main grievances that they — and many other Mexicans — have with the federal government and the broader Morena party-backed “fourth transformation” political movement that was founded by López Obrador and is now led by Sheinbaum.

They included grievances about insecurity, even though the president on Tuesday touted a 51% reduction in homicides (in July compared to the final month of López Obrador’s term).

They included claims that the government is shielding a ruling Morena party governor accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel, even though Sheinbaum has said on repeated occasions that her administration won’t protect anyone who has committed a crime.

And they included accusations that the government is attempting to silence or censor government critics, even though the president says her administration will always respect freedom of speech.

Jorge Álvarez Máynez, national leader of the Citizens Movement party, also offered an appraisal of Mexico almost eight years after Morena first came to power. His remarks, and those of Anaya and Moreno, are covered below.

Ricardo Anaya, National Action Party (PAN) senator and former presidential candidate:

“It was said that Mexico is at peace, that homicides had already gone down. I wish that were true; it isn’t.”

In the Legislative Palace of San Lázaro on Tuesday afternoon, Sen. Ricardo Anaya told his colleagues that he was at the rostrum to “seriously respond” to Sheinbaum’s second government report, which he asserted was “unfortunately riddled with lies.”

In his speech, Anaya sought to demonstrate that the Morena party government is failing to uphold its own ethos: “Don’t lie, don’t steal and don’t betray the people.”

“First they promised not to lie. This morning it was said that Mexico is at peace, that homicides had already gone down. I wish that were true; it isn’t,” the senator said.

“And I don’t say it with my numbers, I say it with yours, with those of the Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System [SESNSP],” he said.

Mi respuesta al informe de Claudia Sheinbaum:

Maquillan las cifras, esconden el robo y protegen a los narcopolíticos. Prometieron no mentir, no robar y no traicionar al pueblo. Fallaron en las tres. pic.twitter.com/mNr6cx12NQ — RicardoAnayaC (@RicardoAnayaC) September 2, 2026

Anaya, who contested the 2018 presidential election as the candidate for the PAN, said that the average daily homicide rate before Morena took office in late 2018 was 70.

“In this six-year term of government, according to you, it’s 63. Seven fewer [homicides per day] is the apparent miracle,” he said.

“But this document — yours, not mine — has another column,” Anaya said as he held up a crime statistics report.

“It’s called ‘other crimes that threaten life and physical integrity.’ There are deaths listed there as well, but those — in a devious and deceitful manner — weren’t counted in this morning’s report. Those deaths, with you [in office], went from 15 to 40 per day,” he said.

Anaya also said that the number of daily reports of disappearances has increased from 16 to 31 under Morena’s rule.

“Disappearances doubled,” he said.

“So, do the math with me because it’s a primary school calculation. Homicides went down by seven per day in one column [but] went up by 40 in the other two,” Anaya said.

“Even though they fudge the numbers, in Mexico no one was brought back to life,” he said.

Anaya apportioned blame for the allegedly fudged numbers to authorities in Mexico’s 32 federal entities, the majority of which are governed by Morena. His claim that homicide statistics are being manipulated has also been expressed by security analysts and others.

Anaya proposed a “public and technical review of the methodology” used by the SESNSP — which compiles crime data it receives from state Attorney General’s Offices — “so that no dead person can change columns.”

“Counting correctly is not a technicality; it’s the first requirement for governing truthfully,” Anaya said.

The PAN senator also accused the government of seeking to silence critical voices with its General Guidelines for the Protection of the Rights of Audiences.

“Huachicol fiscal is the largest robbery in the history of our country.”

Anaya asserted that the government has also broken its “do not steal” maxim.

“Huachicol fiscal is the largest robbery in the history of our country,” he said, referring to a fuel smuggling/tax evasion offense in which high-ranking members of the Mexican Navy and customs officials were allegedly involved.

“And it’s not [just] the opposition saying it. The federal tax prosecutor said it in this chamber: 600 billion pesos (US $35.45 billion),” Anaya said.

“… Six-hundred billion pesos is the hospital that wasn’t built, it’s the medicine that wasn’t supplied,” he said.

“It’s a second promise broken,” Anaya said before proposing the creation of a “special commission to investigate huachicol fiscal,” a crime that Sheinbaum says her government has “practically” eliminated.

The commission, he said, should be “plural,” but chaired by “the opposition.”

Anaya said that the commission could begin by looking into allegations that a company called Portacelis is involved in huachicol fiscal.

“The company is called Portacelis and the name that appears again is that of the friend of Andy, Amilcár Olán,” he said, referring in the first instance to Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, a son of ex-president Andrés Manuel López Obrador and Morena’s former secretary of organization.

“The problem isn’t that Andrés Manuel López Obrador has been stripped of his [U.S.] visa. The problem is that you don’t want to ask a single question. … That is the country you’ve built — one in which your surname determines whether you’re investigated or exonerated,” Anaya said.

“Sovereignty isn’t impunity.”

Finally, Anaya asserted that the government hasn’t fulfilled its pledge to “not betray the people.”

“In a country ravaged by homicides, oppressed by extortion, the worst possible betrayal has a verb, the verb pactar,” he said, alleging that the federal government has a pact with organized crime.

To support his claim, Anaya referred to U.S. prosecutors’ drug trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya, a Morena politician who is currently on leave.

“A grand jury decided to bring criminal charges against Rubén Rocha Moya for drug trafficking. A federal judge issued an arrest warrant. The State Department formally requested his provisional detention for the purpose of extradition. Today marks 126 days, and they keep telling us there is no evidence,” he said.

Anaya asserted that there is indeed evidence linking Rocha to drug trafficking, citing an allegation that he met with Sinaloa Cartel kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, among other supposed examples of proof.

“Proof is not lacking here. What we have in abundance is protection,” he said.

“… Sovereignty is not impunity,” Anaya said, referring to Sheinbaum’s assertion that Mexican authorities can’t detain and extradite Rocha unless they are satisfied that the United States allegations are supported by sufficient proof.

“… The same apparatus that protects Rocha Moya, imprisons Ernesto Ruffo,” he said, referring in the second instance to a former PAN governor of Baja California who faces organized crime, fuel theft and tax evasion charges.

Alejandro Moreno, national leader of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and a federal senator:

“Eight years after the Morena governments began, the outcome is a country that is divided, fractured, indebted, bogged down and engulfed in violence.”

Speaking before Congress on Tuesday, Senator Alejandro Moreno was also highly critical of the current federal government and its predecessor — i.e. the administration led by former President López Obrador.

“Eight years after the Morena governments began, the outcome is a country that is divided, fractured, indebted, bogged down and engulfed in violence,” he said.

Moreno, a former governor of Campeche, asserted that the Sheinbaum administration doesn’t have a “national project” or “answers” to the problems Mexico faces.

Although Sheinbaum has an approval rating of 68% according to the most recent El Financiero poll, the senator claimed that her government is rejected by Mexicans.

Claro, en MORENA sí “Juntos han hecho historia”, pero por haber hecho un pacto inconfesable entre el gobierno y la delincuencia organizada. Un pacto que se ha convertido en un régimen criminal transnacional y que hemos denunciado ante todos los organismos internacionales por… pic.twitter.com/oOeS2Qd8M1 — Alejandro Moreno (@alitomorenoc) September 2, 2026

He asserted that the government is seeking to “put an end to free media outlets” and “destroy the voices of the opposition, canceling the most fundamental freedoms in our country.”

Moreno went on to say that “the Morena government is impunity disguised as false defense of national sovereignty.”

He accused the Sheinbaum administration of protecting Morena governors and other officials wanted by “foreign governments and mainly the government of the United States.”

Moreno also accused the government of making a “shameful pact” with organized crime, a claim that the Trump administration has also made.

He said that if the government had a “modicum of decency,” it would “break its pact with the organized crime cartels and take away the protection of” López Obrador, Andy López Beltrán, Senator Enrique Inzunza, Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila and Tamaulipas Governor Américo Villarreal.

“They’ve ruined peace; they’ve destroyed Mexicans’ quality of life.”

Moreno also claimed that the current government “has ruined peace” and “destroyed Mexicans’ quality of life.”

“They systematically eliminated everything that had a stamp of autonomy,” he said, referring to the government’s abolition of various watchdog agencies, including the now-defunct National Transparency Institute.

Moreno asserted that at elections in 2027, “with a large party and citizens coalition,” the opposition will win a congressional majority.

“And have no doubt, in 2030, with the people of Mexico behind us, we’re going to win the presidency of the republic,” he said.

Jorge Álvarez Máynez, national leader of Citizens’ Movement and a former presidential candidate:

“Hospitals and healthcare centers still don’t have medicine.”

In a video posted to social media, Jorge Álvarez Máynez, MC’s candidate at the 2024 presidential election, said that eight years after Morena took power, “Mexico is not making progress.”

Ya son 8 años de Morena en el poder. Y aún con todo el poder, México no está avanzando. El gobierno prometió mucho y ha cumplido poco. Pero México es más que su gobierno. México tiene alternativa. pic.twitter.com/ywiO7JYpsx — Jorge Álvarez Máynez (@AlvarezMaynez) September 2, 2026

“Insecurity continues affecting the lives of millions of families,” he said.

“Hospitals and healthcare centers still don’t have medicine,” Álvarez Máynez asserted.

“And people continue battling to reach the end of the month,” he said, referring to the challenge of making ends meet.

Álvarez Máynez also said that after eight years of Morena governments, “corruption and abuse of power have not gone away.”

“… They promised to be different from the PRI but they failed to deliver on that too,” he said.

“We have a government that promised a lot but which has achieved very little,” Álvarez Máynez said.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How Taiwanese imports are fueling Mexico’s record tech exports
World.content:
Data came out last week showing that Mexico’s exports were worth a record high US $81.4 billion in July, an increase of almost 44% compared to the same month of 2025.

In the first seven months of 2026, Mexico’s export revenue totaled $471.4 billion, a year-over-year gain of 27.7%, according to the national statistics agency INEGI.

In July, almost three-quarters of Mexico’s export income came from the shipment abroad of non-automotive manufactured goods. Within that category, revenue from the export of electrical and electronic equipment and appliances soared 134% annually. Among those products are inputs for AI servers and other computer equipment. Mexico is currently shipping large quantities of such goods to the United States.

On the surface, the AI-related export boom appears to be great news for Mexico, but the reality is more nuanced.

As Pedro Casas, CEO of the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico, wrote in an article that MND published this week, “a significant share of the inputs” in the AI-related products Mexico is exporting is not Mexican, or even North American, but rather Taiwanese. That means that a significant share of the revenue Mexico receives from the export of such products has already been spent on imported inputs.

In a recent LinkedIn post, economist Gilberto García-Vaquez wrote that “a single trailer of servers” entering the U.S. from Mexico “can be worth as much as a thousand cars.”

“But most of that value entered Mexico as imports before the servers ever left,” he added.

In his article, Casas wrote that Mexico, “in many instances,” is “assembling and integrating components that arrive from Asia, then shipping the finished product north.”

“That’s not nothing — assembly creates jobs and keeps supply chains on this side of the Pacific,” he wrote. “But it’s not the same as manufacturing a vertical regional integrated supply chain.”

In that context, this “Mexico in Numbers” article looks at some of the key numbers related to Mexico’s exportation of AI servers and other electronic products — and the Mexican content (or lack thereof) in those goods.

* The data in this article comes from various sources, each of which is mentioned below. In some cases, the numbers cited are estimates rather than proven figures.

More than 1/3 of US server imports come from Mexico

As we reported on Aug. 14, a report by the Economic Studies Department of Grupo Financiero Banamex found that Mexico’s share of U.S. server imports through the first half of 2026 was 34.5%, just behind Taiwan’s 36%. In the second quarter of 2026, Mexico’s share of the U.S. market for imported servers was nearly 40%.

During the first half of the year, Mexico exported more than US $60.4 billion worth of computer servers to artificial intelligence data centers in the United States, according to Banamex. In May, it surpassed Taiwan in sales.

Banamex said that “Mexico has established itself as an assembly platform close to the U.S. market, while design, technological integration and chain coordination activities (for artificial intelligence computing production) remain concentrated in Asia.”

Taiwan’s exports of artificial intelligence servers to the United States were worth $72.2 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Banamex.

As MND wrote last month, “Mexico and Taiwan have captured the U.S. market for artificial intelligence data center servers, which had previously been dominated by China.”

“In 2017, China accounted for 60.4% of U.S. purchases of computer equipment, while in the first half of 2026 its share fell to 2%.”

The vast majority of inputs in computing and other electronic products made in Mexico are foreign

According to a recent report by Swiss multinational investment bank UBS, more than 95% of inputs used in the manufacture or assembly in Mexico of computing and other electronic products are imported, primarily from Asian countries such as Taiwan. In other words, less than 5% of the content in such “Made in Mexico” products is actually Mexican.

“Mexico is capturing an important role in the North American AI supply chain, but much of the value of the products it exports is still generated abroad. Computers and electronics rely heavily on imported inputs, limiting their domestic value-added and employment multipliers,” UBS says in its report.

The bank also says that “a server assembled in Mexico can have a very high export value without generating a proportionally large amount of Mexican income, employment, or local demand.”

Similarly, the Financial Times (FT) reported in August that the “surge in high-value exports is yet to translate into proportional local benefits” in Mexico.

“Each dollar of investment in the highly automated [AI server] plants creates far fewer jobs than more manual sectors such as car parts,” FT wrote, also noting that “Mexico manufactures very few of the parts” used in the country’s AI server sector.

Fernando Alba, deputy economy minister in the state of Chihuahua, told FT that in current conditions Mexico could realistically aspire to reach 3-7% Mexican content in each server, compared to 39% for autos.

“It could do electronics, cooling and product design but making chips was very unlikely, he said, as the country lacks the engineering and design knowhow, as well as enough energy and water,” FT reported.

Alba also said: “A car is a value chain disseminated up and down the country. … It’s much harder to do that with AI servers. We are much less prepared.”

In its report, UBS says that “Mexico does not need to produce advanced chips to capture more value from the AI boom.”

“The more immediate opportunity is to build a broader ecosystem around the manufacturing capacity already being established. Potential areas include electronic components, cooling and power systems, testing and packaging, design, and other specialized industrial inputs,” the bank said.

Mexico’s imports from Taiwan have surged

FT reported in August that “Taiwanese manufacturers are rapidly expanding factories in Mexico to assemble servers, which are now the country’s top U.S. export, overtaking autos that dominated its trade for decades.”

As noted above, the vast majority of the inputs going into servers assembled in Mexico — whether by Taiwanese manufacturers, Mexican manufacturers or anyone else — comes from abroad. Taiwan is a top supplier of those inputs.

“Much of the increase in technology imports is coming from Taiwan,” UBS notes in its report.

Therefore, it is not surprising that official data shows that Mexico’s imports from the East Asian island have significantly increase.

According to Bank of Mexico data, Mexico’s imports from Taiwan totaled US $43.91 billion in the first six months of 2026, an increase of 200.5% compared to the same period of last year. In all of 2026, Mexico imports from Taiwan were worth $46.58 billion, less than $3 billion above the total in the first half of this year.

As Mexico News Daily reported in April, much of the recent significant rise in trade between Taiwan and Mexico is in the semiconductor industry. In other words, Taiwan is sending large quantities of chips and other electronic components and inputs to Mexico, where they are used in the assembly of AI servers and other computer hardware, much of which is sent across the border to data centers in the United States.

World.title: Chiapas town reclaims Guinness World Record for world’s biggest cheese ball
World.content:
Blessed are the cheesemakers, for they shall … make a cheese ball weighing 1,611 kilos.

Cheese producers in the small town of Pijijiapan, Chiapas, have re-entered the Guinness Book of World Records after stringing together the largest ball of quesillo in history, earning the acknowledgement on Aug. 29 at the city’s Campo Nuevo Milenio field.

Alfredo Arista, official adjudicator of Guinness World Records, verified compliance with the requirements necessary to recognize the new world record and presented an award to Mayor Carlos Alberto Albores.

Mayor Albores said that the eight cheese-producing companies participating conducted three test runs before undertaking the record-setting effort. He said an estimated 15,500 liters of fresh milk were required to produce the giant ball of cheese.

Once the master cheesemaker and cheese producers finished preparing the string cheese, the difficult task of forming the ball got under way. To do it, a special rotating structure with metal platforms was built, allowing the ball to be rotated and manipulated while its dimensions and weight increased.

The strings were progressively wound over almost four hours, until a single piece weighing more than 1.7 tonnes was realized.

The Tourism Ministry lauded the achievement, saying in a social media post that the record was established thanks to “the tradition, talent and hands of Chiapas’ cheese-producing families who are keeping alive one of the special characteristics that distinguishes the region.”

“Behind this large ball of string cheese lies a lot of work, tradition and pride,” said Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez. “This is a great opportunity for more people to get to know Pijijiapan, its flavors, its communities and everything this destination has to offer.”

The Pacific Coast town of Pijijiapan — with a population of just over 18,000 souls and the county seat of the municipality of the same name — is well known for its exceptional dairy products, especially its fresh cheeses, particularly a renowned doble crema.

One goal of last week’s event was to reclaim the Guinness Record it had lost to cheesemakers in Reyes Etla, just 20 kilometers north of Oaxaca city, when cheesemakers there constructed a ball weighing 636.2 kilos in 2024.

Pijijiapan had established the initial record in 2023 (making a cheese ball weighing 558 kilos), and organizers said they planned to climb back atop the cheesemaking mountain by assembling a cheese ball weighing more than 1,500 kilos.

At the same time, municipal officials sought to protect the identity, origin and tradition linked to the production of Pijijiapan cheese by obtaining an official Declaration of Protection of the Geographical Indication “Quesillo de Pijijiapan, Chiapas.”

In support of this goal, the state Economy Ministry filed an application with the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI) requesting the formal designation.

With reports from La Jornada, El Financiero and UnoTV

World.title: Mexico City’s Cutzamala water supply system hits 81%, highest level in a decade
World.content:
Steady August rains have helped replenish the Cutzamala reservoir system, Mexico City’s primary source of water, boosting supply to 81% capacity, its highest volume in a decade.

According to data from the National Water Commission (Conagua), the Cutzamala System has experienced 13 consecutive weeks of recovery, dating to the beginning of the rainy season on June 4.

During the final week of August, 15.02 million cubic meters of water from rainfall and runoff were captured in the Balsas River basin, where the system’s physical infrastructure and reservoirs are located.

The Cutzamala System supplies 5 million inhabitants of the greater Mexico City Metropolitan Area and provides 18% of the water the area consumes, around 422 million liters daily.

Conagua’s monthly report for August indicated that the Valle de Bravo dam was at 86.58% capacity with 341.47 million cubic meters of water; Villa Victoria dam held 78.10% of its capacity with 145.06 million cubic meters; and the El Bosque dam was at 72.98% with 147.71 million cubic meters.

These totals dwarf the numbers the system reported the past three years and come two years after policymakers were faced with concerns that a Day Zero might be approaching.

The current volume of water is roughly equivalent to that recorded in August 2017, but storage steadily declined during the following years. By 2021 and 2022, the system was operating at 50.31% and 50.15%, respectively.

Then, a drought in 2023 reduced the water supply even more dramatically so that in 2023, the system was operating at 36.71% of its capacity. In 2024, it rose slightly to 42%. Ahead of the 2025 rainy season, Conagua reported that storage had reached 56%, but cautioned that the crisis had yet to be averted.

However, plentiful rains boosted the Cutzamala water supply so thoroughly that it remained at nearly 70% by spring 2026.

This year’s August data shows that the three dams had increased their level by more than 30 million cubic meters compared to the same period in 2025, helped considerably by five days in which more than 20 mm of rainfall was recorded in the Balsas and Lerma river basins. Aug. 16 was particularly beneficial to the system, as downpours added 18 mm to Villa Victoria, 34 mm to Valle de Bravo and 26 mm to El Bosque.

On Aug. 1, total storage was 577.56 billion cubic meters, equivalent to 73.81%. By the 30th, the volume had reached 634.25 billion cubic meters, or 81.05%.

Conagua says the system is on track to reach its maximum capacity for the year by Oct. 31 (the date rainfall is expected to drop to near zero in its area of ​​influence), projecting 98% capacity.

With reports from La Jornada, Excelsior, N+, UnoTV and Milenio

World.title: MND Local: From Puerto Vallarta to Punta de Mita, 4 stories of a region in transition
World.content:
Puerto Vallarta and the surrounding region are undergoing rapid change. However, with new investment and infrastructure comes mounting pressure on public services, transportation, housing and the coastline.

In this week’s roundup, we examine questions surrounding the municipality’s growing payroll, the deeper forces behind Vallarta’s worsening traffic, the long-awaited Amado Nervo Bridge, and the continuing debate over development at Punta de Mita.

Questions raised over Vallarta’s growing municipal payroll

Puerto Vallarta’s municipal government is facing questions over the size and cost of its workforce after independent councilor Melissa Madero presented an analysis of the city’s 2026 payroll.

According to reporting by Urritia Comunica, Madero stated the municipal council originally approved 2,707 positions for 2026. Her review of current records alleged there were 3,375 active positions, 668 more than authorized, representing an additional cost of more than 151 million pesos (US $8.8 million).

She also pointed to what she described as 778 unauthorized positions, including assistants, coordinators and other administrative roles, with an estimated annual cost of nearly 180 million pesos.

Perhaps more striking is the contrast she drew between administrative staffing and the city’s operational services. Madero alleged that positions have increased in areas connected to the mayor’s office while other departments responsible for services such as public safety, parks, gardens and municipal infrastructure face staffing and resource pressures.

Madero says she intends to take the matter first to the municipal comptroller and, if necessary, to Jalisco’s Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office.

Although only allegations, the questions are significant.

As Puerto Vallarta spends heavily to keep pace with a rapidly growing city, residents have every right to ask where their municipal money is going, and whether the bureaucracy is growing as quickly as the services people actually depend on.

Vallarta’s traffic problem is about more than cars

If it feels like there are more cars on Puerto Vallarta’s roads every time you leave the house, you’re not imagining it.

Traffic congestion has become one of the city’s defining daily frustrations, with a road network that was never designed for the population and development Vallarta is now supporting. New housing construction and the sheer number of people moving around the metropolitan area are putting additional pressure on already limited routes.

But there’s another part of the story that doesn’t always get enough attention: Who’s living here, and where?

The cost of living in Puerto Vallarta, particularly housing costs, has risen sharply in recent years. For many local workers, remaining in the city is becoming increasingly difficult. As rents push people farther from the center, some workers who once lived close to their jobs are now commuting from places such as Ixtapa, Las Juntas, El Colorado, Bahía de Banderas and farther afield.

That means more vehicles on the road. Not necessarily because more people suddenly decided they wanted a car, but because the geography of everyday life changed, thereby creating a need for one. At the same time, Puerto Vallarta continues to attract new residents, businesses and visitors, adding to demand for roads that were already struggling.

So, the traffic problem isn’t simply about too many cars. It’s another symptom of a city trying to figure out how to accommodate growth without pricing the people who keep it running out of the places where they work.

The still not-quite-ready-yet bridge

For anyone who regularly crosses between Puerto Vallarta and Bahía de Banderas, the Amado Nervo Bridge has become something of a local obsession. And this week, there was another reminder that while the long-awaited connection is getting closer, it isn’t ready for prime time just yet.

The bridge crosses the Ameca River, connecting the Ixtapa area of Puerto Vallarta on the Jalisco side with San Vicente in Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit. When completed, the roughly 2-kilometer project is expected to cut travel times between the two municipalities by about 25 minutes and accommodate thousands of vehicles each day.

Construction is now reported to be about 90% complete, with an opening currently expected later this year.

But that hasn’t stopped some drivers from attempting to get onto the new connection. It is easy to understand the impatience. The Ameca River has long been a bottleneck for a metropolitan area that has grown dramatically on both sides of the bay.

The new bridge won’t solve every transportation problem facing Vallarta and Bahía de Banderas. But once it finally opens, it’ll give commuters another option and, perhaps more importantly, provide a much-needed piece of infrastructure for a region that’s been growing faster than its roads can handle.

Punta de Mita’s coastline is the latest development battleground

The fight over development in Punta de Mita and its coastline isn’t going away.

Last week, the Committee of Punta de Mita and environmental groups called on authorities to move beyond announcements and actually remove the rock barrier at Playa Las Cocinas and begin restoring the affected beach.

The demand follows recent statements from Environment Secretary Alicia Bárcena regarding the site. Local environmental groups say the issue now is what happens next.

Will authorities follow through with restoration rather than simply declaring that action is being taken?

The dispute is part of a larger conversation playing out across Riviera Nayarit. Development has transformed Punta Mita and its surrounding communities into some of the region’s most valuable real estate, but the coastline itself remains a public and environmental resource.

The latest demands from Punta de Mita residents and environmental groups show that the argument isn’t simply about one project or one stretch of beach. It’s about what happens when a coastline becomes extremely valuable, and who gets to decide how much of it can be changed in the name of development.

World.title: United adds direct US flights to Chiapas and Los Cabos starting in October
World.content:
United Airlines will expand its connectivity between Mexico and the United States with two new direct routes launching in late October, including Houston–Tuxtla Gutiérrez and Washington Dulles–Los Cabos.

In addition to expanding flight options, the new routes align with the Tourism Ministry’s goal of connecting Mexican destinations to high-value source markets, diversifying arrival options for visitors, and driving economic benefits for host communities.

The first direct US flight to Chiapas in a decade

Starting Oct. 28, United will operate three weekly flights between the two destinations — on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays — using Embraer E175 aircraft.

The flight will depart from George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston at 9:50 a.m. and arrive in Tuxtla Gutiérrez’s Ángel Albino Corzo International Airport at 12:45 p.m. The return flight will take off from the Chiapas capital at 1:35 p.m. and land in Houston at 4:19 p.m.

With this new service, Chiapas will regain a direct connection to the U.S. for the first time since 2013.

The route will facilitate U.S. and international access to destinations in the southern state of Chiapas, such as San Cristóbal de las Casas, Palenque, Sumidero Canyon and the Lacandon Jungle.

México amplía sus conexiones con el mundo. 🇲🇽✈️🌎 Con nuevas rutas aéreas, fortalecemos la conectividad de nuestros destinos, acercamos a más viajeras y viajeros y abrimos nuevas oportunidades para el turismo y el desarrollo económico del país. Cada nueva conexión impulsa la… pic.twitter.com/GLI91OhzuK — SECTUR México (@SECTUR_mx) August 27, 2026

Washington Dulles – San José del Cabo

This route will operate on Mondays, Thursdays, Saturdays and Sundays starting Oct. 28, although the company plans to increase the frequency to a daily flight during the peak-demand period in December.

The departure flight will leave Washington Dulles at 8:30 a.m., arriving in Los Cabos at 12:08 p.m. The return flight will depart from San José del Cabo at 1:20 p.m. and arrive at Washington Dulles at 7:58 p.m.

The route will strengthen Los Cabos’ air connectivity with the U.S. East Coast market — a key source of international tourists for the Baja California Sur destination.

These new routes will join planned winter seasonal services, including Vancouver-Mazatlán with Air Canada and Puebla-Chicago O’Hare with Volaris.

With reports from Northern Virginia Magazine and Grupo Aeroportuario de Chiapas

World.title: Sheinbaum touts Mexico’s trade position amid US tariff talks: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🕯️ Sheinbaum addresses Atizapán family murders: The president called the killing of musician Jonathan Meléndez, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker a “very sad, terrible situation.” She noted that two alleged perpetrators had been arrested and said the motive for the crime was a dispute between two families.

🏭 Mexico seeks lower US tariffs: Sheinbaum said her government is working hard to secure a better agreement with the Trump administration on tariffs affecting Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles. Her remarks came after Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday.

💬 Sheinbaum discusses politics and AI with Petro in CDMX: Sheinbaum said former Colombian president Gustavo Petro spoke to her about a book he is writing on attempted influence over elections by “the international right.” She said they also spoke about artificial intelligence and its potential impacts. During the meeting, Sheinbaum said she outlined Mexico’s political context and invited the leftist politician to return for a talk at a federal historical institute.

Why today’s mañanera matters

A multiple homicide case and the United States’ trade barriers were among the significant issues President Claudia Sheinbaum spoke about at her Thursday morning press conference.

Official statistics — disputed by some — show that homicides have declined significantly during the term of the current government, but, violence remains a major problem in Mexico, where, on average, more than 48 people were murdered on a daily basis in the first seven months of 2026.

The killing of four people in a México state apartment this week has attracted more attention than many other homicides as one of the victims was a well-known musician.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s comments about her meeting on Wednesday with Gustavo Petro, who served as the first leftist president of Colombia until his four-year term ended last month. As president, Petro held face-to-face talks with Sheinbaum on several occasions, including at Mexico’s National Palace in December 2024.

Sheinbaum comments on multiple homicide in México state

A reporter asked Sheinbaum about the murder of a family in Atizapán de Zaragoza, a municipality in México state that is part of greater Mexico City.

Jonathan Meléndez, keyboard player with the well-known band Camilo Séptimo, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker were found dead on Tuesday in an apartment in an affluent area of Atizapán. A golden retriever was also found dead in the apartment.

Sheinbaum said she was briefed on the case on Wednesday.

“It’s a very sad, terrible situation,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that arrests have been made in connection with the crime. Authorities on Wednesday reported the arrest of two men who are alleged to have committed the murders.

Sheinbaum said that the murders were related to a dispute between two families. She also said that the México state government is supporting relatives of the victims and that the federal Interior Ministry is also ready to provide assistance.

Mexico seeks reduction of US tariffs on steel, aluminum and vehicles

Asked about the meeting on Wednesday between Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard and U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Sheinbaum said her government is working very hard to reach an agreement with the Trump administration that results in a reduction of the U.S. tariffs that currently apply to Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

“There is ongoing dialogue,” she said, noting that Ebrard is a frequent visitor to Washington, D.C.

“… We’re seeking the best possible agreement for Mexico,” Sheinbaum said. “… We’re doing well and we hope to be able to reach a beneficial agreement.”

Sheinbaum reiterated that Mexico is among the “best-positioned countries” in terms of trade with the United States, as its exports — most of which enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA free trade pact — are subject to lower tariffs than those from other nations.

“The majority of [Mexican] goods that are exported to the United States don’t have tariffs, but we want an even better agreement on steel, aluminum and automobiles,” she said.

Sheinbaum summarizes her meeting with Gustavo Petro, former president of Colombia

Asked about her meeting in Mexico City on Wednesday with Gustavo Petro, Sheinbaum told reporters that the ex-president of Colombia spoke to her about a book he is writing.

She said that Petro, in the book, “touches on some issues that we’ve spoken about here.”

“But obviously it’s from his perspective,” Sheinbaum said. “… It has to do with the use of digital platforms [e.g. social media] to externally influence election results.”

She said Petro is writing about how the “international right” has organized itself to exert influence in different parts of the world.

Acabo de salir de hablar con la presidenta de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos, @Claudiashein pic.twitter.com/e9msOf0CZd — Gustavo Petro (@petrogustavo) September 2, 2026

Earlier this year, Sheinbaum agreed with a reporter who suggested that an “international media” campaign designed to “impose narratives in Mexico” was taking place.

“There are a lot of people who have come to an agreement. This international right-wing movement we talk about moves in many places in the world and there are a lot of people who are betting on the defeat and failure of the Mexican government for ideological reasons and for political reasons,” she said on May 13.

On Thursday morning, Sheinbaum said that Petro is also writing about artificial intelligence and “the impact it could have at a national and international level.”

“We spoke about that, about the reflection he’s making in his book [and] I spoke to him about Mexico,” she said.

“[I told him that] our perspective is very different because here there is a large majority of Mexican people who support the transformation and the results we’ve achieved, and the people are happy with the work the government is doing,” Sheinbaum said.

“… They were some of the issues we spoke about,” she said, adding that she had invited Petro to return to Mexico to speak at the National Institute of Historic Studies of the Revolutions in Mexico.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: How to move money into Mexico from abroad without losing a bundle
World.content:
Most foreigners who relocate to Mexico arrive with most of their liquid assets sitting in a bank outside of Mexico’s borders. Before long, they are wondering about the best ways to move money from there to here to fund everyday expenses.

Whether it is money for rent and groceries, or a big-ticket item like a car or real estate, finding the most economical way or ways to move money across borders is not necessarily intuitive.

Below are the best — and worst — ways to accomplish this boring but necessary task.

Factors to consider before choosing a money transfer method

If you’re new to living abroad and have never done a cross-border money transfer, it is natural to feel fear and uncertainty about the safety and reliability of the transaction. And that is before you even consider cost.

The truth is, there is no “one size fits all” best method for moving money across borders. The best option depends on three things. How much you need to transfer? How soon you need the money? In what form do you want the funds?

The best ways to move small amounts across borders

When you have no bank account in Mexico and only need to access small sums from a foreign bank account, a Mexican bank ATM is your best option.

At a Mexican ATM, two different fees are applied to cash withdrawals. The first is a “convenience” fee, which ranges from 30 to 200 pesos per transaction. The second is the exchange rate commission applied when converting money from your home country’s currency to Mexican pesos.

As a non-bank customer, it is wise to test out different brands and locations. BBVA and HSBC tend to charge larger transaction fees to out-of-network users, while fees from Banorte and Santander are typically lower. Even within the same bank, ATMs in touristy areas often have higher fees than those in non-touristy neighborhoods.

While the ATM’s convenience fee cannot be avoided (though some U.S. banks will refund them), foreigners can avoid exchange rate markups at Mexican ATMs that can reach 6%. To protect yourself, always decline the Mexican bank’s conversion rate when withdrawing funds. The transaction will still process, but at your foreign bank’s exchange rate, which is almost certainly better.

In addition, take care to avoid standalone ATMs that are not tied to major banks, such as those in convenience stores, gas stations and other public venues. These are easy for criminals to tamper with and can also apply exorbitant fees.

How to move large sums across borders

Because the daily limit on ATM withdrawals in Mexico is about 11,000 pesos (US $645), there are times when this method will not meet your needs. For transfers exceeding ATM limits — such as US $1,000 to US $50,000 — electronic transfers (also called EFTs or ACH transfers) are the most cost-effective option.

Money transfer specialists like Wise, Remitly, Revolut and others handle a large volume of these transactions. But they are not all the same.

Transaction fees and wait times from one provider to the next vary widely, so it pays to shop around. While Wise can move US $1,000 to Mexico in seconds, with Remitly it could take three to four days. Exchange rate markups with these services can range from 0.8% to as much as 3% over the mid-market rate.

In addition, while most who use these services have a Mexican bank account to receive the funds, some providers like Western Union or Remitly allow senders to pick up cash at Mexican retail chains like Oxxo or Walmart. Others give customers the option to send money to a mobile wallet.

Besides helping foreigners living in Mexico access their funds in overseas banks, these service providers also handle a large share of the nearly US $62 billion in annual remittances sent home by Mexicans working abroad.

In rare cases when a foreigner might need to move an even larger sum of money to Mexico — such as US $500,000 for a home purchase — a standard money transfer service may not suffice.

Among top specialists, platforms like OFX and Wise can accommodate high-value transactions of this size. Even when they do, it is common to experience longer wait times.

International wire transfers

In these cases, the most reliable option is an international bank-to-bank wire.

International wires use the SWIFT payment system and a unique code for each banking institution, ensuring funds reach the correct destination. They may also require a phone call to verify the sender’s identity.

This method is considered the safest of all, though keep in mind that international wires may take several days to reach the destination bank. Additionally, traditional banks add big exchange rate markups (2% or more) and fees (up to US $50) on international wires.

Due to these shortcomings, international wires only make sense when an ACH transfer does not satisfy your needs, or when you insist on having a person assist you for peace of mind.

How to lose a lot of money while moving it into Mexico

Convert physical cash you carried to Mexico

This old-school method of moving cash across borders carries some of the highest commissions. At money changers in Guadalajara, exchange rate markups can reach 5%. At a kiosk inside the arrivals hall of an international airport, it is even worse, with markups reaching 10% to 20% over the spot exchange rate. These places tend to target desperate travelers and should be used only in an emergency.

Choose a money transfer service without comparing fees first

Because quality and reliability are a moving target with money transfer specialists, it pays to collect multiple quotes and periodically check customer reviews. That said, some providers routinely fall short, hitting customers with 3% or higher fees, such as PayPal and its subsidiary, Xoom.

Fail to manage exchange rate risk

For anyone who needs to send large sums of money to Mexico with an uncertain time horizon, managing exchange rate risk is critical. In the case of a foreigner buying Mexican property with funds sourced from abroad, if the peso strengthens against your home currency while you wait months for paperwork to finish, you could end up paying tens of thousands more than intended.

Fortunately, there are now services for this, too.

With MexEdge, it is possible to purchase a forward contract for a fee of about 1% that locks in the current exchange rate for up to two years. While forward contracts do not make sense for small transactions, the savings can add up on larger ones.

Conclusion

No matter which service you use, U.S. citizens should know that banks and money transfer services are legally obligated to report cross-border transfers exceeding US $10,000 under the Bank Secrecy Act. The law applies to U.S. financial firms as well as foreign banks with branches in the U.S. to combat money laundering.

For foreigners living in Mexico without a local bank account, many of the best money transfer options will not be available. It is a key reason to consider opening a local account, which will be the topic of the next article in the “Mexico and My Money” series.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: IHG Brings Its voco Brand to the Cancun Lagoon Side
World.content:
Mexico · TRAVEL

Key Facts — What happened IHG will convert a former Real Inn into a voco hotel in Cancun, two Mexican trade outlets reported.

— How big The hotel has 160 rooms with views of the Nichupte lagoon.

— Location It sits at kilometre 5.5 of Cancun’s hotel zone.

— What comes next Opening is scheduled for October 2026; the hotel was not yet open as of early September.

— The catch The hotel is on the lagoon side, not the beach side.

IHG Hotels & Resorts will open a voco hotel in Cancun in October 2026. The property, a former Real Inn, overlooks the Nichupte lagoon.

IHG Brings Its voco Brand to the Cancun Lagoon Side. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

IHG Hotels & Resorts will bring its voco brand to Cancun with a 160-room hotel on the Nichupte lagoon. The property, a former Real Inn, is set to open in October 2026.

IHG Announces voco Cancun

IHG Hotels & Resorts will open a voco hotel in Cancun, Mexico, in October 2026. The Mexican trade outlet REPORTUR reported the news on 3 September 2026.

The hotel will occupy the former Real Inn building at kilometre 5.5 of Cancun’s hotel zone. It will have 160 rooms with views of the Nichupte lagoon.

A Second Source Confirms the Details

REPORTUR is not the only outlet on this story. Quintafuerza.mx reported the same 160-room count, location, and October opening on 31 August 2026, citing local outlet Novedades de Quintana Roo.

That second report also said the conversion should create about 100 new jobs. Two Mexican outlets now agree on the hotel’s size, site, and timing.

What Is voco?

voco is an upscale hotel brand within IHG’s portfolio, often used for converting existing hotels. It sits above midscale brands but below IHG’s luxury names.

IHG’s own materials describe voco hotels as offering a warm, distinctive style at a premium level. The brand has grown quickly since IHG launched it in 2018.

Location and Lagoon Views

The hotel overlooks the Nichupte lagoon, an inner lagoon opposite the Caribbean-facing beaches. Guests will see water, but not the open sea.

The lagoon side offers a different experience from the beach side. It sits closer to Cancun’s mangrove ecosystem and away from the busiest beach strip.

Former Real Inn Building

The building previously operated as a Real Inn, a midscale hotel brand. Both REPORTUR and Quintafuerza.mx report that it will now run under the voco flag.

REPORTUR said the property was “previously known as Real Inn.” It will now operate under the voco name from IHG Hotels & Resorts.

IHG’s Own Announcements

IHG did announce this Cancun conversion, contrary to an earlier claim in this article. A 2025 IHG press release listed a 160-room, lagoon-view voco for Cancun as part of a six-hotel Mexico deal.

That original release projected a 2027 opening for the wider group of hotels. The October 2026 date now reported by REPORTUR and Quintafuerza.mx suggests this property is opening ahead of that broader schedule.

Opening Timeline

The hotel is scheduled to open in October 2026, per REPORTUR and Quintafuerza.mx. As of 3 September 2026, it was not yet open.

Neither outlet gave an exact calendar date within October. Travelers planning October trips to Cancun should confirm the exact date closer to the time.

Target Guests

The hotel will target both business and leisure travelers, according to REPORTUR. It called the property an option for those visiting for work or rest.

The lagoon location may appeal to travelers seeking a calmer setting. It remains close to the hotel zone’s main attractions.

Global voco Expansion

voco is growing fast worldwide. TOPHOTELNEWS reported on 28 August 2026 that the brand has had “a slew of openings around the world,” including in Asia Pacific.

IHG has also signed a voco hotel for Karjat, in India’s Maharashtra state, under a separate 2026 announcement. That shows the brand’s expansion beyond Latin America.

No Investment Details

No investment figure has been reported for this project. Neither REPORTUR nor Quintafuerza.mx mentioned any cost, budget, or room rate.

The absence of financial details is normal for early hotel-conversion news. Such figures often emerge later, closer to a property’s opening.

What This Means for Cancun

Cancun’s hotel zone will gain a new upscale option once voco opens. The brand adds variety to IHG’s growing presence in Mexico.

Converting an existing building is generally faster than new construction. It also gives the property a fresh identity under a different brand.

Nichupte Lagoon vs. Beach

The hotel faces the lagoon, not the ocean, so it has no direct beach access. Guests would need to cross the hotel zone to reach the sand.

The lagoon still offers water views and a different, quieter setting. That may suit travelers who prioritize calm over beachfront convenience.

Cancun’s Hotel Zone

Cancun’s hotel zone is a narrow strip of land between the Caribbean Sea and the Nichupte lagoon. Most large hotels there face the ocean side.

A voco hotel on the lagoon side is less common than a beachfront property. It gives IHG a foothold in a quieter part of the same strip.

IHG’s Wider Push in Mexico

The Cancun voco is one of six hotels IHG has signed for conversion to the voco brand in Mexico. The others are planned for Guadalajara, Ciudad Juarez, San Luis Potosi, Torreon, and Nuevo Laredo.

That six-hotel plan shows IHG betting on conversions, not just new builds, to grow voco in Mexico. Cancun appears to be moving fastest among the group.

Future of the Property

The former Real Inn will finish its rebrand to voco around the October 2026 opening. Until then, it is not operating under the voco name.

Travelers should wait for an official date before booking around the opening. Details may still change before the hotel welcomes its first guests.

Sources and Verification

This article draws on REPORTUR, Quintafuerza.mx (citing Novedades de Quintana Roo), IHG’s own 2025 and 2026 press releases, and TOPHOTELNEWS. All confirm the core details of this project.

An earlier draft cited Construction World for the Karjat, India voco news. That citation could not be confirmed and has been removed.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will the voco Cancun hotel open?

The hotel is scheduled to open in October 2026, according to REPORTUR and Quintafuerza.mx. As of early September, it was not yet open.

Where is the voco Cancun hotel located?

It sits at kilometre 5.5 of Cancun’s hotel zone. The hotel overlooks the Nichupte lagoon.

What was the building before?

The building previously operated as a Real Inn hotel. It will now run under IHG’s voco brand.

Is the voco Cancun project confirmed by more than one source?

Yes. REPORTUR, Quintafuerza.mx, and IHG’s own press releases all describe this Cancun voco project.

Sources: REPORTUR; Quintafuerza.mx (Novedades de Quintana Roo); IHG Hotels & Resorts; TOPHOTELNEWS.

World.title: Grupo Sura Shares Surge to Fresh Highs in Bogota
World.content:
Colombia · MARKETS

Key Facts — What happened Grupo Sura shares rose 3.87% on 1 September 2026, then another 5.12% in the next session, Colombian outlets reported.

— How big The stock closed at 62,840 pesos (US$19.89) on 1 September, then climbed to about 65,700 pesos.

— The catch That price sits above the 63,940-peso high of 30 January that data providers had listed.

— Who it hits Grupo Sura is a Colombian holding company for insurance, pensions, and financial services across Latin America.

— What comes next No source gives a confirmed reason for the rise, and small price gaps remain between different data pages.

Grupo Sura shares jumped in two straight Bogota sessions, and Valora Analitik called the close a record. The available price data backs that up, showing a close above the previous January high.

Grupo Sura Shares Surge to Fresh Highs in Bogota. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Grupo Sura shares jumped again in Bogota, and Valora Analitik called the close a record. The available price data backs that up: the close topped the previous high from January.

A Two-Day Jump in Bogota

Grupo Sura shares rose 3.87 percent on 1 September 2026, closing at 62,840 pesos (US$19.89) a share. Investing.com reported that Grupo Sura was the best performer on the Colcap index that day.

The Colcap index itself gained 1.86 percent that same day. Grupo Sura led a broadly positive session for Colombian shares.

A Bigger Jump the Next Session

In the following session, Grupo Sura shares climbed a further 5.12 percent, according to Colombian outlet Valora Analitik. The outlet said the shares had closed at “historic highs” for the stock.

Valora Analitik’s report did not give an exact peso price. A separate market-data page, La República, showed a close of about 65,700 pesos (US$20.80) for that same move.
