World.title: Plié toasts a decade of dance
World.content:
Mercy performed by Complextions Contemporary Ballet, choreographed by Dwight Rhoden with music by Phil Kline, Michael Murray, Mendelssohn & Hans Zimmer, was among the highlights at Plie for the Arts’ Amalgamation Global Gala at The Little Theatre on Saturday, August 29, 2026. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

It was an evening of elegance, artistry, and celebration inside The Little Theatre on Saturday as Plié for the Arts marked its 10th anniversary with the Jamaican leg of its Amalgamation Global Gala.

The formal affair, held on August 29, brought together an impressive roster of international and Caribbean dancers for the first of two nights of performances, culminating a regional tour that had already made stops in Trinidad and Tobago and Barbados.

Among the night’s major highlights was the Caribbean premiere of Love Rocks, performed by members of the internationally acclaimed Complexions Contemporary Ballet. Choreographed by Dwight Rhoden and Desmond Richardson to the music of rock star Lenny Kravitz, the piece added another memorable moment to a programme packed with world-class dance.

The evening also featured Christopher Grant of New York City Ballet; Ashley Green of Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater; Adji Cissoko and Shuaib Elhassan of Alonzo King LINES Ballet; dancers from Parsons Dance; and the Plié Caribbean Collective, which placed regional talent alongside some of the world’s leading dance professionals.

Richardson, a celebrated dancer, choreographer, and co-founder of Complexions Contemporary Ballet, was the night’s honoree and received the Icon Award, while renowned ballerina Misty Copeland served as patron of the 10th anniversary celebration.

For Richardson, whose mother is Barbadian, being recognised in the Caribbean made the occasion particularly poignant.

“This is an incredible evening. I’m just honoured and so very blessed to be here. My mother is Bajan, and I grew up with this idea of ‘Caribbean-ness’, and experiencing it really feels quite like homecoming,” he said.

Richardson also used the moment to urge Caribbean audiences to continue investing in the region’s young dancers. “Thank you all for helping to support your young talent because they are amazing. We don’t see this type of talent all the time living in the city. So those of you who have these incredible beings in your midst, please continue to support them. They need you,” he said.

That support took tangible form during the evening when three dancers — Kato Austin, Matthew Johnson, and Lauryn Rickman — were awarded scholarships to attend Complexions.

For Plié for the Arts founder and Artistic Director Marisa Benain, Saturday’s packed house was an emotional validation of a vision she has spent a decade building.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer following the first night’s performances, Benain said she was overwhelmed by how far the organisation had come.

“Just having a vision and seeing the same vision evolve and get bigger and bigger and bigger, and you can’t stop it! Plié is from my soul. There is nothing better that I want to do than do Plié,” she said.

The Kingston engagement followed successful stops on Plié’s 10th anniversary Caribbean tour. The celebrations opened in Trinidad and Tobago on August 23 at the National Academy for the Performing Arts, where the production featured the National Philharmonic Orchestra of Trinidad and Tobago. The tour then moved to Barbados for performances at Frank Collymore Hall on August 25 and 26, presented alongside the National Cultural Foundation.

Benain described the reception across the region as spectacular, but said returning home to a full house carried special significance.

“It’s been wonderful. I mean, you’re talking about going to Trinidad and then you go to Barbados and you see the reception and how they loved it. It really warmed my heart, and to come home and get a full house is very special to me. Jamaica is my home and I want that support here,” she said.

Among her personal favourites from Saturday’s programme were Caught, Ave Maria, Bolero, and Carmina. She also reserved high praise for the Plié Caribbean Collective, whose dancers she said demonstrated the world-class calibre of talent that exists within the region.

World.title: Failing families
World.content:
The data shows that “protective family factors have weakened over time” with only three in 10 students reporting that their parents understood their problems.

A growing disconnect between students and parents who are increasingly taking a more hands-off approach has triggered alarm among analysts who warn of long-term repercussions in the just-released 2026 Global School-Based Student Health Survey.

The data shows that “protective family factors have weakened over time” with only three in 10 students reporting that their parents understood their problems and just four out of 10 saying their parents know what they do in their free time, provide guidance or spend quality time with them.

The survey results were officially released Wednesday morning by Health Minister Dr Christopher Tufton in collaboration with representatives of the National Council and Drug Abuse. It showed that of the 3,058 students between grades seven to 12 who were surveyed, only 25.9 per cent felt their parents understood their issues, 39.2 per cent said their parents knew what they were doing in their free time, 42.7 per cent got guidance or advice from their parents while 40.7 per cent said their parents spent quality time with them.

The researchers in comparing the findings across 2010, 2017 and 2026 for Jamaica said fewer parents understand the problems faced by their children today than they did 16 years ago. The data showed a slide from 31.9 per cent in 2010 to 31.3 per cent in 2017 with the numbers falling even further to 25.9 per cent this year. According to researchers, in 2010, 40.4 per cent of students surveyed said their parents knew what they were doing in their free time compared to 39.7 per cent in 2017 and 39.2 per cent this year.

However, a comparison of the data gathered for parents giving advice or guidance to their children showed an 8.5 per cent decrease between 2017 and 2026. No data was gathered for 2010 for that survey question. In terms of parents spending quality time with their children, there was a two per cent decrease from 2017 to 2026 (from with 42.7 per cent to 40.7 per cent. There was no data gathered for 2010.

The surveyors have in the meantime warned that, if current trends persist, “several systemic pressures and behavioural risks will emerge across multiple areas” which will include “a greater reliance on peers and online influences meaning guidance is shaped increasingly beyond the family”. Furthermore they said “adolescents face increased vulnerability to risky behaviours including substance use, unsafe relationships, violence and exploitation and school disengagement leading to higher risks to health, safety and well-being”. According to researchers there will also be growing pressure on schools and support services as increasing cases place more demands on institutions and systems.

According to the analysts, action in the future should be guided by determining the scope of parenting initiatives to strengthen parent-child communication and help parents remain influential sources of guidance. Furthermore they said the question of how effectively parents are being equipped to recognise, prevent and respond to risks affecting the health, safety and well-being of adolescents must also be answered. Additionally, the canvassers said, it must also be established what strategies exist to strengthen parental engagement with schools to reduce reliance on educational institutions and support services.

World.title: BAILEY’S GREEK ODYSSEY
World.content:
Reggae Boyz winger Leon Bailey signing his contact with Greek giants Olympiakos FC on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, after signing from Aston Villa. .

With Reggae Boyz winger Leon Bailey moving to multiple-time Greek champions Olympiacos FC, Greece-based sports writer Nikos Kotsis says his pedigree makes him a needed addition to the squad.

Bailey, who successfully completed his medical, was presented by Olympiacos on Wednesday. He moves to Super League Greece on a permanent deal, signing a three-year contract which ends a five-year stint with reigning Europa League champions Aston Villa.

“I’m very happy to wear the red and white shirt and I can’t wait to experience the atmosphere at the Karaiskakis Stadium,” he said in a video on the club’s social media.

Olympiacos have won the Greek top flight 48 times in their history, although they finished runners-up to AEK Athens last season. The club, who will compete in the UEFA Europa League season, made the knockout phase play-offs of the UEFA Champions League last season and won the UEFA Conference League title in 2024.

Olympiacos have been busy this transfer window, signing close to 20 players. Kotsis, who writes for several Greek outlets, including Sports 24, says Bailey’s arrival is among the top and believes he can make a real impact.

“Bailey’s arrival in Greece is a move that improves the attacking midfield of Piraeus,” Kotsis said. “If the Jamaican is healthy and has no problems, he will be a player who can make a difference. A winger with rich performances at the top level and a career full of brilliance.

“At 29 years old, the absolute leader of the Jamaican national team, Bailey is in the most mature phase of his career. Olympiacos adds to its roster a pure-blooded killer of the wings, capable of breaking down any defense in one-on-one. And now we are counting down to his arrival in Athens.”

Greek Sports Journalist Kostas Lianos reported that the deal is worth £2million ($427 million) and Bailey is set to earn £1.6 million ($342 million) per year until 2029.

Bailey was thought to be staying in the English Premier League with newly promoted Hull City on the verge of securing his signature. However, the move ultimately broke down with manager Sergej Jakirovic calling it “a mess” while Bailey’s representative Craig Butler told the Jamaica Observer that they were weighing up their options with several clubs interested.

Bailey failed to secure a move before the close of the English transfer deadline on Tuesday, with reports saying that he could be off to Saudi Arabia with Al Diriyah and Al Ittihad among the clubs interested given their transfer window closes on Saturday.

Although he had another year left on his contract with Aston Villa, Bailey was told by manager Unai Emery that he wouldn’t be part of his plans for the season, despite being an active part of their preseason.

Bailey joined Serie A club AS Roma on loan last summer but cut his loan deal short after limited game time and injuries and rejoined Villa in January where he went on to make 19 appearances. He won the Europa League title and saw Villa finish fourth in the league to secure a spot in this season’s Champions League.

Bailey, who joined from German club Bayer Leverkusen for £30 million in 2021, made 163 appearances and scored 23 times in all competitions.

His best season came in the 2023-24 campaign where he registered 10 goals and 10 assists in the Premier League, one of the few players to hit double digits in both categories.

Bailey’s departure means only four Jamaican internationals will be in the Premier League this season. They are Coventry City’s trio of Ethan Pinnock, Joel Latibeaudiere and Ephron Mason-Clark, and Brentford left back Rico Henry.

World.title: Class Act: Smart Lunches for Back-to-School with Reggae Jammin
World.content:
Eleven-year-old Zachary Walker gets ready to take a bite of his mini pizza bagel. First-former or not, a fun homemade lunch like this one makes him the coolest kid in class, no contest! (Photo: Travis Muschett)

Four easy recipes and real tips for keeping lunchboxes exciting once the term settles in.

The first week of school runs on adrenaline and good intentions. By week three, though, that fades, and most parents are staring into an open fridge at 6:00 am wondering what can possibly go into a lunchbox that isn’t a repeat of Monday’s sandwich.

That’s the season Reggae Jammin was created for. The range, snappy chicken franks and juicy burgers, is designed to go from freezer to table fast; the deeply seasoned Reggae Jammin Rotisserie Chicken is ready whenever you need it, which means most of the lunch-planning work is done well before the school-week rush even starts.

“Back to school is really about routine, and routine is where a lot of parents lose steam by week two,” says Navron Henry, brand manager at The Best Dressed Chicken. “We created Reggae Jammin around the idea that a good lunch shouldn’t take a good hour to make. If the hardest part of the morning is choosing what to pack rather than cooking it, that’s a win for everybody.”

Here are four recipes that pack well, reheat well and don’t fall apart by lunchtime, plus a few habits worth building into the school-week routine now, while there’s still time before the term gets away from everyone.

Real Tips For Packing Smarter Lunches

Start the night before. Set an 8:00 pm cut-off for lunch prep. Washing grapes, slicing cucumber and portioning dry snacks into containers the night before saves 10 minutes the next morning, and keeps knifework out of a groggy 6:00 am kitchen.

Cook once, pack three times. Franks are made for batch cooking, and the rotisserie chicken pulls double duty too. Buy it for Sunday dinner and there’s enough left for lunches through the week. Grill a full pack of franks on Sunday night alongside that Sunday chicken, and half the week’s protein is already handled.

Compartments beat one hot dish. Kids eat with their eyes, so skip the single hot dish in favour of a compartmented container. Keep starches, fruit and protein in their own sections and there’s no chance for anything to go soggy against anything else.

Let them dip. Kids love dipping. Instead of dressing a wrap or saucing a protein ahead of time, pack a small container of BBQ sauce, honey mustard or ranch on the side. It keeps the texture of the main dish intact and turns lunch into something closer to an activity.

Pack hot food hot and keep it that way. Anything with rice, pasta or chicken needs to go in steaming hot, not just warm, since it won’t be eaten for another four to six hours. Preheat the container first with a minute of boiling water, tip it out, then fill it right to the top. Packed that way, it stays safely hot until the lunch bell.

Freeze a juice box. A juice box straight from the freezer works as a natural ice pack and is thawed and ready by lunchtime. Bread doesn’t freeze well once it’s already been made into a sandwich, so keep those fresh each morning.

Let them choose. Handing over a little control makes all the difference. Kenya Walker, mother of nine-year-old Kennedy, sees it every day at home. “She loves picking out what goes into her lunchbox,” Kenya says. “Once she’s had some part in choosing it, the box comes back empty. I also try to keep at least one thing in there that’s familiar, because a new lunch and a new school day at the same time is a lot to ask of a child.”

Four Lunches Worth Repeating

BBQ Frank Mac & Cheese

Slice Reggae Jammin Chicken Franks into coins and toss them into a hot pan with a spoonful of smoky BBQ sauce until the edges turn crisp and caramelised. Fold them into a pot of macaroni and cheese, then pack it hot into a preheated insulated container. The franks keep their bite far better than most add-ins, so lunch still feels worth eating by midday.

Sunday Roast Fried Rice

Turn Sunday’s dinner into Monday’s lunch. Shred the leftover Reggae Jammin Rotisserie Chicken and fry it in a hot pan with day-old rice, scrambled egg, spring onion and peas. A splash of soy sauce and sesame oil ties it together, and nobody will guess it’s a repeat.

The Waffle Breakfast Burger

Grill a Reggae Jammin Burger and tuck it between two toasted frozen waffles, with a slice of cheese melted over the hot patty. It sounds unusual until the first bite, and it quickly becomes a regular request. Wrapped tightly in foil, it holds its shape all the way through the school run.

Mini Pizza Bagels

Split a bagel, spread each half with tomato sauce, and pile on sliced Reggae Jammin Chicken Franks or crumbled Reggae Jammin Burger before topping with cheese. Broil until bubbling and golden. These travel well cold or warm, making them the easiest fix for a morning with no time to spare.

In the end, between the batch cooking, the compartments and a rotisserie chicken that’s already done half the work, the goal is a rhythm that works for your household: A lunch that gets packed without a fight, eaten without complaint, and doesn’t need reinventing every single morning. That’s how you get through, and actually enjoy, the school year.

World.title: Farage pledges to slash UK energy bills
World.content:
The cost of energy “represents a national crisis,” Tice said. A cap on energy costs, expressed as the average household's bill and set every quarter by the Ofgem regulator, is set to jump 4 percent next month. The hike is principally driven by the impact of the Middle East conflict on global gas markets.

In a statement, Reform said it will remove charges levied on gas generators, including through the U.K. Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS). The ETS is designed to force down harmful greenhouse gas emissions by the most energy-intensive manufacturers.

The Labour government has made attempts to link emissions trading systems in London and Brussels central to ongoing “reset” talks between the U.K. and EU, arguing that will cut industrial costs and ease trade barriers. Both sides are targeting a deal at the next EU- U.K. summit, expected this fall.

Tice will also pledge to scrap Carbon Price Support (CPS), a tax on power generators introduced by former Conservative Prime Minister David Cameron. The Labour government under Keir Starmer had already pledged to remove CPS costs from bills from 2028.

The party said removing those two levies would shave £90 per year from energy bills.

Reform pledged to scrap other policy costs currently added to household bills, including the remainder of the Renewables Obligation scheme, used to fund legacy net-zero projects. The majority of levies associated with the scheme were shifted into general taxation by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves last year.

World.title: Meta blocks dozens of accounts protesting Kushner-linked Albanian resort project
World.content:
Social media has played a crucial role in the protest, allowing citizens and journalists to report in real time from their own accounts, mobilize protesters, and document scuffles with police. But in the last few weeks, they have found themselves hit with copyright infringement notices, content takedowns, and account suspensions and closures.

Those affected insist they have not violated any of Instagram’s rules, yet received copyright infringement notices for content they filmed or created themselves. Digital rights NGO Repro Uncensored said it has reviewed hundreds of instances and observed no violations of Instagram’s community standards.

“Most cases follow the same pattern: accounts are targeted through repeat copyright infringement reports, and platforms restrict or disable them before establishing whether the claims are legitimate,” says Martha Dimitratou, founder of Repro Uncensored. “Some accounts have been repeatedly targeted, while replacement accounts created after suspension have also been deactivated.”

A Meta spokesperson said in emailed comments that they are reviewing the actions taken against the accounts but have already restored some that were removed by mistake. The parent company of Instagram and Facebook added: “We are sorry for the inconvenience caused,” and noted that Instagram has an appeals process in cases where people think their accounts have been erroneously blocked.

While some users’ access has been restored, others face limits on going live and collaborating with other creators, or experience “shadow bans,” in which their content’s distribution is limited to others, usually without notice.

Agron Shehaj, a member of the Albanian Parliament and the leader of the opposition Mundësia party, had his account disabled on Wednesday evening. “If the rules governing account suspensions and removals are not clear and transparent, the government has every opportunity to extend its censorship into social media, causing potentially irreversible damage to society,” he told POLITICO.

World.title: Germany’s far right gains off VW troubles
World.content:
The far-right Alternative for Germany is blaming the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the EU for VW’s difficulties.

BRUSSELS — Volkswagen’s growing crisis — with the company on Thursday approving factory closures and thousands of layoffs — is turning into political rocket fuel for the far-right Alternative for Germany party ahead of Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

“The end of traditional German car plants is the result of a failed economic and energy policy,” Tino Chrupalla, AfD’s federal spokesperson, said in a statement, putting the blame on the coalition government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

VW's supervisory board on Thursday approved cost-cutting measures proposed by CEO Oliver Blume, agreeing to cut 50,000 jobs by 2030, to trim the company's product line and to shutter four German factories, the company's most radical domestic cutbacks.

World.title: SpaceX, Blue Origin ditch Macron’s space summit after White House pressure
World.content:
But the event comes at a time of strained relations between Europe and the U.S., including over space policy. Washington has lobbied against the European Commission’s EU Space Act, a proposed rulebook for space activities the U.S. sees as targeting American companies by imposing EU rules on them.

A Franco-German push to allocate more mobile-satellite frequencies to European companies, including the EU’s IRIS² satellite network, is also angering the U.S.

Brussels, Paris and Berlin do not want Europe’s satellite connectivity to depend entirely on Starlink or other U.S. providers. For Washington, however, it looks like another example of the EU using regulation and market access to build European champions at the expense of American companies.

French authorities first tried to downplay the Trump administration’s summit threat, arguing U.S. companies were still welcome.

Despite that effort, six French and space industry officials told POLITICO they were not surprised by what they describe as a classic Trump move. The U.S. administration has repeatedly tried to torpedo multilateral initiatives, ranging from global climate measures to quitting the World Health Organization, while also trying to block any European effort to reduce reliance on U.S. companies.



“This is so typical of Trump,” said a space company official who will be participating in the summit. Like others in this story, they were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Trump likes to belittle Europeans … and even more Macron, who somehow embodies European ‘leadership.’”



Lackluster attendance by U.S. companies is a short-term blow to the summit and Macron. But several space and French officials stressed it will also energize European efforts to reduce reliance on the U.S.

“The silver lining is we’re diversifying our partnerships around the world, investing in our own space industry. It’s not about uncoupling but looking at what we can do with other partners,” said a space official.



Two space industry officials also told POLITICO that Trump’s boycott will have a limited impact. Even if the four companies skip next week’s summit, the World Space Business Week taking place a week later in Paris is set, for now, to include major American space companies like Starlink and Blue Origin.

World.title: Slovakia rejects EU’s plan to lock in Russia sanctions for 12 months
World.content:
The bloc’s ambassadors could not find common ground on the proposal on Wednesday, with Slovakia being the sole holdout.

“Apparently, they have some objections. I think we have heard them before,” one EU diplomat said. They were granted anonymity to comment freely on the closed-door negotiations.

A spokesperson for the Slovak government declined to comment and shared a statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs: “Discussions on the regular six-month review of the sanctions regime … are ongoing and are expected to be concluded by 15 September 2026.”

Talks also touched on adding a further 27 individuals and companies to the sanctions list, freezing their EU assets. Technical experts on sanctions policy will now discuss the changes and extension again.

The law is one of the EU’s two main sanctions frameworks: individual and economic sanctions. Originally, both had to be renewed every six months, but the economic sanctions were extended for 12 months in June, after Orbán left office, and will now remain in force until July 2027.

Nicholas Vinocur contributed to this report.

World.title: ChatGPT soumis à de nouvelles règles européennes aux multiples angles morts
World.content:
Un espace hybride

La législation actuelle sur les services numériques, adoptée en 2022, n’avait pas prévu l’essor des chatbots. João Pedro Quintais, maître de conférences en droit à l’université d’Amsterdam, décrit ChatGPT comme une technologie “hybride” qui combine les fonctions d’un moteur de recherche et d’une plateforme en ligne, ainsi que d’autres fonctions plus proches de celles d’un éditeur de ses propres contenus.

La qualification de “moteur de recherche” pourrait limiter la capacité de la Commission à contrôler la manière dont ChatGPT gère les risques liés non seulement à la santé mentale des adolescents, mais aussi à l’intégrité des élections ou aux contenus illicites.

Demander à ChatGPT de citer les noms des candidats à une élection locale devrait désormais relever du champ d’application du DSA. En revanche, une conversation entre un utilisateur et un chatbot sur le choix du candidat pour lequel voter, au cours de laquelle des informations erronées pourraient être diffusées, pourrait ne pas être concernée.

Il a fallu un peu moins d’un an à la Commission pour finaliser la classification de ce chatbot, ses équipes s’étant heurtées à des difficultés pour déterminer dans quelle catégorie le classer. Selon les experts, sans avoir consulté le texte intégral actant cette classification annoncée cette semaine, il est difficile de savoir exactement quelles seront les obligations d’OpenAI.

La qualification de “plateforme” aurait imposé à OpenAI des obligations supplémentaires en matière de modération des contenus au titre du règlement sur les services numériques, mais elle aurait aussi permis à l’entreprise d’échapper à une part importante de ses responsabilités. Le DSA, comme d’autres législations dans le monde relatives aux plateformes, s’articule autour du principe du “safe harbor”, en vertu duquel les entreprises ne sont pas responsables des contenus présents sur leurs plateformes, ceux-ci étant mis en ligne par les utilisateurs. Mais l’avènement des chatbots soulève la question de savoir si une conversation entre une personne et une machine peut être considérée comme un “contenu généré par les utilisateurs”.

Modèles et risques

Si l’attention portée par les autorités de régulation à ChatGPT en tant qu’application grand public est récente, la Commission surveille de près les modèles d’intelligence artificielle qui la sous-tendent via son règlement sur l’IA (AI Act).

World.title: Document: EU Parliament wants tighter fossil fuel exclusions under sustainable finance rules
World.content:
Parliament and member countries disagree on oil and gas exemptions under the revamped Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation.



BRUSSELS — The European Parliament will push for stricter limits on allowing oil and gas companies to be classed as green investments under the EU’s updated sustainable finance rules, according to a document obtained by POLITICO,

The position will set up a fight with member countries, which want to loosen restrictions on fossil fuel companies under the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation — an EU law that aims to prevent greenwashing to support sustainable investment decisions.

Under the SFDR’s new “transition” category — which covers companies that are switching from dirtier to cleaner business models — lawmakers state that fossil fuel companies should only be included if they invest more in green activities than in new fossil fuel projects over a three-year period.

World.title: Trump hints US may not back UK over Falkland Islands, citing lack of Iran support
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has suggested Washington may not support the United Kingdom in the event of a future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.

 

Speaking to GB News, as reported by the BBC, Trump criticised Britain over its response to the US war with Iran, saying the country had "not been there to help me". He later acknowledged that the US military had not required British assistance.

Trump's comments come as Argentine President Javier Milei renews his country's longstanding claim to the islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina.

Milei said he would address what he called the "SACRED issue for Argentines: the Malvinas cause" in a televised speech on Thursday night.

"What cause more important and strategic for the vital interests of the Nation could there be than the Malvinas cause?", he wrote on X.

On Monday, Trump said the US was reassessing its position on the Falkland Islands, following reports that Washington could challenge Britain's sovereignty over the territory unless the UK increases defence spending.

Related UK government calls for FIFA probe into Argentina over World Cup Falklands banner

The reported move was among measures being considered by the Pentagon to encourage NATO allies to meet their defence spending commitments, the Daily Telegraph reported last week.

"I always review every position. That's just one of many," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office when asked if the United States was reviewing its position on the Falklands.

Asked whether he wanted the government of newly appointed British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to increase its defence spending commitments, Trump said: "The UK's got some problems but they'll get solved."

More than four decades after the 1982 Falklands War, the sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina remains a source of tension.

The issue resurfaced at this year's World Cup, when Argentina players displayed a banner reading "The Falklands are Argentine" after their 2-1 semi-final victory over England. FIFA later fined the Argentine Football Association $321,000 (€276,000).

The 1982 conflict began after Argentine forces invaded the British overseas territory, prompting then-UK Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher to send a naval task force to retake the islands.

World.title: 'Highly likely' Russia will escalate attacks on EU, Lithuanian minister says
World.content:
Previous deterrence measures implemented by Brussels against Russia have so far failed to prevent it from carrying out attacks against European countries, intensifying the threat the country poses to the bloc, Lithuanian Foreign Affairs Minister Kęstutis Budrys told Euronews.

 

His comments come days after Germany attributed the presence of a drone rigged with explosives near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which plays a key role in the transport of military goods, to Russia. The Kremlin has rejected these accusations.

While Budrys applauded Berlin's response to the incident, which involved handing Germany's intelligence services greater powers to counter attacks, he argued the overall response from the European Union has fallen short.

"The German services, security intelligence services, they acted really quickly, they prevented this plot, this state terrorism act, and they attributed it to the country and the services responsible for it, so it is a good sign that we have [these] capabilities," the Lithuanian minister said on Euronews' interview programme 12 Minutes with.

However, he argued that the Leipzig operation — the latest in a string of attempted attacks and suspected acts of sabotage by Russia against EU countries in recent months — showed that the measures taken so far to combat threats posed by the Kremlin were insufficient.

"For Russia, our previous responses were not enough to recalculate the whole situation, meaning they are not deterred," Budrys said.

"Russia still sees this as a sort of cheap way to increase the tension in our society, to raise questions of whether we should continue our support for Ukraine. And it means that Russia, highly likely, will escalate [its attacks] in the future."

This was echoed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday. She warned that such incidents had become the "new normal," and that the EU has to "step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better."

Visa limits and increased sanctions

Budrys referred to the recent attacks as kinetic (involving traditional weaponry) rather than hybrid, which he said refers more to disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks.

"How we are stopping it on the field is through our counterintelligence capabilities, our security and intelligence services, which must be strengthened," he said, adding that pressure must also be increased on the political and economic fronts.

After blaming Russia for the drone sabotage at the German airport last month, Berlin took steps on this front, ordering the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, terminating the contract for the Russian House in Berlin, and announcing tougher entry controls for Russian nationals.

Restricting the movement of Russians was also discussed at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland. Russian nationals lost access to multiple-entry Schengen visas in November 2025.

"It cannot be that such a huge number of Russian tourists are still travelling right now in the European Union," Budrys said. More than 477,000 tourist visas were granted to Russian nationals last year.

"How is it that citizens of a country that wages these activities can still travel here? So we have to restrict those," he added.

Following Wednesday's meeting, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said EU member states agreed to press ahead with tougher visa restrictions for Russian tourists and a visa ban for former and current members of the Russian army across the bloc.

Germany's Foreign Minister, Johann Wadephul, also vowed to increase pressure on Moscow's shadow fleet, a group of ageing tankers used by the Kremlin to evade Western sanctions on its oil industry.

Von der Leyen confirmed this week that the EU was preparing additional sanctions against Russia. These are expected to be prepared by foreign ministers at their next meeting.

"We have to increase our sanctions on Russia to show that we are not intimidated and that we won't stop our support for Ukraine," Budrys said.

World.title: France had its hottest summer since records began over a century ago, environment minister says
World.content:
France, this year, recorded its hottest summer since measurements began more than a century ago, the environment minister Monique Barbut said on Thursday.

 

Speaking at a presentation of the climate report covering the months of June, July and August, Barbut said “We have experienced the hottest summer ever recorded since measurements began in 1900.”

According to national weather agency Meteo France, the summer of 2026 recorded an average temperature of 24 degrees Celsius covering day and nighttime. It's 3.6 C above the normal average, and higher than in 2003, when temperatures were 2.7 C above normal.

A firefighter works to extinguish fires near Lege-Cap-Ferret, southwestern France, Friday, July 31, 2026. (AP Photo/Emma Da Silva) Emma Da Silva/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Firefighters relentlessly tackled wildfires through out the summer, even in normally cooler and wetter regions in the north and Brittany, as France experienced one of its driest years ever.

A historic fire devoured forests near Bordeaux and forced a quarter of a million people to evacuate from their homes.

2026 Summer was second driest since records began

Meteo France, said the summer was marked by very low rainfall, with a deficit of nearly 40%, making it the second driest since records began.

There was an unprecedented number of heatwave days, with 53 days across three episodes throughout the season, far exceeding the summer of 2022 with 33 days.

Record-breaking ocean temperatures across all of mainland France and Corsica’s coastlines were recorded, and very hot spells occurred outside the summer months, such as last May and early September, which are a sign of climate change, Meteo France added.

Millions in France, Italy, Spain, the UK and elsewhere across western and southern Europe experienced extreme temperatures this summer.

Scientists say Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, with temperatures increasing at twice the speed as the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.

World.title: Lisbon: MOTELX launches 20th edition with expanded programme and plenty of horror
World.content:
If you walk through the centre of Lisbon from this Thursday, the 3rd, until the 13th, you run the risk of hearing screams coming from a cinema: another horror marathon is kicking off with the return of MOTELX, this time in an expanded format. For the first time, the festival runs for ten days and gains extra space by adding a second venue, the Cinemateca Portuguesa, to its usual home at Cinema São Jorge. This growth has a clear reason, as there is a round-number anniversary to celebrate: the 20th edition.

 

The festival, directed by João Monteiro and Pedro Souto, has reached a respectable maturity and has been gradually gaining in importance since its first edition in 2007.

This year, the opening screening brings us the film Drag (USA), by Raviv Ullman and Greg Yagolnitzer, produced by Danny DeVito. The programme includes a tribute strand to Italian director Sergio Martino, a master of giallo, who will receive the "Master of Horror" statuette, and a celebration of the centenary of the birth of Roger Corman, a guest at the 2017 edition, who will be honoured through his widow Julie Corman, another of the festival's guests of honour. The Noémia Delgado Award, which MOTELX established last year to honour women who have stood out in the genre, is awarded to the Portuguese-Swedish filmmaker Solveig Nordlund, director of films such as Low-Flying Aircraft (2002), based on the work of JG Ballard.

The "Room Service" section, which showcases the most eye-catching films, includes titles such as Fuck My Son! (USA), by Todd Rohal, which the festival presents as "a tasteless X-rated comedy"; AnyMart (Japan), by Yusuke Iwasaki, which exposes the dark side of the Japanese world of work; and two Belgian-French co-productions: Species_,_a piece of body horror by Marion Le Correller, and The Birthday Party, by Léa Mysius, starring Monica Bellucci. These two films are also contenders for the Meliès d'Argent for best European film, alongside Bloody Tennis, by Nikias Chryssos (Germany), Bodyhackers, by Carlos Conceição (Portugal), Ferine, by Andrea Corsini (Italy), No Rest for the Wicked, by Kasper Kalle (Denmark), and The Rest of It, by María Martínez Bayona (United Kingdom/Spain/Norway).

This year's MOTELX also brings to the big screen a season devoted to horror films made in Eastern European countries under communist rule, under the title Lost in Europe: Terror Behind the Iron Curtain, with films from the USSR, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia and the German Democratic Republic. Finally, there is the opportunity to see or revisit some classics, such as the 1979 version of Nosferatu directed by Werner Herzog and with Klaus Kinski in the main role, or the infamous NEKromantik, by Jörg Buttgereit (1988), regarded as one of the most shocking films ever made.

World.title: Former French President Hollande publishes new book with plan for France, but remains undecided about running
World.content:
Former French socialist President François Hollande published his newest book on Thursday entitled "Unite. New World, New Left", in which he outlined a series of 80 proposals for France’s political future — a move widely seen as an effort to appeal to centrist voters.

 

Although his book may read like a manifesto, Hollande is keeping his cards close to his chest: stating that he will wait until December before announcing his decision about whether he will run for the country’s highest office or not.

For now, Hollande will not participate in the left-wing primary set to take place in October, instead declaring that he will assess whether a serious candidate emerges — and only then decide whether he wants to run.

The former president decided not to seek a second term in 2017, in light of very low approval ratings at the end of his five-year term. Almost a decade on, his new book states that France needs to change its methods, outlook and "level of ambition".

Hollande told French public radio France Inter on Wednesday that the current "challenge is to bring the French together", in light of the polarisation across society between "extremists who thrive on division" and a tense international situation in which France must assert its independence from the United States and Russia.

Social and economic proposals at odds with the Socialist Party

According to recent comments made by Hollande on the sidelines of the French Socialist party's (PS) summer conference, the only way to achieve this goal, is to go "beyond political parties."

Several of the proposals outlined in his book distinguish themselves from the positions held by the PS, notably with regards the Zucman tax (a plan to tax the wealth of the ultra-rich), which he dismisses as "a slogan, not a solution", as well as on pensions.

While France's Socialist party wants to restore the legal retirement age to 62, he argues in favour of setting it at 63 and then gradually increasing the required contribution period, in his book.

"The reference age has to take account of rising life expectancy and be adjusted constantly", he writes. The former head of state also wants to "cap pension indexation at 1% for five years, which would deliver savings equivalent to pushing back the retirement age by one year", and to "add a funded component", which would be overseen by the social partners.

Another new idea on the economic front, aimed at boosting take-home pay, is Hollande’s proposal to "increase net wages by cutting employee social contributions".

The resulting loss of revenue for the social security system would be offset by a levy on capital, through "a more progressive tax on financial income" and "a gradual increase in the standard VAT rate from 20% to 24%." According to the former president, this new system would "raise wages by around 10% for everyone".

To offset the impact of the VAT increase, he proposes abolishing the reduced 5.5% VAT rate, which applies to food and energy renovation work, and doing the same, though on a temporary basis, for fuel. He also wants to cut production taxes by reducing aid to businesses, as conservative presidential candidate Édouard Philippe has proposed.

What vision for Europe?

In his book, Hollande paints an alarming picture of the political status quo in the world.

"Democracies are being buffeted by turmoil, struck by the eruption of wars, planetary warming, soaring inequalities, the abuses of drug trafficking and the AI revolution. Fears feed anger, which extremists harness by sowing division."

According to the former president, "The coming year will determine more than our future. It will decide the fate of our continent and our place in the world."

On Europe, he defends France’s role within the European Union while calling for the bloc’s strategic autonomy to be strengthened in an increasingly fragmented international context.

In April, at the Printemps du Souffle breton event organised by the political movement of Brittany’s regional president, Loïg Chesnais-Girard, he warned: "We must not imagine that once Donald Trump is no longer president, the United States will return to Europe as before. That era is over."

He has also advocated a multi-speed European Union, with a small group of six to eight member states steering the "industries of the future, from digital technology to artificial intelligence", as well as defence.

Enough to win over centrists?

In an interview with Radio J, François Bayrou, president of the centrist MoDem party, said that François Hollande was putting forward "ideas that are more compatible than they used to be" with the centre.

A senior figure in the Horizons party, led by presidential candidate Édouard Philippe told AFP that Hollande "gives the impression of being a centre-right candidate. It’s an interesting positioning", while another presidential hopeful observed that he "still sounds very right-wing for a candidate of the left".

But the former president insists that he is "a socialist" and retains left-wing principles, stating in his book that he plans to "tax large inheritances and estates worth more than €10 million before tax", raise employee representation on company boards to 30%, and introduce a €10,000 grant dubbed "entrée dans la vie" for young people doing civic service.

World.title: 'Anti-fast-fashion' law: France rejects China's discrimination claims
World.content:
On Thursday, China claimed that France's new fast-fashion law, targeting major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein and Temu was "clearly discriminatory." Responding to these accusations, a source from a department linked to France's Ministry of Foreign Minister Affairs told Euronews that these claims were false.

 

A source from the French Foreign Trade and Attractiveness office said that the new law was "not discriminatory" and that it was introduced to "protect the environment and consumers."

"It is in everyone's interest, including China's, to have a peaceful relationship with France, with the European Union, and a civil trade relationship", the source said.

Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Chinese commerce ministry spokesperson Huang Ling called for the suspension of the new law, which came into force on Tuesday, after it was voted in July.

The law imposes fees on certain items — which will eventually reach almost 20 euros per garment — as part of a push to curb the industry's environmental and local economic impacts.

"China urges France to immediately halt the implementation of the anti-ultra-fast fashion law," said Huang, adding that China stands in "firm opposition to France's insistence on pushing forward this trade-restrictive measure, which is clearly discriminatory".

"Should France persist in this course of action, China will take necessary measures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises," she stated, while warning that "France will bear full responsibility for all consequences arising from this."

"No discrimination"

According to the source at France's Foreign Trade and Attractiveness Office, while there is "no discrimination", China is within its rights to raise issues around the law with the WTO.

"The fact that China feels targeted is indeed something we have heard. We are of course ready to talk to them to understand to what extent they feel targeted [...] If China has technical issues with the law, it is perfectly entitled to submit them to the WTO."

"Our Parliament is sovereign and has had its say. It has passed this law and we will fully respect its decision. This kind of threat, this challenge to a state's sovereign position, is coercion, economic retaliation. But for now, it remains a threat."

The European Commission has expressed reservations about whether France's "anti-fast-fashion" law is compatible with EU law, particularly relating to its advertising ban, which prohibits promotional campaigns and influencer marketing for fast-fashion brands.

However, according to the source, the law has undergone revisions and is robust. "We have taken the time to respond to the European Commission's concerns, to questions about compatibility with various directives. Questions remain, but we are confident",

"From our point of view, there are no outstanding issues".

For now, China has not said what retaliatory measures it could take, but Beijing has already targeted French interests in the past, imposing anti-dumping measures on European brandy in 2024, after the European Union decided to impose duties on Chinese electric vehicles.

French cognac producers were among the business actors who found themselves at the heart of a customs stand-off between the European Union and China.

What does the law say?

Under France's new legislation, what counts as "ultra-fast fashion" is determined on the basis of two sets of criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.

The per-item fee is set to vary on a set scale, according to how each product scores on both these standards.

Shein, known for its ultra-low prices and rapidly produced clothes, made a tepid Hong Kong Stock Exchange debut on Tuesday, after previous plans for initial public offerings in New York and London were derailed.

The online retailer moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022, which analysts say was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.

World.title: Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs by end of decade
World.content:
The company will carry out the biggest job cuts ever seen in the industry. Volkswagen also plans to restructure and invest in research.

German automobile giant Volkswagen announced on Thursday that it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what is set to be the biggest restructuring ever seen in the global car industry.

The company said that management and trade unions had approved a plan involving the reduction of a further 50,000 jobs, in addition to 50,000 redundancies already agreed.

"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," read a statement from the multi-brand Volkswagen group which, apart from VW itself, also includes Audi and Porsche.

The total of 100,000 cuts amount to about 15% of Volkswagen staff worldwide. The cull eclipses the 50,000 job cuts General Motors made after it declared bankruptcy in 2009.

Unions and management had publicly rowed before signing off on the plans, with the former accusing the latter of not been honest with the workforce after the figure of 100,000 possible job cuts surfaced in the media before being communicated internally.

'The motor of the entire region'

What's more, Volkswagen also said the long-term future of four major German plants – in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be guaranteed. Their closure would mark the first full-scale shuttering of Volkswagen factories in its home country.

"If this plant really were shut down, you could put a big black spot on the map," one long-term employee in Zwickau, Saxony, told the AFP news agency.

"The plant and the jobs outside it, our suppliers, they're the motor of the entire region."

Caught between US tariffs, Chinese competition and a sluggish growth in demand for electric vehicles, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble.

Company reforms to drive profitability

However, CEO Oliver Blume insisted that the decision to cut 100,000 jobs sent "a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group."

Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said that the company will take responsibility for its entire workforce, its partners, and industrial jobs worldwide [FILE: March 2026] Image: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

Volkswagen did not give details as to the timing of the cuts and how they would be distributed across the different regions where it has plants and offices, but the company said its focus will turn to North America and that it is looking to expand exports to the Global South.

The plan also includes a three-digit-billion sum investment over the coming years as VW looks to improve technologically through research and development and become more competitive.

Among the moves is a structural change that should bring about faster decision-making and a cut to the number of businesses and holdings it owns by about one-third.

World.title: FIFA blames UEFA for 'smear campaign' against Infantino
World.content:
The dispute between the two football associations reached a US court, in which UEFA is looking for permission to collect evidence for criminal proceedings in Switzerland.

World football governing body FIFA took a lash at Europe's UEFA for starting a "smear campaign" and "fishing expedition" against FIFA and its President Gianni Infantino.

This comes after a dispute between the two organizations due to FIFA's plan to sell a stake in its commercial rights, with UEFA submitting an ex parte application to the US District Court in New York to obtain testimony and documents from US-based entities. These documents will be used in potential criminal proceedings in Switzerland, where both FIFA and UEFA are based.

"While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of UEFA’s smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership,” FIFA said in a filing in US District Court in Colorado on Thursday.

FIFA's filing in Colorado was a motion to intervene, requesting that the discovery process be postponed or dismissed.



Spain won the 2026 FIFA World Cup [FILE: July 2026] Image: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu/picture alliance

According to UEFA, the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), an entity which would have had the commercial rights linked over the FIFA World Cup to investors was developed without adequate consulting FIFA's 211 member associations, as well as FIFA's own governing bodies.

UEFA threatened to boycott the FIFA World Cup should the move go ahead.

The move would have affected both the men's and the women's tournaments.

FIFA argued that the association representing European football had tried to scupper the proposal with a bid to keep European football's dominance as is.

Demands for Infatino's resignation

Pressure has been mounting on both FIFA and its President Gianni Infantino since the FFE plans were made public.

Criticism is mounting over FIFA's now-scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup's commercial rights [FILE: May 2026] Image: Ethan Cairns/ZUMA/IMAGO

This resulted in several countries saying they will not support Infantino's reelection for a fourth term as president in March 2027, when the Swiss-born FIFA boss looks for a fourth term in office.

Aside from UEFA, two other continental confederations demand Infantino's resignation.

Both CONCACAF, representing North and Central America and the Caribbean, and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) voiced their objections to Infantino. Only the South American and African confederations still support him.

UEFA also demanded a "genuinely independent external review" of how the proposal came about.

"FIFA cannot investigate itself and expect the football community to simply accept its conclusions," UEFA said.

World.title: Berlin: BER Airport Terminal 1 reopened after security scare
World.content:
Police have given the all-clear at Terminal 1 at Berlin's BER Airport following an earlier security scare and evacuation. The airport said some flights had been delayed but they were trying to avoid any cancelations.

Terminal 1 at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) was reopened on Thursday evening following an earlier evacuation due to a security scare.

"The police operation has ended," said an airport spokeswoman.

Federal police, responsible for transportation security in Germany, had evacuated BER Terminal 1 at around 5:45 p.m. after a woman reportedly told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance in her luggage.

"A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the police spokesperson told the dpa news agency.

Police then gave the all-clear at around 8:45 p.m. and confirmed that nobody had been in danger at any point.

Police initially provided no information as to the nature of the substance in question, with analysis results expected in the coming days.

Berlin: BER operations remain restricted

Despite the all-clear, operations at BER remained restricted on Thursday evening.

"Due to the police operation, we will still be experiencing delays and some cancelations until the end of the day," said the airport spokeswoman.

She advised travelers to double-check the status of their flight before arriving at BER and to keep an eye on the boards while at the airport.

"Flights were not stopped," she insisted, emphasizing that there were only delays.

"Regular operations will resume on Friday."

Various emergency services were in action at the scene as dusk fell on Thursday Image: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

What did the airport say about departures and arrivals?

The airport had confirmed the incident itself earlier on Thursday but said planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land.

Passenger processing was "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," a spokesperson said.

Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as delayed on the airport's website.

An airport press officer told DW that around 30 flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid cancellations by redirecting departures to Terminal 2.

Specialist personnel could be seen in action near the building Image: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

Trains were also impacted by the operation for a time. The city's S-Bahn train service confirmed disruptions on both lines to airport, while Deutsche Bahn also reported widespread disruptions to regional trains.

BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year.

The last comparable security disruption at the airport was in March of this year, when flights were disrupted but because of a potentially suspicious aerial object rather than a suspicious item in the terminal.

Personnel responding to the alert went through decontamination procedures on leaving the building Image: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

World.title: Israel releases first of 5 Lebanese prisoners
World.content:
Israel has agreed to release five civilians in exchange for Lebanese assistance in locating the bodies of missing Lebanese Jewish leaders killed in the 1980s. Talks aimed at ending the war with Hezbollah remain stalled.

A Lebanese man who had been held prisoner in Israel was released on Thursday, the first such handover since the outbreak of the latest conflict between Israel and Hezbollah six months ago.

The release of prisoner Malek Ghazi was confirmed by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which facilitated his handover to the Lebanese army in the city of Tyre, Lebanon.

Ghazi is to be first of five Lebanese civilians detained by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon who Israel has agreed to release.

"After their interrogation was completed, it became clear that they are civilians who are not members of any terrorist organization, have not engaged in terrorism, and there is no reason to continue holding them in Israel," read a statement from the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Lebanese officials told the AFP news agency that the four remaining prisoners are expected to be released on Friday.

Lebanon remains main stumbling block to Israel-US-Iran peace To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Lebanon thanks US for prisoner release efforts

"We will continue working until all our prisoners are released, the fate of the missing is revealed, and a complete Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory is achieved," read a statement from Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, who also thanked the United States for its "efforts exerted in this regard."

In Washington, the US State Department said the releases were the "result of US-led mediation between two legitimate governments" and were finalized during a recent trip to Israel by the US ambassador to Lebanon, Michel Issa.

"We commend the government of Israel and the government of Lebanon for demonstrating good faith through these initial steps, and hope this will serve as the basis for expanded discussions on other civilian issues," added the statement.

Dozens of Lebanese prisoners are believed to be held in Israeli detention centers, including several Hezbollah militants but also a number of civilians and at least one Syrian national, according to a list of more than 30 people compiled by the prisoners' families.

Why did Israel agree to release Lebanese prisoners?

As part of the deal to secure the release of the detained Lebanese civilians, Lebanon has been assisting in the search for the bodies of Lebanese Jewish leaders who Israel says were "abducted and murdered by terrorist organizations" during the Lebanese civil war in the 1980s.

A Lebanese official told the Associated Press that Lebanese authorities were "actively searching for the bodies of the Lebanese Jewish leaders."

The statement from Netanyahu's office described these "field operations" as "significant activity."

Could US-backed Israel-Lebanon deal lead to civil war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nevertheless, despite the prisoner release, peace talks remain at an impasse.

In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-mediated framework deal under which Israeli forces were to withdraw from southern Lebanon in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah. But little progress has been made.

Israel-Lebanon talks remain stalled

The news came as Israeli forces reportedly detained more Lebanese citizens.

Lebanese state media reported that troops had entered the town of Halta in southern Lebanon earlier Thursday and seized three men "after the force surrounded several houses and prevented residents from leaving."

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not immediately comment.

"However difficult the negotiation process may seem, we will continue to mobilize all necessary efforts to safeguard Lebanon's rights and the interests of the Lebanese people," said Lebanese Prime Minister Salam ahead of further talks in Rome, Italy, later in September. "Particularly our people in the south."

Hezbollah is not a party to the talks and insists it will not give up its weapons in any area north of southern Lebanon's Litani river.

Israeli officials, meanwhile, have said their forces will not withdraw unless the Iran-backed militia is disarmed throughout Lebanon.

World.title: Indonesia: Thousands fall sick from free school meals
World.content:
Hundreds of new food poisoning cases have been reported this week linked to President Prabowo Subianto's free school lunch program. The costly scheme has been dogged by health concerns and allegations of corruption.

More 1,700 people have contracted food poisoning in Indonesia over the past week after eating free school meals provided by the government as part of a new scheme.

At least 725 pupils and 25 teachers at a school in Lasem on the island of Java complained that they felt unwell on Thursday morning after consuming the free lunch on Wednesday.

"They had diarrhea, they were vomiting, and felt nauseous," said the school's principal. "There was a queue at the bathrooms because two of our toilets are under renovation."

Earlier this week, more than 600 students in Sidoarjo, East Java, were also taken to hospital after eating free lunch meals on Tuesday.

In two other cases on Wednesday, 49 people in the East Java city of Nganjuk and 237 in the West Sumatra region of Agam also fell ill.

Children in Sidoarjo, East Java, were taken to the regional general hospital Image: Suryanto/REUTERS

One lawmaker, Charles Honoris, put the total number of food poisoning cases linked to the free school meals scheme as high as 50,000 since, citing health department data.

"This is a failure of the ⁠system," he said.

What has caused the food poisoning?

The mass outbreaks of food poisoning have been blamed on improper food storage and late delivery of pre-cooked meals.

According to the school principal in Lasem, a food taster found that some of the grilled chicken to be distributed was "slimy" and therefore put aside.

"The kitchen operator said the food was cooked at 3 a.m. and it ​was eaten at noon," she reported.

President Prabowo's free school meals scheme

The $12.94 -billion (€11.13-billion) program, launched in January 2025, is one of President Prabowo Subianto's signature policies, intended to improve nutrition for up to 80 million children as well as pregnant and breastfeeding women.

But the costly scheme has been dogged by allegations of corruption, ​leadership changes and spate of mass food poisoning outbreaks.

It was among the first budget items to be cut back as the Indonesian government moved to counter the economic impact of the war in the Middle East and hundreds of people took to the streets of the capital, Jakarta, last week to call for it to be scrapped entirely.

How Indonesia aims to combat childhood malnutrition To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This has become a national alarm," said Ubaid Matraji, a researcher at the Indonesian Education Monitoring Network.

"The government cannot continue to treat them as mere statistical figures. Behind every number there is a sick child, a panicked family, and the state's failure to guarantee safe food."

The head of Indonesia's National Nutrition Agency, ⁠which oversees the scheme, told a parliamentary hearing that the food poisoning cases would be ​handled "seriously."

World.title: Trump's Iran strategy: Could this become a forever war?
World.content:
The US has launched fresh attacks on military targets in Iran. It wants to prevent Tehran rebuilding its destroyed capabilities, but risks triggering a sustained downward spiral of reconstruction followed by new attacks.

US President Donald Trump has given a fairly clear description of what the next phase of the Iran war could look like. The Iranians had tried to rebuild their radar equipment, Trump stated after the most recent wave of US strikes. "We waited until it was almost built, and then we hit it," he said.

On Tuesday, American forces once again attacked several targets in Iran. According to US Central Command (CENTCOM), the targets destroyed included "air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites."

'Mowing the grass'

Iran responded by firing rockets and drones at US facilities in the region. With this, the war moved on to what CENTCOM had indicated just a few days earlier could be the strategy for the next phase.

What strategy will Donald Trump choose to pursue next in the war with Iran? Image: Ken Cedeno/REUTERS

According to the news portal Axios, it was considering limited strikes, at regular intervals if necessary, to prevent Iran from reconstituting its military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz. An American government representative used a concept from Israeli security policy to describe this idea: He called it "mowing the grass."

The metaphor refers to a strategy that doesn't even attempt to promise that an opponent will be defeated once and for all. It is enough to regularly reduce the enemy's military capabilities to the point where the threat remains manageable. When the grass grows back, you "mow" it again.

Applied to the situation in Iran, this would mean the US keeping an eye on which military capabilities the enemy is reconstituting, and attacking once it crosses a certain threshold.

Successes that won't last

In the past few months, the US has scored some military successes. US forces have significantly reduced Iran's military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz, and have begun clearing Iranian sea mines.

However, these successes will not last. Tehran is repairing or procuring new radar installations, anti-aircraft positions and anti-ship missiles. US bombs could certainly destroy important Iranian positions with targeted strikes. But the knowledge and the industrial basis of Iranian military technology would remain.

This image issued by US CENTCOM shows a precision strike against an Iranian military target in July 2026 Image: US Central Command/AFP

Reconstruction can therefore be delayed, but not prevented. The US will repeatedly be confronted with the same choice: whether to accept that Tehran is regaining its capabilities, or to attack again and destroy them.

Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, warned as early as April that this development could lead to an "enduring low-intensity conflict punctuated by more intensive interventions."

Trump's belligerent warnings

The fact that the strategy of "mowing the grass" is reaching its limits is also because it was never designed for a war with a state. Israel developed the strategy to combat non-state actors like Hamas.

However, as Yacoubian pointed out in her article, the Israeli academics who initially coined the term warned that if the opponent had "statist characteristics and/or more powerful capabilities, 'mowing the grass' might become an outdated military strategy." This is clearly the case with the Strait of Hormuz.

The US needs to keep the strait reliably open. Iran, on the other hand, only needs to make people believe that the passage remains dangerous. In this way, even a significantly weakened opponent can impose substantial costs on Washington.

Keeping the vital shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz open is a priority for the US Image: Atta Kenare/AFP

Another problem for the US is that, while Washington can determine the intensity of its own attacks, it has no control over Tehran's response. This week, Trump warned Tehran not to launch a retaliatory strike, threatening that Iran would be "totally wiped out as a country" if it did.

Nonetheless, the regime in Tehran immediately fired missiles against American facilities in the region. Jordan alone reported 13 ballistic missiles in its airspace, 10 of which it was able to intercept.

The nuclear question

But Yacoubian believes that repeated American attacks carry a far greater risk. She warns that they may lead Tehran to conclude that "pursuit of a nuclear weapon" is the only way to achieve "lasting deterrence." This suggests that, by attacking Iran, the US and Israel could actually accelerate the precise development they sought to bring under control.

The Natanz nuclear facility in Iran was one of the first sites targeted by the US and Israel Image: Planet Labs

From Washington's perspective, the alternatives available to Trump don't look much better. If the president accepts Iran rebuilding its military strength around the Strait of Hormuz, he risks renewed attacks on shipping and disruption of one of the world's most important energy routes.

The consequences for the global economy are well known. In spite of the upheaval and repeated negotiations, a political agreement between Washington and Tehran has so far failed because of apparently insurmountable differences.

America's next 'forever war'?

For Trump, "mowing the grass" has domestic appeal, in spite of the uncertainty it brings to foreign policy. The US president would be able to avoid occupation, nation building and deploying large numbers of American ground troops.

At the same time, it allows him to distance himself from the so-called "forever wars" he repeatedly accused his predecessors in the White House of pursuing.

Ultimately, though, this supposed way of avoiding a forever war could become one of its own. Yacoubian describes it as a "Sisyphean attrition strategy without end." As long as Washington is not prepared at some point to accept the rebuilding of Iran's capabilities, each successful attack merely creates the justification for the next one.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Norway seizes Russian ship in Svalbard to compensate Ukraine
World.content:
Authorities in Norway have seized a Russian ship, the Professor Molchanov, on a court order sought and obtained by Naftogaz in Ukraine. Russia has protested the move, which stems from its refusal to pay Naftogaz damages.

Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014.

Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday.

Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions.

Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

Around two thirds of Svalbard is designated as national parks and nature reserves, but the coal mining settlement of Barentsburg is home to about a tenth of the archipelago's population Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance

What do we know about the Professor Molchanov ship being impounded?

The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023.

Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine, and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead.

"Russia cannot evade ​responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.

Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov, for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived.

The end of coal mining in Svalbard To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard.

"The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement.

Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo.

"Russia can demand that ​the district court reassess the case," the Justice ‌Ministry said.

How did Russia respond?

Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

"We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said.

The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint.

Is Svalbard Russia's real leverage in the Arctic? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Professor Molchanov, a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them.

"The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website.

He said that for the time being, "the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case.

Prior to the war in Ukraine Barentsburg was also home to Ukrainian and other foreign nationals. But most have since left, Ukrainians in particular were told to accept an offer of Russian citizenship or leave. Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance

What is behind Svalbard's special status, and why is it home to the Barentsburg settlement?

Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people.

It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century.

The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa, provided they met certain conditions.

The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades.

Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago.

Edited by: Zac Crellin
