Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili said he did not understand why authorities had summoned him for questioning in the Lazare Jorbenadze death case, as he had made no specific statements about Jorbenadze and only learned of his existence after his death.

“I only learned of Jorbenadze’s existence after his death. I did not comment specifically on the situation involving Jorbenadze. I spoke more broadly about suicide cases that raise questions. Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze should be here instead of me, because Garibashvili named them, but they are not being summoned — I am. And now this has turned into nothing more than a tragicomedy,” Khukhashvili commented.

According to Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, investigators did not ask him about any other subjects during his questioning in the Jorbenadze death case. Gvaramia believes the case may serve two purposes: one could be political propaganda, while the other could involve bringing new charges against the former prime minister.

“The next step, I am sure, will be to bring new charges against Garibashvili, under the article concerning illegal wiretapping. As far as I know, investigators are currently questioning him in prison. Mdinaradze and Kobakhidze should themselves be concerned about such allegations if they are true, although Garibashvili should also provide further explanations,” Gvaramia said after the questioning.

Death of Georgian human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze

World.title: Social assistance is shrinking in Azerbaijan: Is poverty falling, or are low-income people losing support?
World.content:
Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

In Azerbaijan, the authorities have raised the income threshold for classifying families as low-income. It would be logical to expect this to increase both the number of people receiving assistance and the amount of support they receive. However, official statistics show the opposite trend: both the number of families receiving targeted state social assistance and the amount paid per person are falling.

According to the State Statistics Committee, as of 1 July, 349,300 people from 78,900 families received targeted social assistance. A year earlier, the system covered 353,300 people from 80,300 families. This means that over the year, the number of families receiving assistance fell by 1,400, while the number of recipients fell by 4,000.

The decline becomes even more striking over the longer term. In mid-2017, 498,400 people received this type of assistance. Over nine years, that figure fell by 149,100, or about 30%. Meanwhile, the country’s population increased during the same period.

These figures raise an important question: have the incomes of low-income families increased enough for them to no longer need social assistance, or has the system stopped reaching some people who still need support?

The income threshold has risen, but social assistance has fallen

Targeted social assistance is not a fixed payment. The authorities calculate it as the difference between the needs-based threshold for all family members and the family’s average monthly income. The calculation takes into account income from the previous 12 months.

In 2025, the needs-based threshold stood at 285 manats (approx. $167.65) per person. In 2026, the authorities raised it to 300 manats (approx. $176.50), an increase of 5.3%. Despite this, the average payment per person fell from 100.37 to 97.94 manats (approx. $59 to $57.70). In nominal terms, the payment fell by 2.43 manats (approx. $1.43), or 2.4%.

Applying the current formula to the average figures suggests that the system calculated recipients’ average monthly income per person at 184.63 manats (approx. $108.60) in 2025 and 202.06 manats (approx. $118.90) in 2026. This represents a nominal increase of 9.4%. Mathematically, the lower payments reflect the fact that, according to the system’s calculations, family incomes grew faster than the needs-based threshold.

However, these figures do not prove that the financial situation of all low-income families has improved. The average for families that remained in the system in mid-2026 is being compared with the average for families that received assistance a year earlier. Families whose payments stopped or whose applications were rejected no longer form part of the new average.

Our calculations, based on official data, show that total monthly payments to recipients fell from about 35.46 million (approx. $20.86 million) to 34.21 million manats (approx. $20.12 million). The government therefore reduced its monthly spending on this group by about 1.25 million manats (approx. $735,300), or 3.5%, in nominal terms.

The assistance has lost even more purchasing power

According to July 2026 data, annual inflation stood at 5.8%, while food inflation reached 7.3%. After taking price rises into account, the purchasing power of the 97.94-manat payment fell by about 7.8% compared with the 100.37-manat payment a year earlier. If we consider only food price increases, the decline approaches 9%.

After receiving assistance, the system brings a family’s calculated income per person up to the needs-based threshold of 300 manats. However, this represents only a 5.3% increase from last year’s level of 285 manats. That increase falls short of overall inflation and especially of food price growth. As a result, even the minimum income of families that remain in the social assistance system has not increased in real terms.

The number of people receiving assistance is not the number of people living in poverty

The State Statistics Committee’s final data for 2025 put the poverty line at 286 manats (approx. $168.20) and the poverty rate at 5.2%. With a population of 10.26 million, this amounts to roughly 534,000 people.

At the end of the same year, 336,000 people received targeted social assistance, or about 3.3% of the population. The authorities use different methodologies and reporting dates to calculate these figures, so we cannot directly compare them. Nevertheless, the gap of about 198,000 people clearly shows that the number of assistance recipients cannot serve as a measure of poverty in the country.

Moreover, earning less than 300 manats does not in itself qualify a person for assistance. Under the rules, a family must show that factors beyond its control have caused its low income. The official criteria allow authorities to reject an application if the family owns or uses a car, has two properties of the same type at different addresses, or has carried out purchase or sale transactions worth more than 12 times the subsistence minimum over the previous 12 months. Authorities can also reject an application if an able-bodied family member has turned down two suitable job offers.

Based on the 2026 subsistence minimum, the threshold for purchase and sale transactions stands at 3,600 manats (approx. $2,118). Authorities can also reject assistance if a family spends 45 manats (approx. $26.50) or more per person each month on utilities and communications. For a family of four, that amounts to 180 manats (approx. $106) in total. The authorities also count money and gifts from relatives, as well as estimated income from a household farm or garden, when calculating family income.

These criteria may help identify hidden income and assets. However, the same rules can exclude a family with a low cash income if it owns an old car, faces high utility bills or mainly survives on financial support from relatives.

The number of pensioners is falling, while more people receive age-related benefits

Another question arises when we examine other social security figures. On 1 July 2025, Azerbaijan had 1,103,300 pensioners. A year later, the figure had fallen to 1.1 million. At the same time, the average pension rose by 10.5% to 594.4 manats (approx. $350). However, the number of pensioners fell by 3,300.

Meanwhile, the number of people who do not qualify for a labour pension but receive a 220-manat age-related benefit (approx. $130) rose from 166,200 to 177,500. We cannot say that the changes in these two groups involve the same people. However, the fall in the number of pensioners as the elderly population grows, alongside the rise in recipients of a lower benefit, requires a separate explanation in terms of access to labour pensions.

What data the government should disclose

To treat a decline in the number of assistance recipients as evidence of falling poverty, we need more than one headline figure. The Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population should report how many families entered the system over the past year, how many stopped receiving assistance, how many applicants faced rejection and why authorities rejected their applications.

The government should also report how many families failed to qualify under each criterion, including car ownership, purchase and sale transactions, utility costs, discrepancies in income data and refusal to accept an offered job. It should also disclose how many decisions authorities reviewed following complaints and what share of assistance recipients are children.

Without this data, we cannot conclude that poverty has fallen. So far, the official statistics show only this: the number of people covered by targeted social assistance has fallen, the average payment has declined in nominal terms, and its purchasing power has fallen even further.

Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

World.title: Beslan school siege 22 years on: Where does investigation stand and what did victims achieve?
World.content:
Beslan school siege anniversary

Twenty-two years have passed since the Beslan school siege, one of the most tragic events in the modern history of North Ossetia.

Commemorative events are being held across the republic, but there is still no complete clarity over what exactly happened during the attack.

“Three days in hell”: Timeline of the attack

On 1 September 2004, militants took pupils and teachers at School No 1 in Beslan hostage, including children starting their first year at school, their parents and babies who were with them.

In the first hours of the siege, the militants shot dead the adult male hostages. They held the others in the school’s gymnasium for three days, denying them water and making political demands, including the withdrawal of Russian troops from Chechnya.

The militants also demanded the presence of the then president of North Ossetia, Alexander Dzasokhov, Ingush President Murat Zyazikov, and CIS Executive Secretary and former Russian Security Council Secretary Vladimir Rushailo. None of them complied with the demand.

The North Ossetian authorities attempted to negotiate the release of the hostages, but without success. On 2 September, former Ingush President Ruslan Aushev managed to negotiate with the Ingush members of the militant group. He was allowed into the gymnasium and secured the release of around 20 women with babies.

At noon on the third day, two explosions were heard in the gymnasium.

According to some of the hostages and the official account, one of the explosive devices that the militants had placed along the walls detonated. A fire broke out in the gymnasium and the militants began shooting at the hostages.

An unofficial account, however, maintains that the explosion and subsequent fire were caused by an external strike on the school building using a Shmel rocket launcher.

This account remains disputed, with the North Ossetian and wider Russian authorities rejecting it as unfounded. FSB special forces, who were rehearsing an assault plan in a nearby village when the explosions occurred, were then urgently deployed to Beslan. Fighting with the militants ensued, during which most of the hostages were freed.

However, the death toll was still extremely high. A total of 334 people were killed in the attack, including 314 hostages and 20 members of the FSB special forces, Interior Ministry and Emergencies Ministry. Another 783 hostages were injured.

According to the official account, there were 32 militants. All were killed except Nur-Pashi Kulayev, who was detained and later sentenced to life imprisonment.

However, the criminal investigation launched immediately after the attack has still not been concluded. Relatives of the victims disputed the authorities’ official account and demanded an “objective and fair investigation”. According to some former hostages, there were more than 32 militants and some may have escaped.

There were also claims that the attackers had hidden weapons inside the school in advance and that some of the militants had previously gained access to the building by posing as workers carrying out repairs.

Commemoration ceremony in the gymnasium where the hostages were held

22 года спустя

On 1 September 2026, the Mothers of Beslan public organisation held its annual press conference.

The organisation’s leader, Susanna Dudiyeva, reported some progress in the criminal investigation, which she said had been made possible following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin two years ago, when he visited Beslan ahead of the 20th anniversary of the attack. According to Dudiyeva, Putin subsequently issued instructions to the head of Russia’s Investigative Committee, Alexander Bastrykin.

Dudiyeva told the press conference that investigators had established that there were in fact more than 32 militants and that the criminal case remained open because not all of those killed had been identified. In particular, investigators have been unable to identify one of them, a Saudi national, as the Saudi authorities have not been cooperating with Russian investigators.

The health of former hostages was one of the main issues discussed at the press conference. The Mothers of Beslan committee has successfully campaigned for victims of the attack and their relatives to receive regular social and medical assistance. A comprehensive rehabilitation programme for those affected by the attack has been extended until 2030, while funding for their medical treatment has been increased.

“I would say that rehabilitation at health resorts is going well. There are some problems and some issues, but they can all be resolved. It is particularly encouraging that the children of former hostages who were born after the attack are now also receiving rehabilitation. Almost no other victims of terrorist attacks in Russia have access to this kind of rehabilitation,” Susanna Dudiyeva said.

The question of granting victims an official legal status remains a pressing issue. The adoption of relevant legislation would open up significant new opportunities to provide support to survivors and even their children.

Elvira Tuayeva, a member of the Mothers of Beslan organisation, said the group would continue campaigning for a law establishing the legal status of victims of terrorist attacks, not only those affected by the Beslan siege but by all terrorist attacks that have taken place in Russia.

World.title: Georgian businessman, animal rights activist Tamaz Elizbarashvili begins prison hunger strike
World.content:
Activist Elizbarashvili on hunger strike

Georgian businessman, animal rights activist and outspoken critic of the Georgian Dream government Tamaz Elizbarashvili, who was detained earlier, has gone on hunger strike.

Tamaz Elizbarashvili was detained at his home after law enforcement officers searched his car and flat. The Interior Ministry said the search of Elizbarashvili’s car was carried out as part of an investigation into alleged threats and the illegal acquisition and possession of weapons.

According to his lawyer, Elizbarashvili is currently being held in administrative detention.

What is known so far?

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, Iako Siranashvili, her client was detained by law enforcement officers as he was attempting to jump from a balcony and take his own life.

Siranashvili said Elizbarashvili attempted to take his own life after seeing law enforcement officers use force against his lawyer and witnessing his children in distress.

“Tamaz Elizbarashvili was going to take his own life when he saw me being pushed into the building and beaten. When he saw his children crying and in distress, he tried to jump from the balcony. Tamaz was detained over this and charged with disobeying police orders,” Siranashvili said.

According to the lawyer, law enforcement officers tried to take her phone away when she began filming the search. She alleges that around 20 officers then used physical force against her.

“They tried to take my phone away to stop me filming the search. Anyone is allowed to film, especially a lawyer. They probably wanted to plant a weapon or some other prohibited item, but I prevented them from doing so because I was filming. Around 20 people then attacked me: they grabbed me and snatched the phone from my hands. When I resisted their attempts to take it, they twisted my arms, threw me to the ground and began kicking me,” Siranashvili said.

The lawyer said she had sustained injuries to various parts of her body and was having difficulty walking. Siranashvili said she had left the clinic of her own accord.

“My injuries are such that I can barely walk. I have difficulty moving around. My left arm is in severe pain. My hearing has also deteriorated and I have swelling around my facial bone. I left the clinic of my own accord because I did not think it was necessary to remain there,” she said.

According to Siranashvili, an investigation has been launched under Article 333 of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which covers abuse of official powers. She said, however, that investigators should also examine whether offences had been committed under Articles 364 and 365, which concern obstruction of a lawyer’s professional activities.

“What angers me most is not the fact that I was beaten, but that I was prevented from carrying out my professional duties. That is what makes me most angry, as does the fact that violence was used against a lawyer. Other articles must also be applied; the investigation cannot be limited to Article 333 alone,” the lawyer said.

She said her health had so far prevented her from attending the investigative authorities for a medical examination.

“I feel very unwell and have not yet been physically able to get to the relevant authorities. Investigators have ordered a medical examination, and I hope it will be carried out,” Siranashvili said.

World.title: Former head of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee arrested after appearing in court on stretcher
World.content:
Former Armenian revenue chief in court on stretcher

In Armenia, the arrest of former State Revenue Committee chairman Gagik Khachatryan has sparked widespread debate. He faces charges of accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. The Anti-Corruption Court is also considering cases seeking to confiscate allegedly illicitly acquired property from Khachatryan and people linked to him, including his sons.

However, the video that his lawyers shared on social media, rather than the charges against Khachatryan, has caused the biggest public outcry. The footage shows National Security Service officers carrying the 71-year-old Khachatryan, who is groaning in pain, from a bed onto a stretcher during his arrest. His lawyers said they consider the law enforcement officers’ actions equivalent to torture.

Human rights defenders and civil society representatives have also condemned the actions. They said authorities handled the transport of a person with serious health problems “improperly”, causing him physical suffering.

“No legal procedure or procedural necessity can justify violating human dignity,” experts from the NGO Disability Rights Agenda said.

What is Khachatryan accused of: all known details

The Investigative Committee said the previous day that investigators had carried out searches at the homes of the former head of the State Revenue Committee and his son as part of a case involving particularly large-scale bribery and money laundering. They also searched the offices and branches of more than 20 companies linked to them. Shortly afterwards, reports emerged that authorities had arrested Gagik Khachatryan for two months.

According to the case file, Khachatryan faces charges of:

accepting a particularly large bribe from the directors of Progress Armenia and Local Developers,

misappropriating 174 million 581 thousand drams ($482,000) in state funds during the reconstruction of the Dilijan training centre,

illegally transferring property belonging to a local university, worth 208 million 908 thousand drams ($577,000),

and laundering particularly large sums of money. The charge concerns concealing 151 million 126 thousand drams ($417,000) of illegally obtained funds.

Meanwhile, the Anti-Corruption Court is hearing a case seeking the confiscation of allegedly illicitly acquired property. The Prosecutor General’s Office is seeking to confiscate from Khachatryan and people linked to him:

193 properties, including properties in Yerevan’s most expensive central district,

89 properties in Kotayk Province,

stakes in 29 legal entities,

14 movable assets,

bonds worth $1,451,074,

a bank deposit of $147,210,

claims arising from loans worth approximately $23.1 million, 409.8 million drams (more than $1 million) and €9,800, and

7 billion 761 million drams ($49 million).

Defence lawyers and prosecutors disagree over the defendant’s health

The Prosecutor General’s Office says it conducted a forensic medical examination.

“Khachatryan has no health problems that could prevent him from taking part in any procedural actions as part of the criminal proceedings,” the experts concluded.

However, his defence team takes the opposite view.

Lawyer Yerevan Sargsyan told reporters that in June, authorities also took Khachatryan to the investigative body and then to court on a stretcher. At the time, however, the court found that his detention could pose health risks.

“They waited so long until they got the [forensic medical] conclusion they wanted. How they did it is known to them. And now they have organised the arrest in the same way again,” Sargsyan stressed.

Ombudsman’s office examines the case

On 2 September, a day after the lawyers published the video, the Human Rights Defender’s Office issued a statement. It said that the ombudsman had initiated an urgent examination of the case. A team of experts has already gone to the penitentiary to speak with Khachatryan and monitor respect for his rights.

The ombudsman’s office has also asked the relevant authorities for explanations to establish all the circumstances. After it completes the investigation and reviews its findings, the Human Rights Defender will present its position.

Comments

Human rights defender Zaruhi Hovhannisyan believes that the published photograph of the defendant on a stretcher in the courtroom is “not simply a sad scene”. In her view, the situation raises questions about the state’s attitude towards human rights:

“The photograph shows a 71-year-old man with serious health problems lying on a stretcher, completely covered, in the middle of a courtroom. People involved in the proceedings, tables, microphones and documents surround him. On one side stands the entire institutional machinery of criminal justice, organised by the state. On the other stands a person whom the system completely ignores.

The issue is not to make people feel sorry for the man lying on that stretcher, or to discuss why he ended up in court, what case he faces or how many charges he faces. The issue is that this is an extremely dangerous picture. When the state becomes accustomed to subordinating human dignity to a judicial process, it puts not only one person’s rights at risk but also the boundary that should prevent the state from gaining unlimited power over an individual. Human dignity and the prohibition of torture limit the state’s power over a person.”

Former head of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee in court on a stretcher

The NGO Disability Rights Agenda also issued a statement about the videos that Gagik Khachatryan’s lawyers circulated:

“According to the defence, doctors diagnosed Gagik Khachatryan with spinal stenosis in 2015 and implanted special devices in his cervical spine. The footage also shows him in a semi-conscious state while people were moving him.”

The organisation’s experts believe the authorities should structure the court proceedings in a way that prevents harm to a person’s health or humiliating conditions. Appropriate specialists should accompany people with limited mobility at all times. Medical professionals should supervise their movement and authorities should provide the necessary technical equipment.

“Regardless of the nature of the charges or his former position, humanitarian principles and safeguards for physical integrity must remain unchanged,” the statement says.

The organisation called on law enforcement agencies to take the following steps during further procedural actions:

rely only on impartial professional assessments,

provide the necessary medical care,

prevent any actions that cause a person unnecessary physical pain.

Former Armenian revenue chief in court on stretcher

World.title: Amnesty International: Georgia must not deport Denis Kulanin to Russia
World.content:
Denis Kulanin’s case

Amnesty International is calling on the Georgian authorities to prevent the deportation of Russian citizen Denis Kulanin to Russia, where the organisation says he faces a real risk of imprisonment and torture.

The organisation says Georgia should protect Kulanin from being forcibly returned to Russia because he has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for opposition leader Alexei Navalny. According to Amnesty International, both positions could lead to criminal prosecution in Russia.

“Denis Kulanin has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for Alexei Navalny — both actions constitute criminal offences in Russia and can lead to imprisonment. The Georgian authorities must ensure that he is not deported to Russia. Amid the harsh repression of people who oppose the war, he faces a real risk of arbitrary criminal prosecution, imprisonment, torture or other ill-treatment,” said Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s deputy director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia.

He said Georgia must uphold the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning a person to a country where they face a real risk of serious human rights violations.

“The Georgian authorities must also ensure that Denis Kulanin has an effective opportunity to seek international protection, including by allowing him to leave voluntarily for a safe third country,” Krivosheev added.

Who is Denis Kulanin?

Denis Kulanin is a Russian citizen who lived in Georgia and took part in pro-European protests. Police arrested him on 28 March 2025 during a demonstration outside parliament. The authorities accused him of smashing a police car window and sentenced him to two years in prison.

On the Orthodox Christian feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God, President Mikheil Kavelashvili pardoned Kulanin. However, because Kulanin is not a Georgian citizen, the authorities did not release him. Instead, they transferred him to the migration department.

According to his lawyer, deporting Kulanin to Russia would be both unacceptable and dangerous. While in detention, Kulanin sent a letter in which he wished Ukraine glory and peace. His lawyer says that in Russia, authorities can interpret almost any statement about the war in a way that could lead to criminal charges.

Denis Kulanin. Photo: Publica

On 30 August 2026, the Tbilisi City Court ordered Denis Kulanin to be held at the temporary detention centre run by the Georgian Interior Ministry’s Migration Department. He will remain at the centre until the grounds for his detention cease to apply or the authorities enforce the decision to deport him from Georgia, but for no longer than three months.

On 31 August, Kulanin’s lawyer was told that he would not be allowed to leave Georgia voluntarily until the Tbilisi City Court considers his deportation case.

On 1 September, Kulanin’s lawyer said the Migration Department had asked the Tbilisi City Court to deport him to his country of citizenship, the Russian Federation.

Denis Kulanin’s case

World.title: Opinion: ‘An attempt to make Abkhazia’s residents feel part of single political space with Russia’
World.content:
Abkhazia is actively preparing for Russia’s State Duma elections, which will take place on 20 September 2026. Most Abkhazia residents hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, which gives them the right to vote in the elections.

Russia will open 319 polling stations in 152 countries for citizens voting abroad. 35 of them — more than 10% — will open in Abkhazia.

Many people think this is excessive for a small republic with a population of 250,000.

One of those who objects is Akhra Bzhania, a prominent Abkhaz blogger and public figure. He believes that the “excessive” number of polling stations and the active election campaign aim to create a sense among Abkhazia’s residents that they somehow “belong” to Russia.

Akhra Bzhania: “There is a standard procedure for people with dual citizenship who vote abroad.

Usually, two or three polling stations open, plus a polling station at the consulate or embassy. That’s it.

Abkhazia cannot use its budget to cover the costs of holding a constitutional event of a foreign state. That makes no sense.

If someone argues that the Russian side is paying for the campaign, that is even worse!

Let me explain why. Fifty or 60,000 votes from Abkhazia will have no impact on the overall balance of parties in the State Duma.

This means the election campaign here must serve a different, ideological purpose — to create a sense among Abkhazia’s citizens that they share a single political and administrative space with Russia. And from there, a common state is not far away.”

I have no doubt that some Abkhaz citizens with dual citizenship care deeply about the differences between the programmes of Russian political parties. For them, State Duma elections are therefore not only a civic but also a political act.

But in that case, they can plan ahead and vote in Sochi, Krasnodar or Moscow, as Russians living in Armenia, Kyrgyzstan and elsewhere do.

Yet our entire republic is covered with banners urging people to vote for a government body of another country! We plan to open 35 polling stations, just as we do for our own presidential elections!

It seems strange to me — and not only to me — and out of line with the status of our state and the level of Abkhaz-Russian relations.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Abkhazia prepares for Russia’s State Duma elections

World.title: Breaking: Melbourne man jailed for four years for keeping woman as slave
World.content:
A man who beat a woman he kept as a slave in Melbourne's west will spend at least four years behind bars.

Chee Kit Chong, a 47-year-old Malaysian national, bashed and starved the Indonesian woman aged in her 60s between February and October 2022, while she lived with Chong and his family in their Point Cook home.

He was found guilty earlier this year of intentionally keeping a slave and assault, while his wife Angie Liaw was acquitted.

Judge Michael Cahill sentenced Chong to a total of six years' imprisonment for forcing the woman into domestic servitude and assaulting her on at least one occasion, describing the abuse Chong inflicted on her as "callous and cruel".

"You treated her as a slave," Judge Cahill told the court this morning.

"That is, you used her like property you owned."

Slavery, a federal crime in Australia, carries a maximum term of 25 years behind bars.

World.title: 'Supermodel' bull sells for $420k, smashing Australian record
World.content:
An Angus bull from New South Wales has become the most expensive beef animal ever traded in Australia, selling for $420,000 at a Central West bull sale.

Wyatt W50 was just the fourth lot to sell at Millah Murrah's annual sale near Bathurst, where bidding saw the price skyrocket past the former all-breeds bull record of $360,000.

It also surpassed the all-time beef animal record of $400,000 paid for a Wagyu heifer in 2022.

The bull was named after stud principal Ross Thompson's late father, which made the sale emotional for his family.

"I did have sunnies on, but apparently you could see [the tears] streaming," Mr Thompson said.

"He was just simply outstanding and extremely hard to fault. I did consider him the best bull, on balance, that we'd ever put in the sale ring.

"I was wondering why I was selling him by the time we got to the sale."

Auctioneer Paul Dooley said it was an exciting afternoon.

"You can hear the buzz in the crowd as the numbers go up," he said.

"It certainly speaks to the confidence in the cattle industry."

Million-dollar semen sales

Gundungarra Angus purchased the bull at Moss Vale in the NSW Southern Highlands.

In breeding terms, the bull holds genes for everything cattle farmers chase — from calving ease to strong weight gains.

"In human terms, he's supermodel-level looks," Mr Thompson said.

"He's got a pedigree that's globally very diverse and on top of that. He's just an incredibly versatile bull."

The Thompson family, pictured in 2023, has set a number of industry records over the stud's almost 60 year history. (ABC Rural: Hamish Cole )

Millah Murrah retains a 20 per cent share in the bull, and will work closely with Gundungarra Angus to manage the high demand for semen sales.

Mr Thompson said semen from the bull was already attracting interest from Australia, Canada and the USA.

"It's nice to think that people from other parts of the world are looking at Australia as a potential genetic source, so it's quite an exciting moment," he said.

" The semen revenue potential in a bull like that would go into the seven-figure mark. "

Mr Thompson said managing such a valuable animal could be stressful.

"I've got 250 [semen] units in the tank, so if he drops dead, we've got him genetically away," he said.

After a mass sell-off of cattle from drought-hit northern NSW, 2026 was tipped to be a challenging bull-selling season.

But Mr Thompson said the record-breaking bull was in a league of his own.

"You're talking about one particularly elite animal," he said.

World.title: Almost 200,000 people searched for weapons in Qld in the last year
World.content:
A hunting knife and a large machete confiscated from teenagers in Brisbane's Fortitude Valley on the same night are some of the 300 weapons seized by police since Jack's Law was made permanent.

Police have wanded almost 200,000 people and seized more than 1,400 weapons across Queensland since July last year.

Under the legislation police can randomly search people for a weapon without a warrant in a public place.

The law was named in honour of teenager Jack Beasley, who was stabbed and killed on the Gold Coast in 2019 while on a night out with friends.

A samurai sword was among the weapons seized by police. (Supplied: Queensland Police)

Police Minister Dan Purdie said police conducted 54,000 wandings in the Brisbane region and seized 300 weapons, resulting in 700 arrests and 1,400 charges.

"We'll never know what those weapons were going to be used for, but every knife, every weapon, every samurai sword is potentially a life saved," Mr Purdie said.

Police said that recent incidents include a large machete taken from a 17-year-old boy in Fortitude Valley and a hunting knife was confiscated off an 18-year-old in the same area on the same night.

Last weekend, a large machete was taken from a 15-year-old boy at a shopping complex in South Brisbane.

One in 10 people searched for weapons in Qld identified as First Nations In Queensland, police have the power to randomly stop and search people for weapons.

"Jack's Law is making Queenslanders more safe than before," Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said.

"When you walk amongst our community you just don't think people are carrying knives, but they are," Mr Bleijie said.

The seized weapons, which include machetes and a samurai sword, have been crushed at an e-recycling plant.

Laws target 'everybody'

Recent data has shown that more than one in 10 people searched for weapons in Queensland under the expanded powers identified as First Nations.

That's despite Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people making up 4.6 per cent of the Queensland population.

Mr Bleijie said the laws are non-discriminatory.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the laws are making Queenslanders safer. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"Everybody across Queensland in public spaces can be wanded, and we're trying to take knives off everybody," he said.

" We want knives off everybody in every community. "

The increased police powers form part of the LNP's tough on crime agenda, which includes the introduction of new legislation tightening bail laws.

The breach bail, go to jail legislation includes a minimum mandatory one year jail sentence for offenders who breach bail.

World.title: Breaking: De Minaur crashes out of US Open
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has been dumped out of the US Open in the second round, falling in straight sets to Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp 6-4, 7-5, 6-2 in two hours and 43 minutes.

De Minaur had never lost to the 30-year-old world number 70 in their previous four meetings, including earlier this year at the Rotterdam ATP event, which the 27-year-old Aussie won.

But on a night where he committed 29 unforced errors to van de Zandschulp's 21, as well as seven double faults in a sub-par serving display, the Australian world number seven faltered badly.

De Minaur's exit means wildcard Dane Sweeny is the only Australian left in the men's singles draw at Flushing Meadows after his 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 victory against world number 14 Lorenzo Musetti.

World.title: More than 100 motorbikes tear through outback pub in world record attempt
World.content:
The sound of revving engines echoed around the centre of Alice Springs last night as dozens of riders attempted to set the record for the most motorbikes ridden through a pub.

From the leather-clad to the board-short-wearing and everything in between, the riders on commuters and muscle bikes fell just short of their goal at Bojangles Saloon.

Aiming for 125 bikes, only 107 rode through the outback pub, filling it with fumes and noise, as dozens lined the barricades to get a glimpse of the action.

This year's Finke Desert Race motorbike race winner David Walsh, also known as the King of the Desert, led the charge.

Finke Desert Race champion David Walsh led the ride. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

"I was a little bit nervous to be honest," he said.

"It was really cool, something different, it was a great atmosphere, I'm pumped that I did it."

The record attempt was part of Red CentreNATS, the Northern Territory sister festival to Canberra's Summernats, with dozens of car and motorbike events planned over the next few days.

"Alice Springs is full of revheads, there's a lot of nice cars out here so it's cool that we all get to display them … it's just such an amazing event," Mr Walsh said.

Laura Johnson from Red CentreNATS said despite the failed attempt, the fact they even gave it a go was a win.

Bojangles Saloon welcomed the motorbikes, which filled the pub with fumes and noise. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"It might not be a world record, but it is absolutely a record for us and the growth that we've shown from last year, I am so confident that at Red CentreNATS [next year] we are going to smash it out of the park," she said.

She said the atmosphere was electric and Alice Springs locals and volunteers were part of what made Red CentreNATS so great.

"Where else do you shut down the centre of town and ride motorbikes through a pub," she said.

"To be able to be a part of it, for 107 bikes to ride through a venue, that's amazing."

Many riders came from interstate to be a part of the action.

Harley Hall says he will be back next year to try again. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Ngarrindjeri Kokatha-Wirangu man Harley Hall arrived in Alice Springs from South Australia with his family as part of the 3% motorbike group — which he said represented the 3 per cent Indigenous population of Australia.

"That was an adrenaline rush and a half," he said.

" We'll be back next year, we're going to bring more fellas — hopefully we beat the world record. "

Behind the bar after the fog of fumes had lifted, Bojangles Saloon owner Pearl Randhay said she was grateful to have events like Red CentreNATS come to town and bring it to life.

"It was so exciting, I was nervous in a good way, I'm happy everything went well," she said.

Pearl Randhay says the record attempt was exciting. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"Thank goodness we had earplugs."

The event raised money for the Butterfly Connection, an organisation helping central Australians travel interstate for medical treatment.

World.title: Second rider dies after cyclists struck by car in Canberra last week
World.content:
Two lives have now been claimed by a crash in Canberra's north last week, after a 39-year-old man died in hospital yesterday evening.

On Thursday morning last week, at about 6:20am, ACT Policing said a car "ploughed" into a group of five cyclists on Gungahlin Drive in Palmerston, between Wells Station Drive and Kosciusko Avenue.

A 32-year-old female rider died at the scene, while a 39-year-old man was taken to hospital in a critical condition.

Members of the public, including an off-duty nurse and police officer, assisted the injured cyclists ahead of emergency services arriving.

This morning, ACT police confirmed the second cyclist had died in hospital, bringing the number of deaths on ACT roads this year to 11.

A group of five cyclists cyclists were involved in the crash on Gungahlin Drive. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

The cyclists were part of the ACT's triathlon community, with the group last week describing the crash as "shocking".

"This incident is a reminder that the roads are a shared space and all we ever want, whether you're a driver or a cyclist, is to get home safe," ACT Triathlon president Lara Lever said.

Following the crash, Detective Inspector Mark Steel said the driver of the vehicle, a 40-year-old woman, was assisting police with enquiries.

No charges have yet been laid.

Detective Inspector Steel said police were appealing to "anybody with information or dash cam footage of the cyclists on Gungahlin Drive, or a Hyundai Accent, light blue in colour, with ACT registration YND94Q".

World.title: NSW coalmining companies accused of using planning 'loopholes'
World.content:
Coalmining companies in NSW are using loopholes in planning laws to get expansions approved, say the Greens and environmental groups.

Up to 30 million tonnes of additional coal will be extracted from Idemitsu's Boggabri mine after the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) endorsed a modification to the existing plan on Monday.

The decision will keep the New England mine running until 2040, generating an estimated 68 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions.

The modfication will see 84 hectares of native vegetation cleared within the Leard State Forest. (ABC News: Lisa Herbert)

The Greens and environmental groups have accused the NSW government of using the modification process to get around more stringent planning rules for new developments.

Community group People for the Plains (PFTP) was one of 16 objectors to the Boggabri mine modification.

PFTP secretary Sally Hunter said applying for modifications was a "loophole" that mining companies could exploit to avoid the full rigour of applying for a new development.

"Within the NSW planning process, there are certain criteria that need to be met to go through a full process, and these modifications slip under that trigger point," she said.

Sally Hunter believes the state government is allowing mining companies to use "loopholes". (Supplied: Lock the Gate)

"When it goes to a full process, there's a lot more scrutiny, whereas the modifications are reviewed and approved by the department."

Modifications unlocking mining

So far, the government has approved 13 extensions since the 2023 election, including at Mount Pleasant in the Upper Hunter last month.

Greens spokesperson for the environment and climate change Sue Higginson said modifications approved in the Gunnedah basin, the Hunter Valley, and the Upper Hunter were an easy route to unlock more mining.

"It's get in the door, get your approval and then seek the expansion and impact process by modification," she said.

"It's a bit like the death by a thousand cuts analogy.

"Everybody knows we are talking about new coal, new areas for longer periods of time."

Sue Higginson says mine modifications are a slow death. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

The Idemitsu expansion at Boggabri will allow about 84 hectares of native vegetation within the Leard State Forest to be cleared.

PFTP argued the mine would negatively impact the habitat of critically endangered birds such as the regent honeyeater and swift parrot.

Regent honeyeaters are under threat in the region. (Supplied: Dean Ingwersen)

'A full merit-based assessment'

In a statement, Planning Minister Paul Scully said there was no basis for the assertions of loopholes.

"Every mining proposal or modification goes through a full merit-based assessment," he said.

"The modification for Boggabri was on public exhibition from 13 June to 11 July 2025 to allow the community to have their say."

NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully says there is no basis for the assertions of loopholes. (Four Corners)

A DPHI spokesperson said it undertook a rigorous merit assessment of the Boggabri mine, including community input, consideration of greenhouse gas emissions and potential impacts to threatened species, surface water and groundwater.

In the notice of decision, the department imposed several conditions, including reviews and updates of biodiversity and water management plans, and a requirement to prepare a greenhouse mitigation plan before April 2027.

The department considered a previous modification approved in 2019, and found that a new development application was not needed.

Crucial for the community

According to Idemitsu, the Boggabri coal mine provides about 875 jobs, with most workers living locally.

President of the Boggabri business chamber Suzanne Torrens said the expansion would continue to provide crucial jobs for the area.

"Without the mining industry, our community wouldn't survive," she said.

"It's going to help keep our younger generation in the town as it creates job opportunities."

Suzanne Torrens says the Boggabri mine is the largest employer in the area. (supplied)

Ms Torrens said she understood opponents' concerns but trusted the operator to follow environmental impact standards.

"I believe the mines are doing everything in their ability to make sure the area does go back to its natural state," she said.

Idemitsu declined to comment on the modification approval.

World.title: Uneven distribution of class action payments causing havoc in Arnhem Land
World.content:
Organisations in north-east Arnhem Land say they have been left to wear the frustrations of hundreds of local residents who missed a tight registration window for a major class action lawsuit, while lawyers and administrators walk away with millions.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the names and images of Indigenous people who have died, used with the permission of their family.

In 2024, former station worker Minnie McDonald settled a $202 million class action that she led against the Commonwealth for historical wage theft in the Northern Territory.

She brought the lawsuit on behalf of thousands of Aboriginal workers who worked for little or no pay on pastoral stations, missions and other workplaces in the NT between 1933 and 1971.

Minnie McDonald was the lead applicant in the class action against the Commonwealth. (Supplied)

In August 2025, the Federal Court heard that figure was reached based on estimates there were up to 8,750 NT workers paid little or no wages in that time frame.

However at that point only 5,761 of those workers and their descendants had lodged claims, and in February — months after the close of registrations — the court heard the scheme had about 500 less claimants than originally anticipated.

Both of Wanyubi Marika's parents worked during the period of time covered by the class action claim. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Wanyubi Marika, the chair of the powerful Rirratjingu Aboriginal Corporation, which has business interests across the NT's Gove Peninsula, said he was one of many in the region who was unaware when the October 2025 deadline came and went.

Both of Mr Marika's parents worked within the years covered by the class action — his father Milirrpum working as a labourer for the Australian Defence Force (ADF), and his mother Liyapidiny as a nurse's assistant in Yirrkala.

Milirrpum Marika worked as a labourer for the Australian Defence Force. (Supplied: National Museum of Australia)

According to the Australian War Memorial, the ADF employed Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory from 1933 under similar conditions to those at cattle stations, with "long hours, poor housing and diet, and low pay".

"They only get [work] for clean-em-up, cleaning yard or stock works, and all that with very small money, where the Balanda [Westerners], they get higher package level," he said.

Mr Marika said his mother Liyapidiny at times worked all hours of the night as a nurse and midwife, and on Sundays she administered congregations for the local Methodist church.

"Very, very hardworking woman, and for that health djama [work] she received an Order of Australia medal," he said.

Liyapidiny Marika worked as a nurse and midwife at the time and was an ordained Uniting Church minister. (Supplied: Uniting Church)

Mr Marika said in his home community of Yirrkala, there was lingering confusion about the substantial cash payments that had landed in the bank accounts of some residents across the region earlier this year.

He said it was only after some received the payments that others like himself found out about the class action.

"Families [are] getting this stolen wages money, and there's a question mark there," the Rirratjingu elder said.

"How? Why? What's that stolen wages?"

Lawyers and investors pocket millions in fight for stolen wages They are meant to deliver justice for ordinary Australians, but class actions are being used by law firms to profit at the expense of some of the most vulnerable members of society.

Local organisation Aboriginal Resource and Development Services (ARDS) said in a statement it was approached by the class action's litigators, Shine Lawyers, in May last year because "they were finding it difficult to sign Yolŋu up to the class action".

Chief executive Julie Wormer said ARDS had been given eight weeks and "a small amount of funding" to get the message out to communities in north-east Arnhem Land.

She said ARDS staff had been able to help 350 people register, in trips made to about a dozen communities and homelands in the region.

"The applications involved a complicated 12-page form in English and explanation of difficult legal concepts which required upwards of two hours to complete per person including follow up," Ms Wormer said.

On August 29 last year the court granted an extension of the registration deadline to October 3.

ARDS confirmed that it was only contracted to do the outreach work until the end of August, but said they did continue until the October deadline, mostly unpaid.

Workers on cattle stations are among those who have been reported to have experienced stolen wages. (Source: Australian News and Information Bureau)

A Shine Lawyers spokesperson said the court had ordered the involvement of community groups like ARDS in their outreach work, and directed further questions to Deloitte.

Deloitte declined to comment.

Lawyers' fees, registration windows criticised

A large amount of the $202 million settlement cost went to Shine Lawyers ($15 million), litigation funders LLS Fund Services ($30 million), and administrator Deloitte ($3.2 million), while the claimants themselves received "at least $10,000" each as compensation.

In approving the settlement, Federal Court Chief Justice Debra Mortimer criticised Shine for the "excessive" human resources it had devoted to the case, and said it had "elected to plan what I consider was the most expensive way that the outreach and registration process and the book build could have been undertaken".

Debra Mortimer previously criticised Shine Lawyers for how it managed the class action case. (Supplied: Federal Court of Australia)

In the months after compensation reached claimants this year, organisations in north-east Arnhem Land said they had been left to field hundreds of enquiries about how to apply for payments from the class action settlement.

"In March 2026, seeing the spread of misinformation and the confusion amongst Yolŋu in relation to the class action, ARDS shared up-to-date information with Yolŋu both in plain English and Yolŋu Matha [language] about the class action on our ARDS and Yolŋu Radio Facebook pages," Ms Wormer said

"Between the end of October 2025 to present, ARDS have not been funded to do this work."

Glenda Abraham says her organisation has needed to respond to the consequences of people missing out on the class action. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Laynhapuy Homelands Aboriginal Corporation (LHAC) worked alongside ARDS last year to convey information about the class action to residents of homelands and outstations in the region.

"We've got the strongest connection to homelands, the strongest connection to those people who are impacted, and as a result we are the ones who have started to wear the frustration and the questions," chief executive Glenda Abraham said.

Ms Abraham said significant resources had been devoted to standing up programs in homelands specifically to address the consequences of claims being unevenly awarded.

"We're wearing the full cost of all that," she said.

" One of the concerns we have in homelands is eldership abuse and particularly financial abuse, and so we're starting to see that play out. "

She said establishing a national redress scheme for wage theft victims would be "the most logical" way for compensation to be distributed, saying "there are definitely people who have missed out all over the country, and even within the [Territory]".

Thalia Anthony says a national redress scheme is needed for the issue of stolen wages. (ABC News: Jack Ailwood)

University of Technology Sydney law professor Thalia Anthony, who has been researching historical wage theft for 25 years, said she agreed with Ms Abraham that the Commonwealth should set up a national redress scheme, which would stay open for a period of years and pay out compensation based on written and oral evidence.

"It's been a very ad hoc approach where each state has dealt with it in very different ways," Professor Anthony said.

"So we've got really uneven outcomes, and so it needs to be uniform and harmonised, and it needs to be established with the partnership of Aboriginal organisations."

Malarndirri McCarthy says she acknowledges people are frustrated with how the class action was managed. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy did not respond to questions about whether a national redress scheme was warranted, but said she "acknowledged the disappointment of members of the Yolngu community with the Administrators' operation of the scheme".

"Given the independence of the Settlement, the Commonwealth cannot influence the way Deloitte administers the settlement, including to extend the registration date," she said in a statement.

Professor Anthony said there were potentially thousands of people across Australia who had missed opportunities to make claims under various state-based class actions.

"Now that there is some momentum following the failure of the compensation set-up in the Northern Territory, hopefully there'll be ongoing litigation or other forms of campaigning that will bring light to this issue," she said.

World.title: ‘They just want to burn the house down’: Behind the rise of One Nation in the Hunter
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twenty minutes into a One Nation press conference on a sunny Friday, the angular eyebrows of Senator Pauline Hanson begin to furrow, trying – like most attendees – to discern what her party’s new leader in NSW and candidate for Cessnock is saying in fluent Japanese. The event – held at the industrial headquarters of mining equipment supplier Drill Doctor on the outskirts of Singleton, an hour north-west of Newcastle – has been arranged so One Nation could announce the identities of its ambitious campaign for next year’s state election. Despite having no MPs sitting in Macquarie Street, the party talks of taking power. As Sean Bell, Hanson’s former adviser turned NSW senator, exclaims during a fundraiser at the Toronto Hotel that August evening: “I don’t think there’s ever been an opportunity like this.” Even Hanson’s admonishment of Cessnock candidate Mike Newman’s foreign interlude – “Excuse me. I think everyone else would like to know what you’re saying” – is swiftly brushed past, with the 53-year-old calmly explaining he will complete answering the Japanese journalist’s question in her native language before translating for the crowd. One Nation candidate Mike Newman answers a question in Japanese. James Brickwood The vignette is a microcosm of the strange new era of Australian politics. It’s one in which Newman – a cosmopolitan, bilingual investment banker with a Japanese wife, and a preacher of foreign investment – has joined One Nation, a nationalist populist party of the battler whose leader just months earlier rejected multiculturalism in favour of a “monoculture”. It marks another attempt by Hanson’s outfit to evolve from a closed tent mainly composed of insiders and loyalists to one recruiting the talent that it hopes will solidify its status as the nation’s leading conservative party.



Eight years after Hanson enlisted political maverick Mark Latham to be the party’s leader in NSW, One Nation hopes the Newman experiment can succeed where that marriage ended in acrimony. Related Article Updated

WA election ‘This is One Nation heartland now’: Labor shocked in bruising Secret Harbour byelection Less than 28 hours after announcing its first NSW candidates, One Nation easily claimed victory in a byelection in the West Australian state seat of Secret Harbour. Hanson is on the march. And the Hunter will be fertile ground for the party’s populist message in NSW. The Hunter is coal-mining country. It was once a Labor heartland. The eponymously named, blue-collar federal electorate has voted Labor since the electorate was established in the early 20th century. Cessnock, the state seat that sits within the Hunter’s boundaries, has been in the party’s column since 1927 aside from an aberrant result in 1988. One Nation’s Stuart Bonds carved a huge chunk of voters away from Labor in his first electoral outing. James Brickwood That sense of security was shattered in May 2019, when in his first crack at federal parliament, coal miner Stuart Bonds snatched 22 per cent of the primary vote in the Hunter. Joel Fitzgibbon, the veteran Labor frontbencher first elected in 1996, was left with a 3 per cent margin.



Bonds, who will now run at the top of the party’s upper house ticket in NSW, says despite living and working in the electorate, he was initially encouraged to run for the neighbouring seat of Lyne in 2019 because the prospect of winning the Hunter was considered fanciful. Related Article Exclusive

One Nation One Nation candidate launches broadside on NSW Liberal leader “You will never flip the Hunter in a million years,” Bonds says he was told by One Nation. “No one else could see this uprising happening, but I could see it, literally, at the coal face.” Ten people showed up for his first branch meeting in Singleton in 2018, Bonds remembers with a laugh. Since then, support for One Nation in the Hunter has fluctuated. Bonds’ primary vote of 16 per cent in the 2025 election was nearly 6 per cent lower than 2019. Yet, as proven by the South Australian state election in March and the Secret Harbour byelection, people are turning out to vote for One Nation in 2026. Polling by Resolve in August shows more than one in four NSW respondents would vote for the party if an election were held today. Former federal Labor MP Joel Fitzgibbon says voters are angry and want to send a message. James Brickwood But even those unprecedented polling figures understate how well the party is doing in regional seats. Where Bonds once tapped disaffected Labor voters looking to send the party a message, today One Nation has become the brand of choice in the Hunter.



“I’ve no doubt that [Hanson’s] support in the Hunter Valley is very, very strong,” Fitzgibbon says in an interview from his Cessnock home. “The question is: can the juggernaut continue to grow right until March of next year?” Related Article Immigration Five days later, Hanson still struggles to articulate migration policy “They want to send the most powerful message that they can – that they’re as angry as hell, and they’re not going to take it any more.” If anyone wanted to witness the popularity of Hanson in the Hunter, all they needed to do was visit the Singleton Golf Club on a Friday in late August. “She is the most in-demand person in Australia right now,” the host tells a crowd who have taken the Friday off to see Hanson, who is headlining a fundraiser for the Singleton charity shop’s cancer appeal. The 320-seat event, costing $125 a ticket, was sold out two weeks in advance. There was so much demand, Bonds claims organisers could have sold double the number of tickets.



Hanson is mobbed at Singleton Golf Club. James Brickwood The veteran’s popularity is undeniable among fans. James Brickwood It takes the Queensland senator – who walks in with Bonds and his Finnish tattooist wife, Sini – half an hour just to make it into the clubhouse after being swamped by patrons looking for selfies or simply to hold her hand and offer words of support. A heavily tattooed man with a flannelette shirt and handlebar moustache reminiscent of Mark “Chopper” Read sheepishly asks his friend whether he thinks Hanson will take a photo with him. “You can stay at my place,” a woman tells Hanson when asked if she’ll be visiting the Hunter again. If Hanson’s popularity is undeniable, so is the sense that Anthony Albanese is on the nose. The second and third prize of the charity auction are two “Fire the Liar” packages – name-checking One Nation’s campaign against Albanese – each containing a party shirt and cap signed by Hanson and the opportunity for the winner to have their photo taken with her. The room is decorated with One Nation posters. James Brickwood

World.title: What Trump’s decoy plane ruse tells us about poor leadership
World.content:
NationalDonald Trump Opinion What Trump’s decoy plane ruse tells us about poor leadership Bram Connolly Leadership expert September 4, 2026 — 11:30am

September 4, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I suspect I won’t be allowed in the United States again after this but being able to respectfully talk truth to power is a fundamental right of a Western democracy, so I take my chances. Trump arrived for the NATO summit in Ankara on Air Force One but didn’t go home on it. AP Last month, as reported by The Washington Post and CBS News, the president of the US boarded the presidential aircraft Air Force One in front of the cameras at Ankara airport, and then he quietly left it. Facing a credible Iranian missile threat, he was reportedly moved by catering truck to a smaller military aircraft and flown out under a different call sign. The journalists and staff who boarded the original plane were told to keep their window shades down and they weren’t told why, and they also weren’t told the president was gone. Then, as scheduled, they flew home, unknowingly aboard an aircraft a hostile state had decided was a legitimate target. Set aside the politics. I want to look at this through an entirely different lens: leadership.



I have spent three decades now in the Australian army, much of it in Special Forces, and my consultancy teaches leadership to executives. The definition of leadership I use is a demanding one: leadership is compelling other people to do what you want them to do because they want to do it. It’s important to understand that it’s not because they’re ordered to, and not because they’re deceived into it. It’s actually your credibility, your example and your care for them that make following you the thing they choose to do. Bram Connolly, on assignment with the ADF Special Forces. By that definition, what happened at Ankara wasn’t leadership. There’s a simple framework we use to explain how leadership is projected: what leaders say, what they do, what they prioritise and what they recognise. Words are obviously the cheapest of the four, and actions take a bit more energy to demonstrate. But it’s the last two, a leader’s priorities and what they recognise, that are impossible to fake. Let’s run the Ankara decision through that framework. What was said: that the flight was dangerous because of the adversaries “we have to deal with”. What was done: the principal was extracted from the danger while his own press corps and staff were left sitting inside it, shades drawn. What was prioritised: the safety of one man, and the secrecy of the manoeuvre, above the informed consent of his staff and those who convey his messages. And what was recognised? When later asked about the shades, the reported response to the journalists was, in effect, that if he went down, they’d go down, too; followed by the suggestion that perhaps they should change professions. That is recognition of a kind. It recognises that the staff are what made the decoy compelling.



Now, the counter-argument deserves a fair hearing, of course. A head of state is not an ordinary passenger; protective agencies exist precisely to move the principal out of harm’s way, and continuity of government is a legitimate priority. I don’t dispute any of that. The security professionals who designed the switch did their jobs and they did it well. My argument is not with the extraction. It is with what happened to everyone else. The Committee to Protect Journalists put it plainly: people covering the president should be informed of credible threats so they can make their own informed decisions about their own safety. Deciding to accept risk is a personal right. Having risk assigned to you unknowingly, as a decoy for someone else, I would contest that won’t be forgotten, and that’s where he has lost their trust. Moreover, trust is built from three things: credibility (do you know what you’re doing?), reliability (do you do what you say?) and intimacy (can I be safe and honest with you?). And it is divided – divided, not merely reduced – by one thing: self-interest. You can be supremely credible and impressively reliable and have intimate working relationships, but the moment the people behind you conclude that, when it matters most, you will throw them under the bus (a narcissist manoeuvre), nothing else matters. Trust doesn’t just erode in that moment, it actually collapses and it can never be won back. I know this equation from the other side of it. In Afghanistan, commanding soldiers in combat, the one thing I found hardest to do was delegate risk. I did do it – I often delegated risk to a lead vehicle and one driver, and I still haven’t forgiven myself for it – but the driver knew and accepted the risk. Unlike Trump’s staff, my staffer was given the option. Whatever we drove into, we drove into together. Soldiers will forgive a leader almost anything except the discovery that their exposure and the leader’s are valued differently. I’ve just written a book, 100 Ways I Almost Died, and if there’s a thread running through all those moments, it’s this: I was never exposed to risk alone. My men were beside me and they knew everything I knew. The knowledge that the risk is shared is the intimacy in the equation. It’s why they followed me in training and combat. It’s why, years later, I think they still would. Leaders at every level, in every organisation, face a quieter version of the Ankara choice most business days: who absorbs the risk, who gets told the truth and who is left with the shades down. When the pressure comes, your people will not remember your speeches. They will remember which plane you put them on.



Bram Connolly, DSM, is a former Special Forces officer, founder of Hindsight Leadership and Resilience, and the author of 100 Ways I Almost Died (published by Allen & Unwin). Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Raygun’s Netflix doco seems like a mockumentary. It’s actually a disturbing love story
World.content:
September 4, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Minutes into Netflix’s new doco Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly, all I could think of was Christopher Guest’s Best in Show meets Chazz Michael Michaels from Blades of Glory. Mostly because of Rachael Gunn’s husband Samuel Free, breakdancing name Sammy Sex, who speaks to camera with an American twang and what looks to be an elite home perm. By turns, Sammy looks cooked and thrilled, but maintains one thing throughout: that his wife is a world-class B-Girl. Rachael Gunn in a still from the Netflix documentary Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly. Netflix And therein lies the rub. This isn’t a mockumentary of the Raygun kerfuffle that swept the Paris Olympics. It’s actually a love story. And the question it throws up extends to all of us: how much should the people who love you most tell you the truth? Even Raygun’s terrific parents seem bemused by her Olympic selection. Not Sammy. He’s in her corner, from practice sessions to that final unforgettable Olympic routine – yep, zero points, the sprinkler, the move where she lay on the floor opening and closing like a set of tongs, the kangaroo hops.



“I was, like, struck by the beauty of the performance,” he says of her final battle. “It was the essence of creativity.” Well. Risking coming late to the pile-on, but I grew up on Dance Fever, the TV disco dance-off that spun out of Saturday Night Fever, and I know quality dance. Watching Raygun, I had that feeling you get in front of a Jackson Pollock: I could do that. The “essence of creativity” is a bit rich. Raygun’s husband Samuel Free, aka Sammy Sex, in Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly. Sammy’s more interesting than his wife (who at one point says, and I can hardly bear to type it, “We’re not in Kansas any more”) in her own show. He’s doing what a good husband is supposed to do: backing his person. And he seems sincere, which is the worry. A flatterer knows they’re lying. A delusional spouse doesn’t.



Love has a dangerous side effect. It makes the person you adore look like the person you think they could be. Iris Murdoch called love “the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real”. Not just a fella with a blind spot, Sammy’s managed something else: the refusal to see what’s real. Related Article Performing arts ‘Ridiculed’: How Australia’s breaking community was left reeling after Paris When does backing a spouse tip into actively failing them? Perhaps Ryan Reynolds should have had a word with Blake Lively before the Baldoni legal bloodbath. Maybe Harry could have said, Meg, the homemade bath salts are making you ridiculous. Certainly, Melania should have seen the gilt work in the Oval Office and confiscated the glue gun. A good spouse will say you’re smart enough to go on Sale of the Century, that you killed it at karaoke, that you’re legit hilarious, that you smell incredible, that your deadlifting has really come on, that you organise great holidays. A delusional one will say ... you could be Miss Universe and be boss cocky of Mensa and your tailgating doesn’t matter and sure, you could win breakdancing at the Olympics.



Because the love that never says the hard thing doesn’t make the hard part go away. It outsources it. The world eventually delivers the verdict that love withheld, and it has no stake in being gentle. Old story, but fits here: when our middle son hit a junior footy milestone, we made a banner: “48 great games and two poor ones.” Yep, it got a few laughs from one resilient boy and a small crowd. Raygun: not so lucky. Her feedback arrived via a braying audience of millions. Rachael “Raygun” Gunn competes at the 2024 Olympics. Getty Images Maybe Sammy couldn’t say, “darl, you’re not much chop” because he was too close. Maybe Rachael couldn’t hear it, although she did tell a psychologist pre-Olympics she feared being a laughingstock, which suggests self-awareness. Either way, it would have been kinder for someone at her kitchen table to tell her the truth before we all did.
