World.title: NFL stars land in Melbourne with a week to prepare for MCG clash
World.content:
SportNFL 2026 NFL stars land in Melbourne with a week to prepare for MCG clash Josh Dubow September 4, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The San Francisco 49ers have arrived in Melbourne after embarking on the longest road trip in NFL history. Ahead of next Friday’s historic season-opener at the MCG against the Los Angeles Rams, the 49ers were given advice on how to eat and hydrate, what to do after arriving and the best options of when to sleep on the approximately 8000-mile (13,000km) flight that took about 16 hours. Loading The two teams have taken vastly different approaches to the long-haul journey, with the Rams not arriving in Melbourne until 24 hours before the match, whereas the Nines left home on Wednesday (PDT) and arrived at Tullamarine Friday morning (AEST), giving them a hole week to acclimatise. Before the flight, Niners defensive lineman and avid world traveller Keion White outlined his personal approach.



“I don’t know if you can OD on melatonin, but I’m going to try,” he said. “Take five melatonins, go to sleep on the plane. As soon as I wake up, I’m taking five more. Just keep rolling like that.” While some members of the 49ers organisation, including coach Kyle Shanahan, have been lamenting the season-opening trip, White is embracing it after already playing games in Germany and London earlier in his career. The San Francisco 49ers arrive in Melbourne a week early for their game at the MCG. Rhys Duke He plans to watch TikTok before he arrives to get ideas of what to do and then get on public transport and explore after team meetings on the first day to help make sure he stays up all day and gets onto a normal sleep schedule as quickly as possible. “I’m an experience guy,” he said. “If I’m up, walking around, just going to go do stuff, I’ll be up. Just go explore. We will have meetings and everything like that, but once I do that, I’m out exploring Melbourne and getting around town.”



Both the 49ers and Rams studied the process intently in the off-season, even sending advance staffers to Australia to report back on how long it took to adjust to the time change. The Niners will hold a light practice on Saturday, take Sunday off and then have a normal stretch of three practices on Monday through Wednesday before playing the opener on Friday morning. The 49ers looked in good spirits on their arrival at Tullamarine. Rhys Duke They will leave right after the game and are expected to land back in the Bay Area on Friday afternoon. They then will be able to take the weekend off before preparing to play Miami on September 20. “It’s a big adjustment on the body,” Shanahan said. “So, the recommendation for everybody has been to tell us when to go, and it’s made a lot of sense. I know how our players feel also. I was a little bit on the fence. Science wasn’t and what I was reported on and our players weren’t at all. So that helped me get off the fence.”



The Rams consulted with their own scientists and came up with the opposite approach. They will do most of their practice at home and aren’t expected to arrive in Australia until about 24 hours before the game, hoping to bypass jet lag by having a short stay down under. The better option won’t not be known until after the game. The players dressed for comfort on the flight. Rhys Duke The approach by the Niners has made the past few days a whirlwind. The players got the weekend off after playing the final exhibition game on Thursday night in Las Vegas and resumed practice on Monday – the day after their roster was reduced to 53 players. The front office had to make those cuts, put together a practice squad and figure out which players would be healthy for week one to make sure they had the correct roster in place before departing.



“There’s a lot behind the scenes,” general manager John Lynch said. “Our logistics folks, our folks that work in the cafe, have just gone to tremendous lengths, our health and performance team, to make sure that we’re giving our players the best opportunity to feel right when they play down there in Australia. Everything from getting visas, which much more complicated than I ever knew, and they’ve been outstanding. ... Hats off to those guys for pulling off a monumental task, and it’s not done yet.” Lynch said he had to make sure all the practice squad players he wanted to sign had passports with one needing his parents to send it overnight. It was an even bigger scramble for offensive lineman Jarrett Patterson, who was acquired in a trade from Houston on Sunday. The San Francisco 49ers arrived in Melbourne on Friday. Rhys Duke “They were like, hey, do you have a passport? We’re leaving for Australia in three days,” he said. “I was like, ‘Whoa!’ It’s obviously a quick turnaround getting here a couple hours after I found out and now getting ready for Australia.” But in all, the players are welcoming the challenge and opportunity. Cornerback Deommodore Lenoir said he’d travel 30 hours if needed to play in an NFL game and rookie De’Zhaun Stribling has a must-see item on his to-do list before making his debut.

World.title: Coles cuts ties with controversial CIA-linked data giant Palantir
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologySupermarkets Coles cuts ties with controversial CIA-linked data giant Palantir David Swan September 4, 2026 — 11:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Coles will cut ties with Palantir, the controversial US data giant whose software underpins American deportation raids and battlefield targeting systems. The supermarket has confirmed its contract with the company will not extend beyond 2027, ending a partnership signed in early 2024 that gave Palantir access to more than 10 billion rows of data covering every store, every shift and each of the retailer’s 120,000 employees. Coles will cut ties with Palantir, the controversial US data giant whose software underpins American deportation raids and battlefield targeting systems. Eamon Gallagher “Coles and Palantir have agreed to conclude their partnership after three years of collaboration,” the two companies said in an identical statement. Coles said a transition plan was under way and the final timing was not settled. The confirmation follows a campaign launched in February by activist group GetUp, which claimed the outcome as a win.



“Nobody should need a national campaign to find out whether military-grade surveillance tech is watching them buy bread and milk,” interim chief executive Paul Ferris said. Activist group GetUp targeted Coles’ partnership with Palantir. “It’s a shame it took 85,000 people, 700 billboards and a shareholder resolution before Coles did what it should have on day one.” Neither company would say when the decision was made. The campaign gathered more than 85,000 signatures and put digital billboards outside close to 700 stores. One video accusing Coles of watching its shoppers was viewed 3 million times.



Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel. Bloomberg Palantir, co-founded by Peter Thiel, built its business inside the US national security apparatus and sells to militaries, intelligence agencies and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Thiel has said he no longer believes freedom and democracy are compatible. The company is worth about $US330 billion. Its chief executive, Alex Karp, holds a doctorate in social theory from a German university, practises tai chi, and has published a manifesto arguing Palantir is the democratic West’s best hope of staying ahead of authoritarian rivals. Surveillance technology has become a flashpoint in Australian retail since the Administrative Review Tribunal ruled in February that Bunnings could keep using facial recognition to fight theft, while affirming it had breached privacy law by failing to tell customers. Coles has rejected the surveillance characterisation throughout, and says the campaign traded in misinformation.



A spokesman said the software was used for rostering, store operations and supply chain planning, and ran inside Coles’ own environment under Coles controls. “Palantir does not control the data, nor can it independently repurpose it,” the spokesman said. Coles said Palantir had never been involved in CCTV, facial recognition or any of its crime-prevention measures. It does not use facial recognition in any store, and a limited proof of concept was run in a testing environment in response to rising violence against staff. The deal was pitched more expansively in 2024. Coles chief operating officer Matt Swindells said it would “redefine how we think about our workforce”. Palantir’s global head of commercial technologies, Ted Mabrey, said the retailer was not treating the software as a “toy”, pointing to Airbus crediting the company with a 30 per cent acceleration in A350 production.



Much of a recent Coles letter to ethical share trading platform SIX, seen by this masthead, was devoted to an attack on the campaign’s methods. Coles said GetUp had used footage of an identifiable worker at its Pacific Fair store and superimposed an employee number and an “84 per cent” working efficiency score over her image. Both were invented, the letter said, and came from no Coles system. Related Article Updated

Privacy Bunnings wins appeal over use of facial recognition technology to fight crime The worker was recognised by others who saw the  and was left distressed, according to the letter, and her mother lodged a written complaint. GetUp has said it bought the footage from a stock site and later blurred her face. “It is particularly troubling that this was done as part of a campaign being conducted in the name of employee privacy,” wrote Coles general manager of investor relations Anita Healy.



The letter asked SIX to withdraw a shareholder resolution, backed by 189 individual investors, that called on the board to commission a human rights impact assessment ahead of November’s annual general meeting. Coles said SIX had since withdrawn it. SIX environmental, social and governance manager James Alexander said the outcome showed the power of small shareholders acting together. “Hundreds of Coles investors backed planned resolutions asking legitimate questions about data governance and human rights due diligence,” he said. Digital Rights Watch head of policy Tom Sulston said Palantir’s politics were incompatible with Australian values of fairness and equality. GetUp acting chief executive Paul Ferris claimed the outcome as a win. Steven Siewert



“It doesn’t belong in Australia and it certainly doesn’t belong in the places we depend on day-to-day, like supermarkets,” he said. Coles is not the first customer to walk away. Spain has moved to block Palantir from public procurement, French and German intelligence agencies picked a domestic rival, and a British parliamentary committee recommended against renewing a contract. Palantir said its technology had delivered value across Coles’ operations and had helped the retailer put team members in the right place at the right time. Its other Australian clients include Westpac, Rio Tinto and Westrac. Coles was its first Australian retailer. “Our privacy laws are decades behind this sort of technology,” Ferris said. “Coles was chapter one, but every board in the country should be checking its contracts.” Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: Australians are flocking to electric vehicles. There’s a hidden cost
World.content:
BusinessThe economyGDP Opinion Australians are flocking to electric vehicles. There’s a hidden cost Millie Muroi Economics Writer Updated September 4, 2026 — 11:16am , first published September 4, 2026 — 5:00am

Updated September 4, 2026 — 11:16am ,first published September 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You can’t blame Australians for seeing fuel prices over the past few months and deciding to ditch their petrol-powered cars. As Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock pointed out at a recent press conference, petrol prices are one of the most visible — and therefore memorable — prices, with most of us passing a petrol station somewhere on our daily commutes. Electric and hybrid vehicle sales having been revving up the Australian economy as people look for ways to save. Bloomberg While petrol prices have fallen from their peak of about $2.50 a litre in our major cities earlier this year, they’re still hovering at about $2 a litre after the government’s fuel excise discount ended in August. That’s about 20 cents more expensive per litre than the average petrol price across our major cities in 2025. Fuel prices are significant — not just because they make up about 3 per cent of an Australian household’s spending — but because they affect how much it costs for businesses, especially in the transport, farming and aviation sectors, to provide their goods and services.



As we know, inflation, or price growth, is still a big challenge for the Reserve Bank (and many of us paying higher prices for everyday items). In the 12 months to July, prices across the economy grew 3.5 per cent — lower than the 3.8 per cent they were growing at in the year to June, but still well above the bank’s target range of 2 to 3 per cent. Related Article Australian economy Chalmers admits tax reforms helped drag down house prices It’s a rational response for people to look for ways to save money. We know, for example, from the recent earnings season where Australian businesses reported their profits, that customers remain hungry for a bargain. We also know from the most recent “national accounts” — which gives us a snapshot of the economy — that Australians revved up their spending on vehicles across March to June this year. But it wasn’t just splashing cash on any old automotive. “There were record sales of electric and hybrid vehicles as more households looked to lower ongoing operating vehicle costs,” the Australian Bureau of Statistics told us.



Greater consciousness about environmental sustainability, growing proof of — and improvements in — the reliability of electric vehicles and their increasing affordability (helped by the government’s subsidy for EV purchases) have gradually been winning over Australian drivers looking to buy a new car. But this year, that trend has ramped up with nearly one in every two vehicles sold across April, May and June in Australia being either electric or hybrid. Data from the Australian Automobile Association shows fully electric vehicles now make up a fifth of new car sales compared to one-eighth six months ago. Basically, as our hip pockets have been squeezed by rising costs — especially the relatively high cost of fuel — Australians have been spending more…so that they can spend less (on things like fuel) in the future. The Reserve Bank could raise interest rates again last year after economic growth and inflation data came in higher than expected. Brent Lewin But like all other spending, our enthusiasm for EVs has an effect on the broader economy.



That’s because household spending makes up roughly half of our total economy. That means any change in our overall level of spending tends to have a pretty big effect on the direction of our economy. Related Article Opinion

Supermarkets I shopped at Costco to save money. Here’s what I learnt Millie Muroi Economics Writer From March to June, household spending grew 0.4 per cent and contributed to half — or 0.02 percentage points — of the overall growth figure of the economy. While economic growth hasn’t shot the lights out for a while, it has been trundling along at a bit more than 2 per cent annually as of the June quarter. And the most recent 0.4 per cent quarterly figure, while lower than three out of the four quarters before it, did come in slightly stronger than the 0.3 per cent that most economists were expecting. Our love of electric and hybrid vehicles also affects growth in other ways.



For example, there was a build-up in “inventories” — goods that businesses have stocked up — when it came to electric and hybrid cars as sellers prepared themselves for continued strong demand for these vehicles. When inventories increase, that technically adds to our economic growth. Of course, since mining is such a huge part of the Australian economy, that build-up in vehicle inventories wasn’t enough to offset a drawdown in inventories in the mining sector. Coal miners in particular, who faced strong demand for exports (partly due to a bounce back from weather disruptions earlier in the year), drew down on coal that they had stocked up to help meet the higher-than-usual demand. This meant inventories, which fell overall, ended up wiping 0.1 percentage points from economic growth. Meanwhile, the effect was reversed when it came to net trade (exports minus imports): another component of economic growth.



Coal exports have also helped to fire up Australian economic growth in the three months to June. Oscar Colman While the rise in electric vehicle imports took away from economic growth, the increase in coal exports (and their prices) helped to tip the balance so that net trade contributed 0.1 percentage points to economic growth. This was the first time since the December quarter of 2023 that net trade added, rather than detracted, from growth. There was also a step-up in government spending, including on initiatives such as free public transport, which contributed 0.1 percentage points to growth. Business investment spending, which was a major driver of growth in the March quarter, took a step back from the limelight. While it remained at a relatively high level thanks to construction linked to data centres, there was little change, meaning it didn’t contribute to growth ... at least not immediately. The uptake of electric and hybrid vehicles is a clear example of Australians trying to save money. After all, they will be able to reduce or completely wipe out their exposure to fuel prices, instead relying more heavily on electricity.



While electricity prices can also fluctuate, uptake of solar and renewable energy generation has put many Australian households in a better position when it comes to energy costs. In 2025, Australia led the world in per-person household solar, with more than four million homes — or one in three — equipped with solar panels. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street The world is facing a dual threat that could blow up markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That means, especially over the longer term, electric and hybrid vehicles should be deflationary: that is, they should help to put downward pressure on energy prices as demand for petrol drops and electricity demands are met using lower-cost solar power. Crucially, it will also help to act as a buffer against global economic shocks we can’t control (such as the most recent surge in oil prices which came about as a result of the Iran war). But in the short term, the slightly higher-than-expected economic growth and higher-than-expected inflation figures might put the Reserve Bank on edge.



Of course, as the bank often says, one set of numbers isn’t something to be too spooked by – and we have seen unemployment start to rise: a sign of capacity in the economy coming under less pressure. It’s also worth remembering that a lot of this data, especially the economic growth figures, come in with a lag: where we are now might be quite different to where we were a month – or several months – ago. But if demand, especially household spending, keeps coming in stronger than expected, and our productivity (how much we can make or provide for a given amount of resources) doesn’t improve, we might end up, at least in the short term, with higher prices and interest rates. Our enthusiasm for electric and hybrid vehicle purchases is driving economic growth forward, but to see the costs pay off – individually and for the broader economy – we may have to look further down the road. World.title: ‘They just want to burn the house down’: Behind the rise of One Nation in the Hunter
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twenty minutes into a One Nation press conference on a sunny Friday, the angular eyebrows of Senator Pauline Hanson begin to furrow, trying – like most attendees – to discern what her party’s new leader in NSW and candidate for Cessnock is saying in fluent Japanese. The event – held at the industrial headquarters of mining equipment supplier Drill Doctor on the outskirts of Singleton, an hour north-west of Newcastle – has been arranged so One Nation could announce the identities of its ambitious campaign for next year’s state election. Despite having no MPs sitting in Macquarie Street, the party talks of taking power. As Sean Bell, Hanson’s former adviser turned NSW senator, exclaims during a fundraiser at the Toronto Hotel that August evening: “I don’t think there’s ever been an opportunity like this.” Even Hanson’s admonishment of Cessnock candidate Mike Newman’s foreign interlude – “Excuse me. I think everyone else would like to know what you’re saying” – is swiftly brushed past, with the 53-year-old calmly explaining he will complete answering the Japanese journalist’s question in her native language before translating for the crowd. One Nation candidate Mike Newman answers a question in Japanese. James Brickwood The vignette is a microcosm of the strange new era of Australian politics. It’s one in which Newman – a cosmopolitan, bilingual investment banker with a Japanese wife, and a preacher of foreign investment – has joined One Nation, a nationalist populist party of the battler whose leader just months earlier rejected multiculturalism in favour of a “monoculture”. It marks another attempt by Hanson’s outfit to evolve from a closed tent mainly composed of insiders and loyalists to one recruiting the talent that it hopes will solidify its status as the nation’s leading conservative party.



Eight years after Hanson enlisted political maverick Mark Latham to be the party’s leader in NSW, One Nation hopes the Newman experiment can succeed where that marriage ended in acrimony. Related Article Updated

WA election ‘This is One Nation heartland now’: Labor shocked in bruising Secret Harbour byelection Less than 28 hours after announcing its first NSW candidates, One Nation easily claimed victory in a byelection in the West Australian state seat of Secret Harbour. Hanson is on the march. And the Hunter will be fertile ground for the party’s populist message in NSW. The Hunter is coal-mining country. It was once a Labor heartland. The eponymously named, blue-collar federal electorate has voted Labor since the electorate was established in the early 20th century. Cessnock, the state seat that sits within the Hunter’s boundaries, has been in the party’s column since 1927 aside from an aberrant result in 1988. One Nation’s Stuart Bonds carved a huge chunk of voters away from Labor in his first electoral outing. James Brickwood That sense of security was shattered in May 2019, when in his first crack at federal parliament, coal miner Stuart Bonds snatched 22 per cent of the primary vote in the Hunter. Joel Fitzgibbon, the veteran Labor frontbencher first elected in 1996, was left with a 3 per cent margin.



Bonds, who will now run at the top of the party’s upper house ticket in NSW, says despite living and working in the electorate, he was initially encouraged to run for the neighbouring seat of Lyne in 2019 because the prospect of winning the Hunter was considered fanciful. Related Article Exclusive

One Nation One Nation candidate launches broadside on NSW Liberal leader “You will never flip the Hunter in a million years,” Bonds says he was told by One Nation. “No one else could see this uprising happening, but I could see it, literally, at the coal face.” Ten people showed up for his first branch meeting in Singleton in 2018, Bonds remembers with a laugh. Since then, support for One Nation in the Hunter has fluctuated. Bonds’ primary vote of 16 per cent in the 2025 election was nearly 6 per cent lower than 2019. Yet, as proven by the South Australian state election in March and the Secret Harbour byelection, people are turning out to vote for One Nation in 2026. Polling by Resolve in August shows more than one in four NSW respondents would vote for the party if an election were held today. Former federal Labor MP Joel Fitzgibbon says voters are angry and want to send a message. James Brickwood But even those unprecedented polling figures understate how well the party is doing in regional seats. Where Bonds once tapped disaffected Labor voters looking to send the party a message, today One Nation has become the brand of choice in the Hunter.



“I’ve no doubt that [Hanson’s] support in the Hunter Valley is very, very strong,” Fitzgibbon says in an interview from his Cessnock home. “The question is: can the juggernaut continue to grow right until March of next year?” Related Article Immigration Five days later, Hanson still struggles to articulate migration policy “They want to send the most powerful message that they can – that they’re as angry as hell, and they’re not going to take it any more.” If anyone wanted to witness the popularity of Hanson in the Hunter, all they needed to do was visit the Singleton Golf Club on a Friday in late August. “She is the most in-demand person in Australia right now,” the host tells a crowd who have taken the Friday off to see Hanson, who is headlining a fundraiser for the Singleton charity shop’s cancer appeal. The 320-seat event, costing $125 a ticket, was sold out two weeks in advance. There was so much demand, Bonds claims organisers could have sold double the number of tickets.



Hanson is mobbed at Singleton Golf Club. James Brickwood The veteran’s popularity is undeniable among fans. James Brickwood It takes the Queensland senator – who walks in with Bonds and his Finnish tattooist wife, Sini – half an hour just to make it into the clubhouse after being swamped by patrons looking for selfies or simply to hold her hand and offer words of support. A heavily tattooed man with a flannelette shirt and handlebar moustache reminiscent of Mark “Chopper” Read sheepishly asks his friend whether he thinks Hanson will take a photo with him. “You can stay at my place,” a woman tells Hanson when asked if she’ll be visiting the Hunter again. If Hanson’s popularity is undeniable, so is the sense that Anthony Albanese is on the nose. The second and third prize of the charity auction are two “Fire the Liar” packages – name-checking One Nation’s campaign against Albanese – each containing a party shirt and cap signed by Hanson and the opportunity for the winner to have their photo taken with her. The room is decorated with One Nation posters. James Brickwood

World.title: What Trump’s decoy plane ruse tells us about poor leadership
World.content:
NationalDonald Trump Opinion What Trump’s decoy plane ruse tells us about poor leadership Bram Connolly Leadership expert September 4, 2026 — 11:30am

September 4, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I suspect I won’t be allowed in the United States again after this but being able to respectfully talk truth to power is a fundamental right of a Western democracy, so I take my chances. Trump arrived for the NATO summit in Ankara on Air Force One but didn’t go home on it. AP Last month, as reported by The Washington Post and CBS News, the president of the US boarded the presidential aircraft Air Force One in front of the cameras at Ankara airport, and then he quietly left it. Facing a credible Iranian missile threat, he was reportedly moved by catering truck to a smaller military aircraft and flown out under a different call sign. The journalists and staff who boarded the original plane were told to keep their window shades down and they weren’t told why, and they also weren’t told the president was gone. Then, as scheduled, they flew home, unknowingly aboard an aircraft a hostile state had decided was a legitimate target. Set aside the politics. I want to look at this through an entirely different lens: leadership.



I have spent three decades now in the Australian army, much of it in Special Forces, and my consultancy teaches leadership to executives. The definition of leadership I use is a demanding one: leadership is compelling other people to do what you want them to do because they want to do it. It’s important to understand that it’s not because they’re ordered to, and not because they’re deceived into it. It’s actually your credibility, your example and your care for them that make following you the thing they choose to do. Bram Connolly, on assignment with the ADF Special Forces. By that definition, what happened at Ankara wasn’t leadership. There’s a simple framework we use to explain how leadership is projected: what leaders say, what they do, what they prioritise and what they recognise. Words are obviously the cheapest of the four, and actions take a bit more energy to demonstrate. But it’s the last two, a leader’s priorities and what they recognise, that are impossible to fake. Let’s run the Ankara decision through that framework. What was said: that the flight was dangerous because of the adversaries “we have to deal with”. What was done: the principal was extracted from the danger while his own press corps and staff were left sitting inside it, shades drawn. What was prioritised: the safety of one man, and the secrecy of the manoeuvre, above the informed consent of his staff and those who convey his messages. And what was recognised? When later asked about the shades, the reported response to the journalists was, in effect, that if he went down, they’d go down, too; followed by the suggestion that perhaps they should change professions. That is recognition of a kind. It recognises that the staff are what made the decoy compelling.



Now, the counter-argument deserves a fair hearing, of course. A head of state is not an ordinary passenger; protective agencies exist precisely to move the principal out of harm’s way, and continuity of government is a legitimate priority. I don’t dispute any of that. The security professionals who designed the switch did their jobs and they did it well. My argument is not with the extraction. It is with what happened to everyone else. The Committee to Protect Journalists put it plainly: people covering the president should be informed of credible threats so they can make their own informed decisions about their own safety. Deciding to accept risk is a personal right. Having risk assigned to you unknowingly, as a decoy for someone else, I would contest that won’t be forgotten, and that’s where he has lost their trust. Moreover, trust is built from three things: credibility (do you know what you’re doing?), reliability (do you do what you say?) and intimacy (can I be safe and honest with you?). And it is divided – divided, not merely reduced – by one thing: self-interest. You can be supremely credible and impressively reliable and have intimate working relationships, but the moment the people behind you conclude that, when it matters most, you will throw them under the bus (a narcissist manoeuvre), nothing else matters. Trust doesn’t just erode in that moment, it actually collapses and it can never be won back. I know this equation from the other side of it. In Afghanistan, commanding soldiers in combat, the one thing I found hardest to do was delegate risk. I did do it – I often delegated risk to a lead vehicle and one driver, and I still haven’t forgiven myself for it – but the driver knew and accepted the risk. Unlike Trump’s staff, my staffer was given the option. Whatever we drove into, we drove into together. Soldiers will forgive a leader almost anything except the discovery that their exposure and the leader’s are valued differently. I’ve just written a book, 100 Ways I Almost Died, and if there’s a thread running through all those moments, it’s this: I was never exposed to risk alone. My men were beside me and they knew everything I knew. The knowledge that the risk is shared is the intimacy in the equation. It’s why they followed me in training and combat. It’s why, years later, I think they still would. Leaders at every level, in every organisation, face a quieter version of the Ankara choice most business days: who absorbs the risk, who gets told the truth and who is left with the shades down. When the pressure comes, your people will not remember your speeches. They will remember which plane you put them on.



Bram Connolly, DSM, is a former Special Forces officer, founder of Hindsight Leadership and Resilience, and the author of 100 Ways I Almost Died (published by Allen & Unwin). Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Raygun’s Netflix doco seems like a mockumentary. It’s actually a disturbing love story
World.content:
September 4, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Minutes into Netflix’s new doco Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly, all I could think of was Christopher Guest’s Best in Show meets Chazz Michael Michaels from Blades of Glory. Mostly because of Rachael Gunn’s husband Samuel Free, breakdancing name Sammy Sex, who speaks to camera with an American twang and what looks to be an elite home perm. By turns, Sammy looks cooked and thrilled, but maintains one thing throughout: that his wife is a world-class B-Girl. Rachael Gunn in a still from the Netflix documentary Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly. Netflix And therein lies the rub. This isn’t a mockumentary of the Raygun kerfuffle that swept the Paris Olympics. It’s actually a love story. And the question it throws up extends to all of us: how much should the people who love you most tell you the truth? Even Raygun’s terrific parents seem bemused by her Olympic selection. Not Sammy. He’s in her corner, from practice sessions to that final unforgettable Olympic routine – yep, zero points, the sprinkler, the move where she lay on the floor opening and closing like a set of tongs, the kangaroo hops.



“I was, like, struck by the beauty of the performance,” he says of her final battle. “It was the essence of creativity.” Well. Risking coming late to the pile-on, but I grew up on Dance Fever, the TV disco dance-off that spun out of Saturday Night Fever, and I know quality dance. Watching Raygun, I had that feeling you get in front of a Jackson Pollock: I could do that. The “essence of creativity” is a bit rich. Raygun’s husband Samuel Free, aka Sammy Sex, in Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly. Sammy’s more interesting than his wife (who at one point says, and I can hardly bear to type it, “We’re not in Kansas any more”) in her own show. He’s doing what a good husband is supposed to do: backing his person. And he seems sincere, which is the worry. A flatterer knows they’re lying. A delusional spouse doesn’t.



Love has a dangerous side effect. It makes the person you adore look like the person you think they could be. Iris Murdoch called love “the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real”. Not just a fella with a blind spot, Sammy’s managed something else: the refusal to see what’s real. Related Article Performing arts ‘Ridiculed’: How Australia’s breaking community was left reeling after Paris When does backing a spouse tip into actively failing them? Perhaps Ryan Reynolds should have had a word with Blake Lively before the Baldoni legal bloodbath. Maybe Harry could have said, Meg, the homemade bath salts are making you ridiculous. Certainly, Melania should have seen the gilt work in the Oval Office and confiscated the glue gun. A good spouse will say you’re smart enough to go on Sale of the Century, that you killed it at karaoke, that you’re legit hilarious, that you smell incredible, that your deadlifting has really come on, that you organise great holidays. A delusional one will say ... you could be Miss Universe and be boss cocky of Mensa and your tailgating doesn’t matter and sure, you could win breakdancing at the Olympics.



Because the love that never says the hard thing doesn’t make the hard part go away. It outsources it. The world eventually delivers the verdict that love withheld, and it has no stake in being gentle. Old story, but fits here: when our middle son hit a junior footy milestone, we made a banner: “48 great games and two poor ones.” Yep, it got a few laughs from one resilient boy and a small crowd. Raygun: not so lucky. Her feedback arrived via a braying audience of millions. Rachael “Raygun” Gunn competes at the 2024 Olympics. Getty Images Maybe Sammy couldn’t say, “darl, you’re not much chop” because he was too close. Maybe Rachael couldn’t hear it, although she did tell a psychologist pre-Olympics she feared being a laughingstock, which suggests self-awareness. Either way, it would have been kinder for someone at her kitchen table to tell her the truth before we all did.

World.title: NFL stars land in Melbourne with a week to prepare for MCG clash
World.content:
SportNFL 2026 NFL stars land in Melbourne with a week to prepare for MCG clash Josh Dubow September 4, 2026 — 11:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The San Francisco 49ers have arrived in Melbourne after embarking on the longest road trip in NFL history. Ahead of next Friday’s historic season-opener at the MCG against the Los Angeles Rams, the 49ers were given advice on how to eat and hydrate, what to do after arriving and the best options of when to sleep on the approximately 8000-mile (13,000km) flight that took about 16 hours. Loading The two teams have taken vastly different approaches to the long-haul journey, with the Rams not arriving in Melbourne until 24 hours before the match, whereas the Nines left home on Wednesday (PDT) and arrived at Tullamarine Friday morning (AEST), giving them a hole week to acclimatise. Before the flight, Niners defensive lineman and avid world traveller Keion White outlined his personal approach.



“I don’t know if you can OD on melatonin, but I’m going to try,” he said. “Take five melatonins, go to sleep on the plane. As soon as I wake up, I’m taking five more. Just keep rolling like that.” While some members of the 49ers organisation, including coach Kyle Shanahan, have been lamenting the season-opening trip, White is embracing it after already playing games in Germany and London earlier in his career. The San Francisco 49ers arrive in Melbourne a week early for their game at the MCG. Rhys Duke He plans to watch TikTok before he arrives to get ideas of what to do and then get on public transport and explore after team meetings on the first day to help make sure he stays up all day and gets onto a normal sleep schedule as quickly as possible. “I’m an experience guy,” he said. “If I’m up, walking around, just going to go do stuff, I’ll be up. Just go explore. We will have meetings and everything like that, but once I do that, I’m out exploring Melbourne and getting around town.”



Both the 49ers and Rams studied the process intently in the off-season, even sending advance staffers to Australia to report back on how long it took to adjust to the time change. The Niners will hold a light practice on Saturday, take Sunday off and then have a normal stretch of three practices on Monday through Wednesday before playing the opener on Friday morning. The 49ers looked in good spirits on their arrival at Tullamarine. Rhys Duke They will leave right after the game and are expected to land back in the Bay Area on Friday afternoon. They then will be able to take the weekend off before preparing to play Miami on September 20. “It’s a big adjustment on the body,” Shanahan said. “So, the recommendation for everybody has been to tell us when to go, and it’s made a lot of sense. I know how our players feel also. I was a little bit on the fence. Science wasn’t and what I was reported on and our players weren’t at all. So that helped me get off the fence.”



The Rams consulted with their own scientists and came up with the opposite approach. They will do most of their practice at home and aren’t expected to arrive in Australia until about 24 hours before the game, hoping to bypass jet lag by having a short stay down under. The better option won’t not be known until after the game. The players dressed for comfort on the flight. Rhys Duke The approach by the Niners has made the past few days a whirlwind. The players got the weekend off after playing the final exhibition game on Thursday night in Las Vegas and resumed practice on Monday – the day after their roster was reduced to 53 players. The front office had to make those cuts, put together a practice squad and figure out which players would be healthy for week one to make sure they had the correct roster in place before departing.



“There’s a lot behind the scenes,” general manager John Lynch said. “Our logistics folks, our folks that work in the cafe, have just gone to tremendous lengths, our health and performance team, to make sure that we’re giving our players the best opportunity to feel right when they play down there in Australia. Everything from getting visas, which much more complicated than I ever knew, and they’ve been outstanding. ... Hats off to those guys for pulling off a monumental task, and it’s not done yet.” Lynch said he had to make sure all the practice squad players he wanted to sign had passports with one needing his parents to send it overnight. It was an even bigger scramble for offensive lineman Jarrett Patterson, who was acquired in a trade from Houston on Sunday. The San Francisco 49ers arrived in Melbourne on Friday. Rhys Duke “They were like, hey, do you have a passport? We’re leaving for Australia in three days,” he said. “I was like, ‘Whoa!’ It’s obviously a quick turnaround getting here a couple hours after I found out and now getting ready for Australia.” But in all, the players are welcoming the challenge and opportunity. Cornerback Deommodore Lenoir said he’d travel 30 hours if needed to play in an NFL game and rookie De’Zhaun Stribling has a must-see item on his to-do list before making his debut.

World.title: Coles cuts ties with controversial CIA-linked data giant Palantir
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologySupermarkets Coles cuts ties with controversial CIA-linked data giant Palantir David Swan September 4, 2026 — 11:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Coles will cut ties with Palantir, the controversial US data giant whose software underpins American deportation raids and battlefield targeting systems. The supermarket has confirmed its contract with the company will not extend beyond 2027, ending a partnership signed in early 2024 that gave Palantir access to more than 10 billion rows of data covering every store, every shift and each of the retailer’s 120,000 employees. Coles’ decision came after a campaign that collected more than 85,000 signatures and placed digital billboards outside stores. Eamon Gallagher “Coles and Palantir have agreed to conclude their partnership after three years of collaboration,” the two companies said in an identical statement. Coles said a transition plan was under way and the final timing was not settled. The confirmation follows a campaign launched in February by activist group GetUp, which claimed the outcome as a win.



“Nobody should need a national campaign to find out whether military-grade surveillance tech is watching them buy bread and milk,” interim chief executive Paul Ferris said. Activist group GetUp targeted Coles’ partnership with Palantir. “It’s a shame it took 85,000 people, 700 billboards and a shareholder resolution before Coles did what it should have on day one.” Neither company would say when the decision was made. The campaign gathered more than 85,000 signatures and put digital billboards outside close to 700 stores. One video accusing Coles of watching its shoppers was viewed 3 million times.



Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel. Bloomberg Palantir, co-founded by Peter Thiel, built its business inside the US national security apparatus and sells to militaries, intelligence agencies and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Thiel has said he no longer believes freedom and democracy are compatible. The company is worth about $US330 billion. Its chief executive, Alex Karp, holds a doctorate in social theory from a German university, practises tai chi, and has published a manifesto arguing Palantir is the democratic West’s best hope of staying ahead of authoritarian rivals. Surveillance technology has become a flashpoint in Australian retail since the Administrative Review Tribunal ruled in February that Bunnings could keep using facial recognition to fight theft, while affirming it had breached privacy law by failing to tell customers. Coles has rejected the surveillance characterisation throughout, and says the campaign traded in misinformation.



A spokesman said the software was used for rostering, store operations and supply chain planning, and ran inside Coles’ own environment under Coles controls. “Palantir does not control the data, nor can it independently repurpose it,” the spokesman said. Coles said Palantir had never been involved in CCTV, facial recognition or any of its crime-prevention measures. It does not use facial recognition in any store, and a limited proof of concept was run in a testing environment in response to rising violence against staff. The deal was pitched more expansively in 2024. Coles chief operating officer Matt Swindells said it would “redefine how we think about our workforce”. Palantir’s global head of commercial technologies, Ted Mabrey, said the retailer was not treating the software as a “toy”, pointing to Airbus crediting the company with a 30 per cent acceleration in A350 production.



Much of a recent Coles letter to ethical share trading platform SIX, seen by this masthead, was devoted to an attack on the campaign’s methods. Coles said GetUp had used footage of an identifiable worker at its Pacific Fair store and superimposed an employee number and an “84 per cent” working efficiency score over her image. Both were invented, the letter said, and came from no Coles system. Related Article Updated

Privacy Bunnings wins appeal over use of facial recognition technology to fight crime The worker was recognised by others who saw the  and was left distressed, according to the letter, and her mother lodged a written complaint. GetUp has said it bought the footage from a stock site and later blurred her face. “It is particularly troubling that this was done as part of a campaign being conducted in the name of employee privacy,” wrote Coles general manager of investor relations Anita Healy.



The letter asked SIX to withdraw a shareholder resolution, backed by 189 individual investors, that called on the board to commission a human rights impact assessment ahead of November’s annual general meeting. Coles said SIX had since withdrawn it. SIX environmental, social and governance manager James Alexander said the outcome showed the power of small shareholders acting together. “Hundreds of Coles investors backed planned resolutions asking legitimate questions about data governance and human rights due diligence,” he said. Digital Rights Watch head of policy Tom Sulston said Palantir’s politics were incompatible with Australian values of fairness and equality. GetUp acting chief executive Paul Ferris claimed the outcome as a win. Steven Siewert



“It doesn’t belong in Australia and it certainly doesn’t belong in the places we depend on day-to-day, like supermarkets,” he said. Coles is not the first customer to walk away. Spain has moved to block Palantir from public procurement, French and German intelligence agencies picked a domestic rival, and a British parliamentary committee recommended against renewing a contract. Palantir said its technology had delivered value across Coles’ operations and had helped the retailer put team members in the right place at the right time. Its other Australian clients include Westpac, Rio Tinto and Westrac. Coles was its first Australian retailer. “Our privacy laws are decades behind this sort of technology,” Ferris said. “Coles was chapter one, but every board in the country should be checking its contracts.” Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: Australians are flocking to electric vehicles. There’s a hidden cost
World.content:
BusinessThe economyGDP Opinion Australians are flocking to electric vehicles. There’s a hidden cost Millie Muroi Economics Writer Updated September 4, 2026 — 11:16am , first published September 4, 2026 — 5:00am

Updated September 4, 2026 — 11:16am ,first published September 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You can’t blame Australians for seeing fuel prices over the past few months and deciding to ditch their petrol-powered cars. As Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock pointed out at a recent press conference, petrol prices are one of the most visible — and therefore memorable — prices, with most of us passing a petrol station somewhere on our daily commutes. Electric and hybrid vehicle sales having been revving up the Australian economy as people look for ways to save. Bloomberg While petrol prices have fallen from their peak of about $2.50 a litre in our major cities earlier this year, they’re still hovering at about $2 a litre after the government’s fuel excise discount ended in August. That’s about 20 cents more expensive per litre than the average petrol price across our major cities in 2025. Fuel prices are significant — not just because they make up about 3 per cent of an Australian household’s spending — but because they affect how much it costs for businesses, especially in the transport, farming and aviation sectors, to provide their goods and services.



As we know, inflation, or price growth, is still a big challenge for the Reserve Bank (and many of us paying higher prices for everyday items). In the 12 months to July, prices across the economy grew 3.5 per cent — lower than the 3.8 per cent they were growing at in the year to June, but still well above the bank’s target range of 2 to 3 per cent. Related Article Australian economy Chalmers admits tax reforms helped drag down house prices It’s a rational response for people to look for ways to save money. We know, for example, from the recent earnings season where Australian businesses reported their profits, that customers remain hungry for a bargain. We also know from the most recent “national accounts” — which gives us a snapshot of the economy — that Australians revved up their spending on vehicles across March to June this year. But it wasn’t just splashing cash on any old automotive. “There were record sales of electric and hybrid vehicles as more households looked to lower ongoing operating vehicle costs,” the Australian Bureau of Statistics told us.



Greater consciousness about environmental sustainability, growing proof of — and improvements in — the reliability of electric vehicles and their increasing affordability (helped by the government’s subsidy for EV purchases) have gradually been winning over Australian drivers looking to buy a new car. But this year, that trend has ramped up with nearly one in every two vehicles sold across April, May and June in Australia being either electric or hybrid. Data from the Australian Automobile Association shows fully electric vehicles now make up a fifth of new car sales compared to one-eighth six months ago. Basically, as our hip pockets have been squeezed by rising costs — especially the relatively high cost of fuel — Australians have been spending more…so that they can spend less (on things like fuel) in the future. The Reserve Bank could raise interest rates again last year after economic growth and inflation data came in higher than expected. Brent Lewin But like all other spending, our enthusiasm for EVs has an effect on the broader economy.



That’s because household spending makes up roughly half of our total economy. That means any change in our overall level of spending tends to have a pretty big effect on the direction of our economy. Related Article Opinion

Supermarkets I shopped at Costco to save money. Here’s what I learnt Millie Muroi Economics Writer From March to June, household spending grew 0.4 per cent and contributed to half — or 0.02 percentage points — of the overall growth figure of the economy. While economic growth hasn’t shot the lights out for a while, it has been trundling along at a bit more than 2 per cent annually as of the June quarter. And the most recent 0.4 per cent quarterly figure, while lower than three out of the four quarters before it, did come in slightly stronger than the 0.3 per cent that most economists were expecting. Our love of electric and hybrid vehicles also affects growth in other ways.



For example, there was a build-up in “inventories” — goods that businesses have stocked up — when it came to electric and hybrid cars as sellers prepared themselves for continued strong demand for these vehicles. When inventories increase, that technically adds to our economic growth. Of course, since mining is such a huge part of the Australian economy, that build-up in vehicle inventories wasn’t enough to offset a drawdown in inventories in the mining sector. Coal miners in particular, who faced strong demand for exports (partly due to a bounce back from weather disruptions earlier in the year), drew down on coal that they had stocked up to help meet the higher-than-usual demand. This meant inventories, which fell overall, ended up wiping 0.1 percentage points from economic growth. Meanwhile, the effect was reversed when it came to net trade (exports minus imports): another component of economic growth.



Coal exports have also helped to fire up Australian economic growth in the three months to June. Oscar Colman While the rise in electric vehicle imports took away from economic growth, the increase in coal exports (and their prices) helped to tip the balance so that net trade contributed 0.1 percentage points to economic growth. This was the first time since the December quarter of 2023 that net trade added, rather than detracted, from growth. There was also a step-up in government spending, including on initiatives such as free public transport, which contributed 0.1 percentage points to growth. Business investment spending, which was a major driver of growth in the March quarter, took a step back from the limelight. While it remained at a relatively high level thanks to construction linked to data centres, there was little change, meaning it didn’t contribute to growth ... at least not immediately. The uptake of electric and hybrid vehicles is a clear example of Australians trying to save money. After all, they will be able to reduce or completely wipe out their exposure to fuel prices, instead relying more heavily on electricity.



While electricity prices can also fluctuate, uptake of solar and renewable energy generation has put many Australian households in a better position when it comes to energy costs. In 2025, Australia led the world in per-person household solar, with more than four million homes — or one in three — equipped with solar panels. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street The world is facing a dual threat that could blow up markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That means, especially over the longer term, electric and hybrid vehicles should be deflationary: that is, they should help to put downward pressure on energy prices as demand for petrol drops and electricity demands are met using lower-cost solar power. Crucially, it will also help to act as a buffer against global economic shocks we can’t control (such as the most recent surge in oil prices which came about as a result of the Iran war). But in the short term, the slightly higher-than-expected economic growth and higher-than-expected inflation figures might put the Reserve Bank on edge.



Of course, as the bank often says, one set of numbers isn’t something to be too spooked by – and we have seen unemployment start to rise: a sign of capacity in the economy coming under less pressure. It’s also worth remembering that a lot of this data, especially the economic growth figures, come in with a lag: where we are now might be quite different to where we were a month – or several months – ago. But if demand, especially household spending, keeps coming in stronger than expected, and our productivity (how much we can make or provide for a given amount of resources) doesn’t improve, we might end up, at least in the short term, with higher prices and interest rates. Our enthusiasm for electric and hybrid vehicle purchases is driving economic growth forward, but to see the costs pay off – individually and for the broader economy – we may have to look further down the road. World.title: SPCA issues new welfare standard after RNZ questions about so-called 'frankenchicken'
World.content:
The SPCA has issued a new voluntary standard for chicken welfare after questions from RNZ about fast-growing "frankenchickens".

Currently, the SPCA's welfare standards for chicken farms have no rules on fast-growing breeds. This has sparked concern that the chickens bred for meat on New Zealand farms grow so fast they can have difficulty walking or get stuck on their backs.

"These guys get bigger and bigger and bigger and bigger in a very fast time frame, and if they tip over, it can be a little bit like a turtle being on its back," says avian veterinarian Jodi Salinsky.

RNZ referred footage from two farms taken in 2024 by activists to the SPCA. The footage shows some birds apparently stricken on their backs. Both farms go above and beyond what's legally required and are SPCA certified. This tells buyers "they are helping raise standards of care well beyond legal requirements as well as providing a good life for New Zealand's animals" according to the SPCA.

SPCA chief scientific officer Arnja Dale says it has not required slower growing breeds because they don't exist commercially here. Making it a requirement would risk producers leaving the voluntary SPCA certification scheme altogether.

"The fast-growing chickens would still be in those sheds, but SPCA certified's standards, oversight and auditing would not," Dale says.

However, SPCA-commissioned research in 2025, which has not been previously released, found more than half (59 percent) of people surveyed wanted fast-growing chickens phased out, and only 11 percent were opposed.

One quarter of respondents wouldn't be prepared to pay more, but 28 percent indicated they would pay 10 percent more for slow-growing breeds. A further 17 percent said they would pay five percent more. The SPCA has developed a new "enhanced" standard, which calls for a transition to slower-growing chickens.

The new Welfare Plus+ standard was published this week in response to the questions raised by RNZ. There is no timeline to make the new standard part of the baseline SPCA certification.

"SPCA will always take a stand. We work with industry to improve animals' lives today. This does not stop us challenging industry to do better tomorrow," Dale says.

Animal welfare standards need to "progress on many fronts".

"We cannot focus so exclusively on one goal that we turn our backs on the millions of chickens we can help today."

The rise of the so-called 'frankenchicken'

Since the 1950s the shape and size of commercial meat chickens has changed massively. Once svelte birds have ballooned to be barrel-like.

Their rapid growth isn't a result of growth hormones. Chickens were selectively bred over decades to be bigger and eat less.

One of the biggest changes has been in their main breast muscle, which one study says increased by approximately 80 percent between 1957 and 2005.

Activists have nicknamed them "frankenchickens" and all of New Zealand's commercially-produced meat chickens, even organic chickens, are these fast-growing breeds.

A meat chicken's life-span before slaughter is now 34 to 39 days. In the 1950s it took 16 weeks to reach roast-ready size. RNZ / Creative Commons

This rapid growth can come at a cost. The same scientific paper that tracked the size changes over the decades noted there were unintended effects of the rapid growth including skeletal defects, metabolic disorders and altered immune function.

Another issue common among fast-growing breeds is difficulty walking. A Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) study found approximately 30 percent of birds' ability to move was affected.

A study carried out in commercial sheds has compared the gaits and welfare of a slow-growing Hubbard Redbro bird against a Ross 308, a common fast-growing breed. It found the slower-growing birds had better leg health than their counterparts and fewer died before they were large enough to slaughter. The slower growing birds took an average of 5.5 days more to grow and were a lighter weight than the fast-growing birds.

Poultry industry's response

Poultry Industry Association New Zealand (PIANZ) executive director Fiona MacMillan says there's no need to switch breeds.

"The birds that we farm have been bred, by a process of selective breeding, to be both healthy and fast growing."

They grow fast but also have "strong bones, good overall resilience and health." Welfare flows from good flock management by ensuring food, conditions and stocking density are optimal, MacMillan says.

Tegel told RNZ it's confident in the genetics of its chickens. The companies supplying the breeds have spent decades selecting for a range of characteristics, not simply growth rate.

"We therefore do not consider growth rate in isolation to be an appropriate measure of welfare."

It says the "broad body shape" and "developed breast muscle" of its birds can affect the centre of balance, which could be why the birds in the video were unable to right themselves.

"Under normal circumstances, our growers conduct regular shed walks and would identify any bird in this position and return it to an upright position."

Activist videos

Animals Aotearoa, a welfare lobby group, supplied footage to RNZ it says was taken in 2024 by "investigators" entering two different farms without permission in the dead of night.

The group released the footage to advocate for a move to slower-growing breeds that are part of a Better Chicken Commitment it wants companies to adopt. It says these breeds would be less likely to get trapped on their backs or experience lameness.

Tegel confirmed both farms identified by Animals Aotearoa were Tegel suppliers at the time the footage was taken, though it couldn't verify if the footage was taken at those locations. RNZ has verified the location of the farm where chickens were on their backs.

The second farm was visited by the SPCA after being given the location by Animals Aotearoa, although it says it wasn't able to independently verify the footage was taken there, or even in New Zealand.

Avian veterinarian Jodi Salinsky told RNZ, without being able to examine the birds, she couldn't diagnose the exact issue each was experiencing, but she thought the video raised welfare concerns.

Jodi Salinsky. Sharon Brettkelly

"A bird laying on its back is going to be in distress if they're there for a significant amount of time. They do not rest on their back in any way, shape, or form."

She says it's likely the birds were stuck because of the large breasts and rapid growth rate, which are a feature of fast-growing chicken breeds. The footage did not show anything illegal, however.

Farms are required to check chickens daily and treat or euthanise sick chickens. As a snapshot in time it's impossible to tell if this was being completed from the footage, Salinsky says.

No birds were on their backs in footage from a second farm, but Salinsky observed some of the birds appeared to have fluid in their abdomens. She also noted the birds often only walked for a few steps, before stopping and sitting, a behaviour she says is common because their bodies grow so quickly.

"Pop holes" to the outdoors were visible in some of the footage and images, which means the chickens are considered free range.

"[Free range] just means they have access to outdoors. But how many chickens can even walk that far to get there?"

PIANZ's MacMillan says the activists recording the footage were intruders, which can distress birds.

"The birds would have been really disturbed by the presence of strangers in the shed, appearing out of the dark and shining lights on them."

Vets have told her that birds prone on their backs are occasionally seen in farms in small numbers.

"If any birds should end up like this, farmers will spot this and correct the situation on their regular visits to the sheds. But again, it needs to be stressed, it is not common," she says.

Tegel's spokesperson says birds trapped on their backs is an "unacceptable welfare outcome" but it agrees the birds in the video could have been startled by the activists in the shed causing them to "tumble" over each other in fright as they moved away from strangers.

It is irresponsible for people to enter sheds without permission, Tegel says.

"It creates a serious biosecurity risk and can significantly stress the birds. Poultry farms operate under strict biosecurity requirements to prevent disease and protect bird health, and anyone entering a shed must follow strict biosecurity procedures."

Salinsky says it's plausible some birds may have been knocked over when people entered the shed but noted some appeared to have a large amount of poo next to them and thought it likely to have been in the same position for some time. "I don't think a bird would have pooped that much if they just got scared and fell over."

Activists entered two SPCA approved chicken farms to collect footage in 2024 Supplied / Animals Aotearoa

Animals Aotearoa executive director Marianne Macdonald says the investigators take precautions to avoid spreading disease. Boots were cleaned before entry and disposable boot covers and gloves were worn. They don't travel between farms and don't have contact with any birds for at least a week before they enter a farm.

She says investigators pause after entering a shed and wait until the chickens are used to their presence before moving around to film.

Most people would be surprised that the chickens in the footage are considered to be free-range and living a "good life," Macdonald says.

Improving conditions in sheds by adding perch space or doors to the outside is no use if the birds aren't physically capable of using them, she says.

"We've got to transition away from these birds that have suffering coded in their genetics."

Macdonald welcomes the new SPCA welfare standard, but says it doesn't go far enough.

"What's critical now is a firm deadline to phase out their current SPCA Certified standard. Right now, they're still certifying preventable suffering. They need to commit to real change."

The current welfare standard

SPCA certified farms are visited four times a year by a third party auditing company. One visit is announced and the other three are surprise visits. In addition, farms must meet other criteria including providing perches, reduced stocking in sheds and a limit on hours of light.

Marcelo Rodriguez Ferrere is an associate professor at the University of Auckland and the president of the New Zealand Animal Law Association. He says the Animal Welfare Act and a code of welfare for meat chickens has minimum standards, but there are no rules that expressly stop fast-growing breeds from being farmed.

The current 2018 code recommends that the selection of genetics "should be encouraged to promote physical traits that support the expression of normal behaviours in meat chickens". It does note concerns around trends in the industry, "particularly in relation to rapid growth rates" and says the industry should take steps to ensure welfare problems don't become "ethically unacceptable" to New Zealanders.

This code of welfare is due to be reviewed.

"We have remarkably little visibility about what happens behind closed doors on farms in New Zealand," Rodriguez Ferrere says. This is why people enter farms without permission and take footage to show people what's happening.

"I don't think people would go to Kentucky Fried Chicken and think that that's the way that chickens are farmed in this country, but it's entirely the way that chickens are farmed in this country, and so perhaps there's a broader systemic problem at issue here."

Animals Aotearoa has been agitating for change since 2021 when it championed a voluntary welfare code called the Better Chicken Commitment, which includes a move to slower-growing breeds.

It has rattled the doors of food meal services, fast-food chains and supermarkets aiming to create demand for slow-growing breeds in hatcheries.

Macdonald claims progress getting food brands on board with slower-growing breeds has been stymied by the SPCA's existing certification.

"Food businesses come back to us and say, 'Well, we're using free-range SPCA-certified chickens, and the SPCA said this is okay, so we're not going to do anything else'."

The blue badge of certification provides a "shield" for the chicken industry, she says.

The role of supermarkets and takeaway stores

The adoption of slower-growing breeds has been mixed around the world. In the Netherlands, all free-range chicken meat sold in supermarkets comes from slower-growing breeds.

In New Zealand, Woolworths says it has no plans to transition to slow-growing breeds.

"We remain committed to continuously improving animal welfare across our supply chain - as reflected in our 2030 Sustainability Strategy and the fact that 100% of Woolworths brand fresh chicken is SPCA certified," a spokesperson told RNZ.

Foodstuffs, which owns New World, says chicken producers are better placed to comment on breed selection than they are.

In the United Kingdom, KFC and other takeaway brands committed to moving to slower-growing breeds by 2026. The plan was abandoned, however, in favour of a new industry standard that permits fast-growing chickens, which they say create less greenhouse gas.

In New Zealand, Domino's has previously committed to using slow-growing chickens by 2026. It wouldn't comment on whether it has been able to meet its deadline, or challenges it has faced trying to meet the goal.

Another pizza brand, HELL, has committed to switching to slower-growing breeds.

There are very few companies in New Zealand that supply chicks to chicken producers. Aviagen didn't respond to RNZ's queries about the availability of slow growing breeds.

Bromley Park Hatcheries general manager Brent Williams says in 2018 the company did bring in a slower-growing breed, but it didn't sell well. It has since sold part of the company to Inghams, and focuses on egg-laying chickens.

World.title: Push for long-term solar energy plans that survive elections
World.content:
Push for cross-party plan on solar energy Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The Sustainable Energy Association is pushing for a cross-party government plan for solar energy that will last longer than an electoral cycle.

Solar energy has moved from the margins of mainstream political debate into a fully fledged election issue in 2026 - with Labour, National, the Greens and other parties making solar commitments.

The Sustainable Energy Association's COO Gareth Williams hoped future governments could develop long-term solar plans that survived electoral cycles.

Williams told Morning Report, the association's annual conference on Friday, was being attended by all the political parties this year.

"Our theme last year was 'this is our time', and we were right I think... we're being aspirational but for good reason, I think, but it's probably exceeded out expectations these last 12 months."

Solar energy in homes had really taken off in February, Williams said, in large part due to the fuel and energy crisis caused by the Iran war.

A house with a new solar system. (File photo) Supplied by Lightforce Solar

"We saw a jump around March and that momentum has just continued and it's really taken off."

In the past, Williams said there had been policies from parties about solar energy, but this year every party now had an interest in it.

"It's painful out there for people and solar is by far the cheapest way of people having electricity into their homes."

There had been a lot of work installing solar in some areas of the country, Williams said, especially around Wānaka, but the number of homes with solar in Auckland remained surprisingly low, with less than 2 percent of homes with solar installed.

"Auckland is near the bottom for some reason and about to be overtaken by the West Coast of the South Island, which is ironic, really."

Williams feared too much government involvement in solar energy could be a hindrance and said it needed to be understood how significant solar energy would be to New Zealand's infrastructure.

"The growth is coming, what's really important is quality, we don't want to see what happened in Australia where every man and his dog suddenly became a solar installer and there were all sorts of issues."

Roughly 4 percent of homes in New Zealand have solar panels installed, whereas in Australia it was roughly 40 percent.

World.title: Party drug MDMA gets official approval as PTSD treatment
World.content:
Two New Zealand psychiatrists have been approved by MedSafe to prescribe and administer MDMA for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder.

MDMA is a synthetic psychoactive drug used recreationally, often called 'ecstasy', 'E' or 'molly'.

It is the first time Medsafe has granted approvals for this type of therapy.

Until now, MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD has not been available as a treatment option in New Zealand. Australia became the first country to allow authorised psychiatrists to prescribe MDMA for PTSD in July 2023.

The two psychiatrists with approval are Wellington's Dr Gary Wynn and Auckland's Dr Tom Paterson. The pair spent more than a year working through the regulatory process, they said in a statement.

Wynn specialises in PTSD and trauma, and Paterson in addiction.

Wynn, who had more than 20 years' experience, explained the drug was often referred to as an empathogen - a kind of psychoactive drug which increases empathy, emotional openness, and connectedness towards others.

"In therapy, that really allows someone who's been traumatized to connect to their therapist, to feel safe, and to get into the heavy work of the traumas that they've experienced in their life in a much safer environment facilitated by the drug.

"The same thing does happen over many years of therapy," he said. "You can get there over many years. This sort of accelerates that into a very short period of time because of the effect of the drug."

But the projected cost of the therapy could reduce the number of people who had access.

Each round of treatment was expected to cost about $15,000. A standard course would be three rounds, totalling 54 hours of therapy. No public funding has yet been allocated.

Associate Health Minister David Seymour said MDMA "can be very effective at treating [PTSD] through psychedelic-assisted therapy".

Associate Health Minister David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"Recent changes have put New Zealand's settings in line with Australia, where authorised prescribers have been providing MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD in clinical settings for some time.

"MDMA remains an unapproved medicine, but two experienced psychiatrists have already been granted authority to prescribe it to patients with PTSD.

"This is very good news for their patients, who will have been suffering for some time."

He said there would be safeguards in place to ensure it was prescribed safely.

"Treatment with MDMA occurs as part of a comprehensive treatment plan and occurs in the prescriber's clinic. Patients don't get dispensed MDMA to take home.

"Practitioners must also meet a series of requirements to gain approval, including demonstrating expertise in the area and providing a detailed proposal of how they will administer the treatment."

A trial completed in 2023 found MDMA-assisted therapy significantly reduced symptoms in people with moderate to severe PTSD, compared to those who received a placebo. There were no serious adverse effects or deaths in the 104 patients who took part.

What does a therapy session with MDMA look like?

Wynn said a standard dose of MDMA would last between four and six hours, so a therapy session could take a whole day.

"You come in and you meet beforehand and you talk and you sort of get the person into the right frame of mind. You might do some yoga, you might do some meditation, you might do some music or arts.

"You want to get the person really in the right headspace as they enter that space that they can really connect with the therapist, feel safe and explore the bounds of the traumas that they've experienced."

What are the risks?

Usually, the risk associated with MDMA use came from overdose - but in a clinical setting, the dose was carefully measured.

"We're talking 120, 160 milligrams of MDMA during a dosing session," Wynn said.

According to scientific literature, that was on par with what people took recreationally - perhaps a little less.

"Everything has risks," Wynn said - but in this case, they were "very minor".

The usual side effect warnings printed on the back of even the most common medicines would also apply - the potential for elevated heart rate, sweating, dizziness, headache and nausea.

"You can experience all of that, but it tends to be temporary and pass quite quickly."

When it came to longer-term effects, the therapy itself was more likely to leave a mark.

"If you bring up your trauma and you don't process it well, if you can have sort of this residual effects for a period of time afterwards until you integrate it. So it can destabilise someone temporarily, but that's actually can be good... because we can then work on that trauma together."

Have any patients expressed an interest already?

Wynn said he had deliberately kept the option off the table until the application was approved. Now, he expected a lot of people to come out of the woodwork.

Anywhere from 1 to 5 percent of the population would experience PTSD during their life.

"There are a lot of people who are really desperate feeling about their PTSD," Wynn said. "You know, they've gone to therapy, they've done meds, nothing works."

But this option would likely only be accessible for a small number for patients.
