"It's expensive, intensive, and takes quite a bit of time to do properly. So I think there's going to be a lot of interest. Who can actually spend the time and the money or get the support to do it? It's going to be a question that shakes out over the coming months."

The Ministry of Health said in a statement the decision brought New Zealand into line with Australia, where authorised psychiatrists had been able to provide MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD since 2023.

"While MDMA contains the same active ingredient found in the illicit drug commonly known as ecstasy, the product used in treatment is manufactured to a pharmaceutical standard and used under strict clinical supervision."

Patients must be over 18 and undergo a comprehensive clinical assessment before treatment was considered.

World.title: Police cordon off roads amid 'serious incident' in Nelson
World.content:
Police are responding to what they describe as a serious incident in Nelson this afternoon.

Officers were called to Quarantine Road around midday. There was also a police presence on Parkers Road.

A police spokesperson said there was no threat to public safety, however members of the public should avoid the area.

Cordons were in place.

Police would not provide any further information.

World.title: ACT promises to axe millions in roadside art spending
World.content:
ACT is promising to stop motorists' money being spent on roadside sculptures, cultural monuments and decorative artwork, saying fuel taxes and road-user charges should pay for roads instead.

Under the party's new transport policy, announced on Friday, such "non-functional art" would no longer be eligible for money from the National Land Transport Fund (NLTF).

ACT infrastructure spokesperson Simon Court said iwi, businesses or environmental groups could pay for them instead through sponsorship or fundraising.

He said motorists should not have to pick up the bill.

"Communities can still add extras - just not on the road user's tab."

Court pointed to $3.7 million spent on 35 pou (carved wooden posts) and two taonga artworks on Te Ara Tupua cycleway between Wellington and Lower Hutt.

Hine te Iwaiwa sculpture designed by Warren Warbrick on Te Ahu a Turanga Highway. Supplied/NZ Transport Agency

He also highlighted $2.2m for a cultural artwork trail along the Oaro-to-Clarence corridor and $1.88m for five sculptures on Te Ahu a Turanga, the new highway replacing the closed Manawatū Gorge road.

'No-frills, fit-for-purpose design'

The crackdown was one of six key changes promised by ACT as part of its election transport policy.

ACT would also require officials to properly investigate the cheapest safe option for all major transport projects, and publish it alongside their preferred design, showing the price, construction time and expected benefits of each.

"No-frills, fit-for-purpose design will be the default," the policy said. "Not every project needs to be bespoke or gold-plated at the expense of the people paying for it."

ACT would also introduce automatic traffic triggers designed to get road upgrades underway before congestion became entrenched.

On major two-lane growth corridors, 10,000 vehicles a day would trigger moves to protect surrounding land. At 15,000 vehicles, consenting and design work would start, and at 20,000, extra lanes would start being built.

The party would also ring-fence road maintenance funding to stop it being "raided" to cover cost blowouts on new projects.

ACT would block Crown funding from going to projects which gave preference to contractors based on ethnicity, making "equal treatment" a condition.

It singled out Auckland Transport, pointing to a $1.39m marae carpark contract which was tendered only to registered Māori-owned businesses.

"Public contracts should be awarded on price, capability, safety and delivery - not ethnicity," the policy said.

World.title: Weather: Wind warning in place for Wellington, heavy rain for the South Island
World.content:
A strong wind warning is in place for the capital on Friday, while parts of the central and northern South Island are being drenched with heavy rain.

MetService said a front impacting parts of the South Island and the Tararua Range had hit on Friday and strong northwesterlies could reach a severe gale in eastern areas from Canterbury all the way up to Hawke's Bay.

Drivers in Canterbury and the West Coast are being warned to expect delays as rain and strong winds hit the regions.

MetService has forecast severe westerly gales reaching 90km/h near Arthur's Pass.

State Highway 7 is down to a single lane with stop/go traffic management in place because of fallen trees near Heslop Creek Bridge, between Rahu Saddle and Springs Junction.

An area warning for slips and flooding is in place on State Highway 73 from Arthur's Pass to Kumara Junction.

MetService has also issued a strong wind watch for the Canterbury high country from 11am until 9pm on Saturday.

It said the winds could approach severe gales in some areas.

A strong wind warning has been issued for for Wellington. MetService screenshot

Wind gusts of 137km/h on Remutaka hill

A strong wind warning has been issued for Wellington and Wairarapa, excluding the Tararua District, from 4am on Friday through to 12pm.

Severe gales gusting up to 120km/h in exposed places were possible, the forecaster said. This could bring damage to trees, powerlines and unsecured structures and make driving difficult for high-sided vehicles and motorcycles.

Wellington was the windest place overnight - but the warmest at the same time.

MetService meteorologist Braydon White said gusts reached 137km/h at the Remutaka Summit around 7am.

Mount Kaukau followed closely at 136km/h gusts.

Urban areas also saw high winds, with the suburb of Kelburn getting gusts as high as 120km/h.

"We're well into the classic Spring westerlies," White said.

While he said these winds were normal for the start of Spring, it was warmer than average.

Both Wellington and New Plymouth were 14 degrees overnight.

Some areas quickly got warmer on Friday, like Napier rising from 7 degrees to 17 degrees within about an hour.

The strong wind dragging warm air will make its way across the country today, finishing in Auckland and Northland this evening.

"These fronts are continuing their march across the country, weakening as they do so."

Heavy rain warnings were also in place for the headwaters of the Canterbury Lakes and rivers until 8am on Friday, and the Tararua Range until 1pm.

The road into Milford Sound. (File pic) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

A road snowfall warning is also in place for Milford Rd (SH94) until 6pm on Friday, with the possibility of 2cm to 5cm of snow accumulating by the tunnel.

The weekend was looking more settled, according to MetService, with some rain. The North Island would see a few showers in the west on Saturday, but be mainly fine while the South Island could expect rain or showers in the west and south with possible heavy falls.

On Sunday, MetService said rain would be developing in the west with possible heavy falls for the North Island and rain the west and south with heavy falls for the South Island.

Wind threatens Auckland Harbour Bridge closure

Travel across the Auckland Harbour Bridge might be disrupted on Friday, transport officials have warned.

Gusts of up to 80km/h have been forecast between midday and 4pm.

"Motorists are advised to drive to the conditions and pay attention to electronic message boards on the motorway, which will advise if any lane closures and reduced speed limits are required," the New Zealand Transport Agency said in a statement on Thursday.

World.title: Politicians urged to listen, not 'dangle lollies' at Koroneihana
World.content:
Politicians arriving at Tūrangawaewae Marae are being urged to listen, as the third day of the annual Koroneihana celebrations gets underway.

The gates of the marae crooned to the sound of the Pacific on Friday morning; chiefs from around the region gathered en masse to pay their respects to the Māori monarch, Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po.

Political parties from the coalition - National, ACT, New Zealand First - and the opposition - Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori - are due to be welcomed onto the marae later this afternoon.

However, none of the coalition party leaders will attend.

Christopher Luxon is returning from Palau after attending the Pacific Islands Forum, and Winston Peters, who was also at the forum, was due to attend but has fallen sick.

Earlier this week, David Seymour told reporters he "sadly" would not be attending but Karen Chhour would speak on the party's behalf.

"Oh, I'd love to go, but I can't this week. I can't this year," he said.

Speaking to media before the politicians arrived, Kiingitanga kaikōrero Rahui Papa said those who had decided not to come were missing a "golden opportunity" to hear the "actual manifesto of Māori".

He warned that they should come with an "open mind" and a "bulletproof vest".

"What we are seeking is for them to come and listen, rather than come and dangle lollies in front of te iwi Māori."

"We want them to come and listen and influence their manifestos as they go forward into an election."

He said issues around honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi were "always top of mind", especially when they impacted on existing Treaty settlements.

"We have had settlements for a long time, and pieces of legislation that make policy decisions that unpick those [settlements] will not be tolerated."

Papa said the upcoming election was "hugely important" and would "shape" the country heading into the 200th anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi, 2040.

He said the government had done some good for Waikato since taking power in 2023, like housing development and the "opportunity to have a talk about fast track".

"We're not going to get all the way there with our aspirations and our wants... but the door is open.

"The support for places like Ruakura, the support for the highway, for example, has meant that a whole lot of things are being able to be done, and so there is silver linings to dark clouds," he said.

The government is planning to pause Plan Change 1 provisions until 2032, which Waikato-Tainui says undermines its Treaty settlement and the health of Waikato and Waipā rivers.

Papa said his people would raise the issue directly.

"We're opportunists, and we're not backward about coming forward."

World.title: Pacific Islands Forum winds up by rebuking China nuclear test
World.content:
Leaders in the Pacific have registered their concern over a nuclear-capable missile test conducted by China in July, calling on all states to provide advance warning ahead of any testing.

Nauru - one of the 18 Pacific Island Forum (PIF) members - noted its dissent from the statement.

Partners to the forum will also be split into two tiers in future, and member states agreed to a declaration for urgent and inclusive climate action to keep 1.5 degrees of warming within reach.

The Pacifc Islands' Forum in Palau has concluded, with leaders taking part in a daylong meeting on Thursday to discuss various issues, releasing a joint statement outlining their conclusions.

The Pacific Islands Forum has been winding up discussions in Palau. Ohanna Rabo Galo/TMC Palau

Specifically, the forum noted an intercontinental ballistic missile test that had "overflew" a number of members "without adequate notice".

The members called on all states undertaking testing of intercontinental ballistic missiles to provide transparency and reassurance, including advance notification of at least 24 hours.

Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr who read the statement concluded by saying: "I might note that the Republic of Nauru has dissented."

The forum has been overshadowed with the tensions between China and Taiwan.

One local told RNZ all he'd been hearing about was "China, Taiwan, and how the outside world, outside countries are ... making certain nations either afraid to talk or not standing up boldly."

"All I hear is about just drama, and that defeats the whole purpose."

He said he wanted to hear more about what other countries were going through, whether that matched up with the problems facing Palau - like outmigration, cost of living, and drugs - and see what could be done by working together.

New Zealand Prime Minister Chirstopher Luxon said on Thursday that China-Taiwan hadn't been a focus inside the PIF.

"It's a piece of a conversation, but it's not the dominant conversation."

But another geopolitical issue was the lingering desire by many in the forum to reach consensus on condemning the intercontinental ballistic missile test by China.

It's understood Nauru and Kiribati, both closely aligned with China, stood in the way of full consensus on a statement earlier in August.

Even as the meeting on Thursday was taking place, China's foreign ministry made accusations toward Palau, after the host of the forum urged the group to condemn China's launch.

"Palau has repeatedly raised this issue in an ill-intentioned attempt to hijack the position of other member states of the Pacific Islands Forum. It will not have its way," the ministry said.

Prime Minister Chistopher Luxon says it;s important to push back over nuclear missile tests that are not signalled in advance. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Luxon himself felt strongly about the matter, telling reporters later it was important to push back so the behaviour wasn't normalised.

"Given all the history in our part of the world with nuclear testing … that's just not something we want to see."

Luxon described Nauru as being "in the room", and wanting to be "disassociated with the statement".

"We said, look, that's great, but we're not going to not make a statement as a Pacific Island Forum because of the objection of one country, and you'd have to ask them as to what their rationale for that was.

"Suffice to say, everyone else was fully on board."

When pressed on whether Kiribati was also on board, Luxon said Kiribati had no representation in the room.

Even stranger was the delayed recognition during the closing ceremony of Kiribati's representative to the forum, David Teaboo, well after all the other leaders had received applause.

The forum also confirmed it would run a tiered system next year, splitting around 30 partners into two streams: one for strategic partners, and one for sector partners.

"Everyone's a partner, but we just need to make sure that we can manage it well going forward," said Luxon.

"We have to acknowledge that as we go forward, we can't treat them all the same or give the same sort of effort."

Foreign Minister Winston Peters at the forum. Supplied / screenshot

Taiwan remains a development partner, and while its foreign minister, Lin Chia-lung, was attending the forum this year after being invited by Palau, New Zealand's Foreign Minister indicated on Thursday that wouldn't be the case next year.

New Zealand adheres to the One China policy, which means it doesn't have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

That would prevent the foreign minister being invited - instead representation at a lower level would be likely at next year's forum.

Despite the geostrategic tensions at play throughout the forum, Luxon said PIF was at its "strongest."

Before setting off to Palau, Luxon denied PIF was being weakened as a mechanism for resolving region-wide difficulties.

"No, I think it's about strengthening it, though," Luxon said.

After his hours' long meeting on Thursday, he said he wanted to see PIF "continue to evolve and strengthen and move - it's the arc of progress that we're focused on".

World.title: Kyrgios free to compete after accepting one-month cocaine ban
World.content:
Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive to cocaine.

After admitting his "huge mistake" when initially suspended for failing a drugs test on June 22 at an ATP 250 tournament in Spain, Kyrgios is allowed to compete again from Friday.

Kyrgios, who had been provisionally suspended since August 4, had faced a ban ranging from a baseline three-month period to up to four years.

During an interview with International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) investigators, Kyrgios explained his use of cocaine had occurred socially during a night out, days before he was due to play in Mallorca.

The ITIA consulted an independent scientific expert at a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory, who stated the explanation was consistent with the level of cocaine found in his sample.

As a result, the ITIA accepted Kyrgios's use of cocaine was outside of competition.

Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Under WADA rules, the default suspension for a breach of this type is three months, which can be further reduced to one month if the individual commits to a treatment program approved by the ITIA.

The 2022 Wimbledon finalist also forfeited the 6,570 Euros he won in Mallorca for losing in the first round to countryman Adam Walton.

But his suspension was reduced for agreeing to enter a treatment program.

The ITIA said Kyrgios, whose career world ranking peaked at number 13, could appeal against the provisional suspension, but he opted against doing so.

"I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine," Kyrgios posted on Instagram last month.

"I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it.

"I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I'm sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed in myself."

Kyrgios, who played only four official singles matches on the elite ATP Tour this year, has battled knee and wrist injuries in recent years and has all but conceded he is finished as a singles force.

"I'm not going to make excuses, but I do want to give some context about where I've been," he wrote.

"The last couple of years of injuries have taken a huge toll on me, both physically and mentally.

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined."

Nick Kyrgios has been beset by injuries. (AP: Charles Krupa)

But the polarising Canberra-born drawcard said that did not excuse his actions.

"I've always said I didn't choose tennis — tennis chose me," he wrote.

"But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I've ever had to face. At times I've felt helpless and alone.

"None of that excuses what I did."

Kyrgios said "the good news is that this has given me a wake up call".

"For the next 28 days, I'll be stepping away from social media and public life while I focus on getting myself right.

"I'd ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly the privacy of my family.

"I'm sorry. I'll do the work and come back better."

The ITIA said Kyrgios was suspended for a ‌positive test for benzoylecgonine, a cocaine metabolite, with a World Anti-Doping Agency laboratory confirming the positive result on July 17.

The 31-year-old was banned from playing, coaching or attending any tournaments sanctioned by the men's and women's tennis tours worldwide and national-level events in Australia.

Kyrgios last played in the men's doubles at Wimbledon in London on July 2, when he and partner Alexander Bublik lost in the first round.

AAP

World.title: Australian battler crushes Italian star in US Open boilover
World.content:
Dane Sweeny has won a real-life David-versus-Goliath battle to rock the US Open with a stunning second-round upset over dual grand slam semi-finalist Lorenzo Musetti.

The unheralded Australian wildcard took down the 14th seed 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 on Friday morning (AEST) for the biggest win of his career.

Standing only 170cm high, Sweeny rose to the occasion to reach the third round of a grand slam for the first time and earn a minimum pay day of $US290,000 ($A402,750).

For a couple of heady hours it looked like his underdog countrymen Tristan Schoolkate and Alexei Popyrin would join Sweeny in round three.

Osaka, Keys mount thrilling fightbacks Naomi Osaka wobbled through the second set to fight back and beat Kateřina Siniaková in three, while Madison Keys staved off five match points to keep her US Open dreams alive on day of high drama at Flushing Meadows.

But Schoolkate's inspired run from qualifying finally came to a halt at the hands of fifth-seeded French Open runner-up Flavio Cobilli.

Schoolkate snatched the first set before the Italian showed his class to prevail 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, 7-5 after two hours and 41 minutes in New York's scorching summer heat.

And two years after upstaging Novak Djokovic in the US Open's third round, Popyrin fell short of a place in the last 32 once again, losing a tense four-set battle with Chilean Alejandro Tabilo.

Like Schoolkate, Popyrin took the opening set before the 25th-seeded South American claimed two pivotal tiebreakers, then the match 2-6, 7-6 (7-4), 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 to seal a likely third-round date with German top seed Alexander Zverev.

But ranked more than 100 places below his world number 14 opponent, Sweeny is savouring a mighty breakthrough after bossing Musetti into submission.

He ran the 14th seed ragged and had the Italian looking in particular distress when he required a medical time-out after falling behind a double break at 0-3 in the all-important third set.

Even after clawing one break back, Musetti — who has made the Wimbledon and French Open semi-finals over the past two years — continued remonstrating animatedly to his courtside box.

Despite sporting a massive ice pack on his right elbow after his first-round win, Sweeny continued diving like Boris Becker for acrobatic winning volleys at the net.

And the 25-year-old was duly rewarded with a last-32 shot at another Italian, world number 22 Luciano Daredri on Saturday (AEST) — and a rankings rise to a career-best 115 in the world, or better.

"I'm just grateful to be even able to compete in grand slams. The tennis journey is such a rollercoaster," Sweeny said.

"And to soak up the atmosphere and get a win, a couple of wins, in front of this crowd, is awesome."

Australia's sixth seed Alex de Minaur was scheduled to play Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp on The Grandstand after Schoolkate's match.

AAP

World.title: Fox makes golden return to Paris Olympic venue
World.content:
Jess Fox has made a triumphant return to the Vaires-sur-Marne Nautical Stadium on the outskirts of Paris, claiming yet another gold medal in the ICF Canoe Slalom World Cup series.

Returning to the venue where she won two Olympic gold medals in 2024, Fox was once again unstoppable in the K1 event.

The now five-time world champion even overcame a two-second penalty to top the standings for her second World Cup win of the season.

"I have great memories here in Paris. It's always a pleasure to race here with the amazing crowd," Fox said in a bilingual post-race interview.

"The course was hard. It was very challenging, very physical — I'm still out of breath.

"I gave it everything and I'm so happy to take the win today."

Noémie Fox finished fifth, just one-tenth of a second off the podium. (Supplied: Romain Bruneau)

Fox, who was born in Marseille and is the daughter of French 1996 Olympic bronze medallist Myriam Fox-Jerusalmi, claimed victory by 0.73 seconds from Slovakian Eliška Mintálová, who was the only paddler in the top six to complete a clean run and not suffer a penalty.

Paris Olympic silver medallist Klaudia Zwolińska of Poland finished third, edging Ukraine's Viktoriia Us out of the medals by just 0.05 seconds.

Fox came into the event off the back of winning three gold medals at the world championships in Oklahoma, capping a superb comeback season after she had surgery to remove a tumour from her kidney nine months ago.

Noémie Fox, who enjoyed her own golden moment on the Vaires-sur-Marne course in 2024, was a further 0.05 seconds back in fifth.

In the men's event, Australian Lucien Delfour finished in 10th place, having been hit with four seconds' worth of penalties, while Italian Giovanni de Gennaro claimed gold with a clean run.

The Fox's will have another chance to win gold in the C1 event, set to take place Friday night (AEST), an event where Jess has won back-to-back Olympic golds in Tokyo and Paris.

World.title: After his Broncos ending, a new beginning looms for Payne Haas
World.content:
A dead rubber game in an empty stadium was no way for Payne Haas's time as a Bronco to come to an end.

To match what he's produced in nine seasons with Brisbane that averaged out to magnificent, Haas's last game would've needed to feel like a life and death struggle where the winners touched the heavens and defeat sent the fallen screaming into hell.

Such contests have been where Haas has enjoyed some of his finest hours and those are the games of 159 appearances for Brisbane that have made him a living legend.

NRL live The Broncos win a final-round contest against the Bulldogs, in a game that doubled as Payne Haas's farewell from Brisbane. Follow live.

But for the last before he heads to South Sydney, he had to settle for purgatory.

Brisbane's 34-20 win against Canterbury on Thursday night felt like so many other games that happen as non-finals teams grimly march to the end of the season.

Tackles were made, tries were scored and whistles were blown on a night that felt flat and lonely, as the citadel of Stadium Australia often can be with nearly 70,000 empty seats.

Brisbane did send Haas out a winner, and that still matters. Josiah Karapani played a blinder and the Broncos found a little of the football that marked that championship season last year.

Haas got in the action early, smashing his way through four defenders to score the opening try of the night and later spent time in the sin bin after being pinged for repeated infringements.

With 152 metres across 71 minutes the numbers were strong, as they always are for Haas, but it's important not to get lost in them.

While the match as a spectacle and a contest was not a fitting finale for Haas's Brisbane career as a whole, it made much more sense as the close for what has been an uneven year in comparison to his other campaigns.

Haas has not played poorly and even if he had, a poor Payne Haas game would be a stand-out performance for many other props.

You could say he's good enough on a bad day but he hasn't had enough truly bad days for us to be sure.

Haas has still averaged 156 run metres and just under 35 tackles a game, marks many players would be proud to call their own.

In 2026, Payne Haas has not quite hit the superhuman form he's become known for. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

He has still had big moments, like his rampaging try against the Bulldogs on his last night, or his similar effort against Canberra two weeks ago that kicked off a rollicking Broncos comeback win.

Australia and Samoa would still both crawl over broken glass to have him in their World Cup sides because he is still the best prop on the planet.

But Haas has not quite been superhuman, and that is what we have become accustomed to during his Bronco years.

We are used to him being closer to a miracle than a man — 156 metres per game, somehow, is the second-lowest average of his career as a starter.

His offloads have plummeted, from 70 last year to just 21 this season. So too his tackle busts, which have fallen from 130 to 64 with the wide-running charges that became such a feature of his game in recent years seemingly hard to find.

In similarly short supply are the inexplicable, gut-busting efforts to cover the defensive mistake of a teammate or clean up a loose ball or just generally be where no prop forward ever should be to do a little extra that no other prop forward can ever really do.

After making the Dally M team of the year four of the past five seasons, Payne Haas will miss out in 2026. (AAP: Jono Searle)

After making the Dally M team of the year four times in the past five seasons — with a 14-match year in 2024 marking his only exclusion — Haas will miss out this year and rightly so.

The Roosters' blunt-force artist Naufahu Whyte and New Zealand's James Fisher-Harris have both enjoyed better seasons.

So too has the old iron Cowboy himself, Jason Taumalolo, and the greatest forward of an age now past got the better of Haas in both of North Queensland's wins over their southern rivals.

Mitch Barnett, Haas's replacement in Brisbane for next year, did the same last month when the Warriors beat the Broncos up like they owed them money.

Even players outside the top eight have got a bit of a turn to put one on the living legend.

Haas barely ever misses tackles — he made 40 without a single miss against Canterbury — but last week against Melbourne Stefano Utoikamanu brushed past him for a try the Storm man can tell the grandkids about because it's not every day you get one on the king.

Haas is not the only player at Brisbane who has struggled to deal with the premiership hangover but he is the only player who seemed above such things. Motivation is fleeting, it comes and it goes and that is why it's for humans, not heroes.

Haas is the player who goes all day, every day, no matter what and he has done it on worse Bronco teams than this.

In the final game of the 2020 season, when Brisbane lost to North Queensland to confirm their first wooden spoon on as low a night as the club has ever had, it was a breakaway try to Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow that confirmed the result.

Chasing Tabuai-Fidow, then or now, is to put in maximum effort for a futile cause at the best of times, let alone in the dying stages of the final game of a nightmare season.

But there going after him, as sure as the sun will rise tomorrow, was Payne Haas. It didn't make a difference, but Haas did it just in case it might.

Last year's premiership was Payne Haas's ultimate reward. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

He kept going like that until it felt like a way of life, until years later when he lifted the premiership trophy and confirmed a legacy that meant he could stand alongside the likes of Glenn Lazarus, Shane Webcke and Petero Civoniceva as the greatest forwards in Brisbane's history.

That journey to greatness is in starker relief given his first Brisbane years began in low-down valleys, making the trail he forged all the way to a premiership his Everest.

His sense of triumph and relief was palpable after that grand final win even amid the throng of family, friends and backslappers that filled the Brisbane sheds as the air felt thick with emotion and cigar smoke.

The player who always found more to do at last had some satisfaction. The seemingly endless appetite for the grind and the fight was satiated.

It was the culmination of Haas's entire footballing life and if anyone had earned the right to look a little more mortal in the aftermath, it was him.

Why Haas's move changes the fate of two NRL giants Payne Haas's decision to leave Brisbane for South Sydney in 2027 didn't just shock the rugby league world, it transformed the futures of two of rugby league's most powerful clubs in an instant.

This version of Payne Haas is still more than good enough to impact the premiership race. If this is the new normal he will still be mighty for South Sydney in a way few players can ever dream of and regardless of what happens next, his greatness is already assured.

But there's every chance the move now creates the chance for another rise, in a new city with new colours and a fresh start amid new challenge that will, from time to time, demand he again pushes himself beyond reasonable limits.

As hyperbolic as we can get about players of Haas's ilk, they are still human. They still need something to chase and last year, after so much effort and so much time, Haas made his ultimate catch.

Perhaps it meant that his farewell season as a Bronco, and particularly his final night, could not match what has come before.

But even if it wasn't a fitting end to what was, it is still an end — which means a new beginning can follow.

World.title: So good for so long this year, Dockers wilt at inopportune time against Hawks
World.content:
So good for so long this year, Fremantle chose an inopportune time to put in — by some distance — its worst shift of the AFL season.

But that assessment is unkind to a Hawthorn side who were nothing short of brilliant in Thursday night's qualifying final at Perth Stadium.

The Hawks dominated on the ground, in the air and particularly down back, holding Fremantle to 40 points, its lowest score of the season.

The victory was built on manic pressure, the visitors forcing the Dockers into turnovers and denying them the chance to get their running game going.

Hawks complete stunning upset over Freo to clinch prelim berth Hawthorn will host an MCG preliminary final after an upset 32-point win over minor premier Fremantle in Perth.

Hawthorn's 32-point win puts it into a home preliminary final, the club now two MCG wins away from its 14th premiership.

Fremantle, meanwhile, toppled from joint-premiership favouritism, and will have to do it the hard way if the club is to bring a first flag to the port city.

The concerning thing for the Dockers was the manner of the defeat.

No Wharfie Time

Other than the first two minutes of the game, the result rarely looked in doubt.

There would be no Wharfie Time comeback against the Hawks this time, as there had been in round nine when the Dockers emerged from a titanic scrap with a 15-point win.

The Hawks came, saw and conquered the Dockers at Perth Stadium. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

Last night Fremantle, who had been unbeaten at home all year, just couldn't get close enough to push the button.

So good was Hawthorn's defence that the Dockers' three-headed forward line leviathan — Josh Treacy, Jye Amiss and Pat Voss — combined for only two goals.

Voss and Treacy managed just one mark between them.

Credit must go to Hawthorn's three-headed beast of its own — backmen James Sicily, Josh Battle and Tom Barrass proving majestic in getting their blend of destruction and creativity just right.

James Sicily was masterful in defence for the Hawks. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

After Fremantle kicked the opening goal of the match, Hawthorn then banged on the next six to take a 33-point lead into the long break.

The Dockers needed to make a move in the third quarter, and they emerged from the sheds with renewed vigour.

But every time Freo struck, the Hawks replied.

The Dockers failed to kick two goals in a row all night, and most of the 59,446 fans who poured through the turnstiles would have been resigned to their fate long before the final siren.

On a night when few Dockers beat their direct opponents, Jordan Clark was outstanding — the All Australian defender notching up 38 disposals and dragging down a spectacular mark.

Sicily was Hawthorn's best with 26 touches, while Jack Gunston, Dylan Moore and Nick Watson kicked two goals apiece.

'Not dead and buried'

Speaking after the match, Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir backed his decision to select Brandon Walker for his first game since round one to curtail the influence of Nick Watson, describing their contest as a "pretty good tussle".

But Walker's rolled ankle ended that tussle early, the dashing defender in tears on the bench after being ruled out of the game.

Watson capitalised on his absence, kicking a goal late in the third quarter and then producing a moment of pure wizardry early in the fourth, handballing to himself before burning off Luke Ryan to set up a goal for Harry Morrison, who extended the lead to 38 points.

Nick Watson prepares to activate the jets to get past Luke Ryan and send Hawthorn inside 50. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

There was no way back for the Dockers, who have now lost three of their past four games.

But Longmuir denied his side was out of form.

"Go back and have a look at the Adelaide game [in round 23], I thought we played a good brand of footy against a really desperate team who had it all to play for," he said.

"We had a couple of away games where we didn't play our best footy, but I've got a lot of faith in this group to bounce back from that."

The coach, who has preached the value of "process" all year, backed his men to get the process spot on over the next week ahead of a cut-throat home semi-final against either Carlton or Geelong.

"It's not the way we wanted it to go, but we're not dead and buried," he said.

Emotional win

For Hawks coach Sam Mitchell, the overwhelming feeling was one of pride.

Teams like Geelong, Sydney and Adelaide had been able to meet Fremantle's fire for quarters and halves this season, but no one has been able to douse it completely for an entire game at Perth Stadium like the Hawks.

Sam Mitchell was proud of the intensity his players showed. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"The relentless pressure that we had on them in that game was what we thought would be required," Mitchell said.

" Full credit to the players for being able to produce that level of effort for that long. "

The coach paid tribute to Will Day, the midfielder outstanding in his first final after a dreadful run with injuries.

An emotional Day let the tears flow on the final siren, and Mitchell said he was feeling it too.

"He's so resilient, he's been through so much," Mitchell said.

"He showed it more than I did, but I felt exactly the way he looked after the game."

World.title: Kiss makes selection gamble for Wallabies-Argentina rematch
World.content:
Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been thrust back into the Wallabies' starting side while Ben Donaldson will steer the ship in Mendoza for his first start at fly-half in two years.

After a tight win a week earlier, coach Les Kiss has again tinkered with his side for their Argentina rematch on Sunday morning (AEST).

After a run of six losses, the side is chasing five-straight wins for the first time since 2021.

Carter Gordon, reportedly under an injury cloud during the week, has been shifted to the bench to give perennial back-up Donaldson a rare start in the number 10 jersey.

Ryan Lonergan will remain at scrum half, and Tom Wright will play his 50th Test after being named at fullback.

Billy Pollard and Josh Nasser will share the hooking duties, with Brandon Paenga-Amosa rotated out.

It's otherwise a full-strength pack with Angus Bell, Taniela Tupou, Josh Canham and Jeremy Williams all starting, while Harry Wilson has been recalled at number 8 alongside Fraser McReight and Rob Valetini.

Kiss has switched his centres though, with Isaac Henry benched and Hunter Paisami left out to make room for star pair Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii will line up at centre. (Getty Images: Marcos Brindicci)

It will be the first time that pair, who were midfield regulars under Joe Schmidt, start together under Kiss, who is 3-0 as Test coach.

Fililipo Daugunu will earn his first start of the season on the wing, replacing Harry Potter, while Kalani Thomas takes Reds teammate Tate McDermott's spot on the bench as back-up scrum-half.

Prop Aidan Ross and lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto also come into the side on the bench, with Charlie Cale the back row back-up.

Meanwhile, Argentina coach Felipe Contepomi has made a number of changes as they look to square the series.

Locks Efraín Elías and Franco Molina come in to replace Tomás Lavanini and Guido Petti, who shifts to the flank in place of Benjamín Grondona.

Pedro Delgado comes in at tighthead prop in place of Francisco Moreno, who drops to the bench in the last of the four changes in the pack.

In the backs, the inexperienced 26-year-old Benetton 10 Nicolás Roger comes into the side at fly-half, outside Newcastle scrum-half Simón Benítez Cruz, while Bath 15 Santiago Carreras switches to fullback to replace Gerónimo Prisciantelli.

Two uncapped players — Facundo Cardozo and Mateo Soler — are in line to make their international debuts off the bench after being named among the replacements.

Pablo Matera, winning his 126th cap, continues as captain in the absence of Julián Montoya, who is one of several overseas-based players unavailable for selection, having not been released by his French side, Section Paloise Béarn Pyrénées.

Wallabies team to face Argentina: Angus Bell, Billy Pollard, Taniela Tupou; Josh Canham, Jeremy Williams; Rob Valetini, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson; Ryan Lonergan, Ben Donaldson; Filipo Daugunu, Len Ikitau, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen; Tom Wright. Bench: Josh Nasser, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Charlie Cale, Kalani Thomas, Carter Gordon, Isaac Henry.

AAP/Reuters

World.title: Osaka, Keys overcome mid-match stumbles to fight on at US Open
World.content:
Two-time champion Naomi Osaka overcame mid-match mistakes to progress while Madison Keys saved five match points to keep her campaign alive in the US Open second round, as fans eagerly awaited Coco Gauff and Alexander Zverev in the late program.

A perennial fan favourite in New York, Osaka survived an up-and-down affair against Czech Kateřina Siniaková to win 6-2 5-7 6-1, harnessing the mental resolve she has taken years to hone on the court where she claimed her maiden major eight years ago.

Sweeny soars into US Open last 32 Australian wildcard Dane Sweeny has posted the biggest win of his career, upsetting dual grand slam semifinalist Lorenzo Musetti to make the US Open's last 32.

"I just told myself that it's an honour to play on this court," Osaka told the crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I just want to keep playing in front of you guys if possible."

The 28-year-old Japanese player's match was not the only nail-biter across the sprawling Flushing Meadows plaza, as American Keys mounted an epic comeback against Hungarian Anna Bondár to win 5-7 6-4 7-6 (5) to delight the home fans on the outer courts.

The 2017 finalist sent over a remarkable 34 forehand winners to get the job done and gave all credit to her adoring fans after forcing Bondár into an error at the net on match point.

Madison Keys saved five match points in her three-set epic. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

"That was something, huh?" Keys, 31, told the crowd after the win.

"No stress though — we all knew I had it, right?"

Her compatriot Taylor Fritz had a far easier time, swatting aside Italian Mattia Bellucci 6-0 6-1 6-1, while Amanda Anisimova's 6-3 3-6 6-1 defeat of Austrian Lilli Tagger added to the American joy.

Canadian third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime, a semi-finalist last year, took the first set but was then swept away in a 6-7(5) 6-3 6-2 6-2 defeat by Russian Karen Khachanov, becoming the highest-seeded man to exit the tournament so far.

The Philippines' wildly popular Alex Eala capped the early programme at Louis Armstrong Stadium with a comprehensive 6-1 6-4 defeat of Ukraine's Oleksandra Oliynykova.

Days of stubborn rain gave way to sunny skies in New York, where Iga Świątek enjoyed a relatively drama-free 6-3 6-2 win over Argentina's Nadia Podoroska, in a rare appearance on the outdoor courts for the 2022 champion.

Fans will eagerly await another evening programme packed with talent as fourth-seeded 2023 champion Gauff kicks off the night on Ashe against Paula Badosa, followed by the men's top seed Zverev, who plays France's Quentin Halys.

Frenchman Gaël Monfils will hope to make magic again in his farewell season when he faces 14th-seeded American Learner Tien in the first night match at Armstrong before second seed Elena Rybakina plays Spain's Jessica Bouzas Maneiro.

Reuters

World.title: FIFA accuses UEFA of 'smear campaign' over World Cup sell-off plan
World.content:
FIFA accused UEFA of waging a "smear campaign" against it and president Gianni Infantino, escalating a dispute over the abandoned proposal to sell a stake in the world governing body's commercial rights, according to a court filing seen by Reuters.

UEFA last week submitted an ex parte application in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York seeking permission to obtain testimony and documents from US-based entities for use in potential criminal proceedings in Switzerland.

"While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of UEFA's smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership," FIFA said in the filing.

Reuters has contacted FIFA and UEFA for comment.

UEFA said it was considering criminal proceedings against Infantino and other FIFA officials over FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a proposed entity that would have held commercial rights linked to the men's and women's World Cups.

UEFA alleged the proposal was developed without adequate consultation with FIFA's governing bodies and 211 member associations.

In a motion to intervene seen by Reuters filed on September 1 by FIFA (AMERICAS) Inc. and FWC2026 US, Inc., FIFA asked the court to defer ruling on UEFA's application or allow it to oppose the request.

FIFA argued that UEFA was seeking discovery for "purportedly contemplated (but non-existent) Swiss criminal proceedings". The world governing body also alleged UEFA had sought to derail the FFE proposal from the outset.

The proposal was withdrawn on July 31 after opposition from UEFA and other regional governing bodies.

"Rather than participate in that democratic process, UEFA issued a press release, the beginning of a weeks-long smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership," FIFA said in the filing.

FIFA further argued that UEFA's opposition was motivated by a desire to preserve European football's dominance.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded The FIFA president has faced more than a fortnight of international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

Infantino, up for re-election for a fourth term in March 2027, has been criticised since tabling the now-abandoned proposal, with several countries withdrawing their support for his candidacy.

The Swiss-Italian administrator is under pressure from three confederations to resign, including UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean.

The regional governing bodies have discussed a potential vote of no confidence in Infantino.

Infantino, who retains support from the African and South American confederations, has sought to sideline the confederations and appeal directly to individual members.

UEFA, in a statement last week, said that it would work with partner confederations to ensure member associations are offered a "credible alternative" committed to reform, if Infantino seeks another term.

UEFA also provisionally suspended plans to boycott FIFA competitions, paving the way for all qualified teams to participate in next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup in Poland, the first major tournament that could have been affected by the stand-off.

However, the body said its members had unanimously mandated the confederation to pursue "every available institutional, political and legal avenue" to secure reforms and restore limits on presidential authority.

The confederation also called for "a genuinely independent external review" of the failed FIFA proposal, saying: "FIFA cannot investigate itself and expect the football community simply to accept its conclusions."

Reuters

Tech.title: The unusually muted Tesla Cybercab launch
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

At a private, closed-door event in Austin, Texas today, Tesla officially launched its gilded car of the future. It’s a huge milestone for Elon Musk, who has been hyping the imminent arrival of driverless cars for years and has bet the future of his company on AI, autonomous vehicles, and humanoid robots.

It was an unusually muted event: with no livestream, pro-Tesla accounts on X.com were left streaming the webpage that tracks the number of Tesla robotaxis in Texas. Like last year’s robotaxi launch, the invite list was mostly pro-Tesla influencers, so as to blunt any possible criticism of its new products. Invitee Chuck Cook said the company had him sign an NDA and agreed to an embargo requiring to wait to post content until after the event was over. On X, pro-Tesla accounts who weren’t invited grumbled aboutthe decision; Not a Tesla App accused the company of “dropping the ball.”

As of this week, Tesla has 45 Cybercab vehicles registered with the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles — though its not clear how many will be put into commercial service right away. Several vehicles were made available to Tesla influencers in Austin for content creation; the company has been testing them in various cities for months now. Tesla also launched a new website for its Robotaxi service, which includes the rules for riding in the new vehicle. For example, children under the age of 13 are currently banned from riding in the Cybercab. Several videos were posted, highlighting the interior, crash test worthiness, and accessibility. (The accessibility video was especially befuddling, showing a wheelchair user getting up to fold and stow his own wheelchair.)

With the new Cybercabs, Tesla now has 256 unsupervised autonomous vehicles in operation across six cities, according to Robotaxi Tracker. By comparison, Alphabet’s Waymo is currently operating approximately 4,000 vehicles across 14 cities.

But there were still many lingering questions about the Cybercab. Two years ago, Musk said the two-seater would be available for purchase, perhaps for a price as low as $30,000. But the company still has yet say when the Cybercab would go on sale. There is a new online form for those interested in “future Robotaxi opportunities,” such as purchasing a fleet of Cybercabs or building “mobility hubs and infrastructure.”

For the past year, Tesla has been operating a robotaxi service in Texas and Florida using several dozen modified Model Y vehicles, some of which are supervised by human safety drivers and some of which are not. With the introduction of the Cybercab, the company is embarking on a risky new phase that will pit Musk’s stripped-down, less costly approach to autonomy against more established players like Waymo.

The Cybercab, which was first introduced in 2024, is a two-seat sedan with gullwing-style doors and eight cameras that it uses to navigate the world without a driver. The vehicle lacks traditional controls, like steering wheel, pedals, and mirrors — as well as sensors commonly found on other robotaxis, like radar and lidar.

The Cybercab is also the lightest, most range-efficient vehicle Tesla has ever produced. According to documents filed with the Environmental Protection Agency, the Cybercab runs on a single front-mounted 219 horsepower permanent magnet motor with front-wheel drive, a compact 48kWh battery pack running at 326 volts, and a curb weight of just 3,113 pounds — making it roughly 700 pounds lighter than the lightest Model 3 on the market. That’s roughly the same as a gas-powered compact car, despite the fact that it’s still carrying a relatively heavy lithium-ion battery.

For years, Musk has been promising the imminent arrival of Tesla’s driverless cars, only time and time again to fall short of those predictions. He claimed that 50 percent of the US population would have access to Tesla’s robotaxis by the end of 2025. Today, the vehicles are only available in six cities in Texas and Florida. (Tesla is running a human-driven ridehail service in the San Francisco Bay Area, but has yet to apply for a driverless testing permit from California.)

For Tesla’s vehicle owners, there’s been a string of broken promises. In 2016, Musk promised that every vehicle Tesla produced from then on would have all the technology necessary for self-driving. Years later, he was forced to retract that claim, acknowledging that the hardware in some older vehicles was insufficient to support autonomous capabilities. Musk promised to retrofit those customers’ vehicles, but has yet to offer any details as to how that would work. Tesla is currently facing multiple lawsuits from customers and regulators claiming it has misled the public about its self-driving capabilities.

Today, the company’s $99-a-month Full Self-Driving feature is still just a Level 2 driver-assist system that requires constant human supervision. During Tesla’s first quarter earnings call this year, Musk promised that “unsupervised” FSD would be available to customer vehicles by the end of 2026 “at the earliest,” admitting that complex intersections, bad road markings, and weather were likely to slow the rollout.

Tesla’s fans will likely point to today’s Cybercab launch as a moment of enormous significance for the company. Investors already seem to agree, with Tesla’s stock price trading up nearly six points over the past five days. Analysts view robotaxis as one of the primary justifications for Tesla’s $1.18 trillion valuation, and the key that will unlock the company’s future. Tesla’s EV sales have slowed down in the face of rising competition, especially from China. And Musk has made massive investments in AI and robotics, with some speculating he could try to merge Tesla with the recently public SpaceXAI.

Developing…

Tech.title: Steve Ballmer got suspended by the NBA because of a podcast and a jumbotron corruption scandal
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Last September, Steve Ballmer insisted in an ESPN interview that the Clippers weren’t involved in a shady-looking $28 million endorsement deal for his star player, Kawhi Leonard, that involved no actual endorsing. Now, the former Microsoft CEO has been suspended by the NBA for a year, while the league says his team will forfeit five future draft picks and pay a $30 million fine, among other penalties.

A year later, an NBA-commissioned 35-page report by Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz is basically calling him a liar, saying those claims were “inaccurate (at best) with respect to Mr. Ballmer” and “clearly false” when it came to Clippers president of business operations Gillian Zucker, who is also suspended for a year. Leonard has accepted the punishment of a $700,000 fine and a ban for his business manager.

Now the Clippers are writing angry letters to the NBA, claiming a biased investigation spurred by “a podcaster’s baseless claims” has cost Ballmer $50 million for lawyers, cost more for his reputation, and upset partners like Daktronics, the company that built a massive 4K scoreboard for the team’s new arena, with its many, many bathrooms.

That unnamed podcast, of course, is Pablo Torre Finds Out, which is cited at the beginning of the document for kicking this whole thing off one year ago today.

The episode made largely unknown fintech startup / green bank / massive fraud Aspiration a household name, and launched a series by the former ESPN reporter and his team. Now the league’s report is filling out the role partners like Daktronics played in getting Leonard money above and beyond the NBA’s mandated salary cap and how it was tied to that massive scoreboard.

In the spring of 2020, and in response to a request-for-proposal process initiated by the Clippers, Daktronics began to compete to obtain a lucrative contract to supply digital scoreboard and signage technology at the Intuit Dome. In May 2020, the Clippers informed Daktronics that it was the team’s preferred provider for this project, but that the team wanted to agree on a “spend back” arrangement whereby Daktronics would provide some amount of business back to the Clippers—which Daktronics told investigators is not uncommon in its industry. Ms. Zucker thereafter suggested to a Daktronics senior executive that this “spend back” could be accomplished through an endorsement agreement between Daktronics and Mr. Leonard.

The report says that an unnamed Clippers executive told Daktronics exactly how much to pay Leonard ($3 million for two years), and eventually told the company in 2021 “that, because the team had decided to increase the amount it would spend on the scoreboard, Daktronics should correspondingly increase the amount it would pay to Mr. Leonard.”

As we mentioned at the time, costs for the eventual Intuit Dome had reportedly ballooned to over $2 billion, including the Daktronics-built “Halo Board,” a double-sided 44,000-square-foot wraparound 4K screen with a price said to be over $100 million. Said the now-suspended executive Zucker when it was announced, “We are excited to partner with Daktronics, an innovator in video displays, to develop a Halo Board that will create one of the most intense live experiences in sports.”

Daktronics, according to the investigators, along with now-incarcerated Aspiration cofounder Joe Sanberg and what remains of the company in bankruptcy proceedings, cooperated with the investigation. However, there are two other Clippers-affiliated companies apparently involved in paying Leonard an extra $18 million, including Lockton Insurance, which refused to cooperate, and Boingo Wireless, which should probably add an anti-snitching policy to its terms of service. According to investigators, Boingo “purported initially to cooperate, but then supplied information that was inconsistent or not credible to investigators and ultimately refused to cooperate further.”

Aspiration, which kicked the whole thing off and had advertised itself as “Wall Street greed’s worst nightmare,” turned into just that for investors including Ballmer, as reported sham endorsement deals by cofounder Joe Sanberg were part of a scheme to create fake revenue. He would eventually be sentenced to 14 years in prison for costing investors $248 million.

While the league’s punishment for Ballmer and the Clippers largely ignores the details of Aspiration’s deal and Ballmer’s $50 million investment, the report now includes a note that at the time, Sanberg explained the curious arrangement to other executives differently, emailing an employee to say that “[the Forum is] going to purchase $7mm of reforestation capacity each year from Aspiration to make the ticket experience carbon neutral and potentially carbon negative. To be clear, the $7mm figure per year is set so what’s variable is how they choose to use it.” That figure matched Leonard’s endorsement payments.

Other explanations were even more clear about the connection to Kawhi Leonard:

When these concerns were conveyed to Mr. Sanberg, he told the Aspiration executives that “the Clippers are asking us to do this with Kawhi Leonard” and that the team would provide additional business back to Aspiration to help offset the financial impact on Aspiration. In an email exchange among Aspiration’s CEO, CFO, and general counsel, one wrote, “[Mr. Sanberg said] that the Clippers are promising to increase the amount they pay us per quarter in line with what we pay this guy [i.e., Mr. Leonard].” Another responded: “Thanks for verifying. . . . We should be fine if it’s cashflow neutral.”

One Clippers executive called its stadium deals with Aspiration “super shady” and full of red flags in text messages to the team’s CFO, and the investigation revealed that while Ballmer and Zucker claimed the $7 million annual arrangement was the result of a study done by a team consultant, the consultant disagreed.

No Clippers witness could provide a credible alternative explanation for the initial appearance of the $7 million annual payment from the team to Aspiration in the Forum Agreement. Mr. Ballmer and Ms. Zucker both claimed that it was based on a study done by a team consultant who had determined that the Forum needed $28 million to offset its carbon emissions and that the team would pay Aspiration for these offsets over four years. But investigators spoke directly with this consultant, who said that the Clippers had given him a $28 million budget with which to address the Forum’s emissions—not the other way around.

After untold hours of podcasts (including Torre’s triumphant two-hour live reaction to the report), repeated blanket Clippers denials, and at least one fraud conviction, the investigation still isn’t over. The investigators are looking into a claim that “the consulting agreement one company signed with the Clippers was in fact a ruse, designed and intended to be a vehicle for the team to provide the company with funds to be paid to Mr. Leonard.”

Ballmer’s lawyers say they are “exploring every legal remedy to address this gross injustice,” but if I were on the investigation I’d just want to know which one is a bigger regret — giving up 10 draft picks and the rights to a future two-time MVP in the Shai Gilgeous-Alexander trade or launching Windows Vista?

Tech.title: You can watch the coolant flow inside Ugreen’s liquid-cooled power bank
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Does your power bank have “CryoPulse technology” or a “Cyber Window”? If you disappointingly answered “no” to both, you might want to consider upgrading to Ugreen’s new MagFlow Pro Magnetic Power Bank. It’s available starting today for $149.99, which puts it on the really expensive end of power banks with only a 10,000mAh battery, but those fancy-sounding features are part of what Ugreen is claiming to be the world’s first liquid-cooling system on a power bank with wireless charging.

Inside the MagFlow Pro is a micro-pump that’s used to circulate coolant and draw heat away from components including the power bank’s Qi2.2-compatible wireless charging coil. You can see the coolant flowing through a (cyber) window on the front of the power bank. That system works alongside copper foil and a design that keeps charging components separated to help reduce heat buildup to prolong the life of the power bank’s battery, the life of your phone, and to help maintain up to 25W of power delivery. It should result in leaving the MagFlow Pro cooler to the touch after a long charging session.

The power bank’s lanyard doubles as a built-in USB-C charging cable, while an additional USB-C port can be used to charge a third device. Image: Ugreen

In addition to charging devices wirelessly, the power bank has a built-in USB-C cable lanyard and a USB-C port that can both charge devices at up to 45W, but that’s also the maximum output of the MagFlow Pro, so connecting multiple devices will reduce charging rates.

Tech.title: Congressman says TikTok backed out of a meeting to avoid child safety questions
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

TikTok backed out of a congressional committee’s “public roundtable” set for this month over concerns it would be asked about child safety practices, the chair of the committee said.

After negotiating “in good faith” to bring TikTok’s chief security officer before the House Select Committee on China to answer questions about Chinese government access to Americans’ data and the TikTok algorithm, Chair John Moolenaar (R-MI) said in a statement Thursday that the company reversed course. “Now, TikTok is refusing to appear citing its own desire to avoid broader scrutiny of its child safety practices,” Moolenaar wrote. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

TikTok reneged on its commitment on August 27th, Moolenaar told Bloomberg in an interview — a day after Meta reached its sweeping settlement with state attorneys general and called on TikTok and YouTube to follow suit. All three of those tech platforms still have many pending suits focused on their child safety practices. “They claimed that in light of Meta’s settlement with state attorneys general, they wouldn’t be able to answer questions on child-safety issues,” Moolenaar told Bloomberg, even though he said the meeting was not set to focus on that topic.

“They claimed that in light of Meta’s settlement with state attorneys general, they wouldn’t be able to answer questions on child-safety issues”

Moolenaar said in his statement that the committee would attempt to reschedule. “We will continue to work in good faith to protect the American people and ensure TikTok executives publicly address the Committee’s questions regarding its operations and safeguards – consistent with the requirements of the Protecting Americans From Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act – before the end of the year.”

The law Moolenaar references is the one that briefly banned TikTok from the US, before enforcement was repeatedly delayed by President Donald Trump. Ultimately, a deal to make its US service part of a new entity closed in January, theoretically resolving the security issues the law cited. But lawmakers on the Select Committee had lingering concerns even after that happened. In a statement after the deal closed, Moolenaar said TikTok would need to answer questions about Chinese government influence on the algorithm and US data protection to the committee directly.
